german: From Marder (marten; mustelid) and a play on Guck mal da ("Look over there!")
korean: From 볼 bol (looking) and groundhog
chineseMandarin: From 步哨 bùshào (sentinel) and 鼠 shǔ (rodent)
chineseCantonese: From 步哨 bouhsaau (sentinel) and 鼠 syú (rodent)

name: Lillipup
english: Lillipup may be a combination of lilliputian and pup.
japanese: From Yorkshire Terrier
german: From Yorkshire Terrier and kläffen (to yap)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (little) and 約克夏㹴 / 约克夏㹴 Yuēkèxià Gēng (Yorkshire Terrier)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (little) and 約克夏㹴 Yeukhākhah Gāng (Yorkshire Terrier)

name: Herdier
english: Herdier and Herderrie may be a combination of herding dog and terrier.
japanese: From herding dog and terrier
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From the partial transcription of the Japanese name and 約克夏㹴 / 约克夏㹴 Yuēkèxià Gēng (Yorkshire Terrier)
chineseCantonese: From the partial transcription of the Japanese name and 約克夏㹴 Yeukhākhah Gāng (Yorkshire Terrier)

name: Stoutland
english: Stoutland may be a combination of stout (bulky, in reference to its fat figure) and Newfoundland (breed of large working dog) or Scotland, in reference to it being based on a Scottish terrier.
japanese: From 尨犬 mukuinu (shaggy dog), ムチムチ muchimuchi (plump) and Newfoundland or Scotland
french: From mastiff and touffe (slang term for shaggy hair)
german: From Biss (bite) and bark, and possibly a pun of Bismarck
korean: From 방 (尨) bang (shaggy dog, generally referring to the sapsali breed) or bark and land or Scotland
chineseMandarin: From 長毛狗 / 长毛狗 chángmáo gǒu (shaggy dog)
chineseCantonese: From 長毛狗 chèuhngmòu gáu (shaggy dog)

name: Purrloin
english: Purrloin may be a combination of purr (a sound a cat makes) and purloin (to steal).
japanese: From ちょろまかす choromakasu (to pilfer) and 猫 neko (cat)
german: From the genus Felis and filou (French for "rascal")
korean: From 쌔비다 ssabida (to steal) and 고양이 goyang-i (cat)
chineseMandarin: From 扒手 páshǒu (pickpocket) and 貓 / 猫 māo (cat)
chineseCantonese: From 扒手 pàhsáu (pickpocket) and 貓 māau (cat)

name: Liepard
english: Liepard may be a combination of lie and leopard.
japanese: From leopard and λεόπαρδος leópardos (Ancient Greek for "leopard") or leopardus (Latin for "leopard")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 酷 kù (ruthless) and 豹 bào (leopard)
chineseCantonese: From 酷 huhk (ruthless) and 豹 paau (leopard)

name: Pansage
english: Pansage may be a combination of Pan (the genus of chimpanzees) and sage (an herb). Sage can also refer to a wise person, relating to the "three wise monkeys" motif of the elemental monkeys.
japanese: From 柳 yanagi (willow), 野菜 yasai (vegetable), 菜 na (greens), and ape
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 花 huā (flower), 花椰菜 huāyécài (cauliflower), and 猴 hóu (monkey)
chineseCantonese: From 花 fā (flower), 椰菜花 yèhchoifā (cauliflower), and 猴 hàuh (monkey)

name: Simisage
english: Simisage may be a combination of simian and sage (an herb). Sage can also refer to a wise person, relating to the "three wise monkeys" motif of the elemental monkeys.
japanese: From 柳 yanagi (willow), 野菜 yasai (vegetable), 菜 na (greens), and monkey
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 花 huā (flower), 花椰菜 huāyécài (cauliflower), and 猿 yuán (ape)
chineseCantonese: From 花 fā (flower), 椰菜花 yèhchoifā (cauliflower), and 猿 yùhn (ape)

name: Pansear
english: Pansear may be a combination of Pan (the genus of chimpanzees), sear, ear or seer (relating to the "three wise monkeys" motif), and pan searing.
japanese: From 爆 bào (Chinese for to burst; to explode), burst, and ape
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 爆香 bàoxiāng (Tempering (spices)) and 猴 hóu (monkey)
chineseCantonese: From 爆香 baauhēung (Tempering (spices)) and 猴 hàuh (monkey)

name: Simisear
english: Simisear may be a combination of simian, sear, and ear (relating to the "three wise monkeys" motif).
japanese: From 爆 bào (Chinese for to burst; to explode), burst, and monkey
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 爆香 bàoxiāng (Tempering (spices)) and 猿 yuán (ape)
chineseCantonese: From 爆香 baauhēung (Tempering (spices)) and 猿 yùhn (ape)

name: Panpour
english: Panpour may be a combination of Pan (the genus of chimpanzees) and pour.
japanese: From 冷や hiya (cool water) and ape
korean: From 앗 차가워 at chagaweo (Oh, it is cold!) and ape
chineseMandarin: From 冷水 lěngshuǐ (cold water) and 猴 hóu (monkey)
chineseCantonese: From 冷水 láahngséui (cold water) and 猴 hàuh (monkey)

name: Simipour
english: Simipour may be a combination of simian and pour.
japanese: From 冷や hiya (cool water) and monkey
french: From flotte (slang term for water or rain) and orang-outan (orangutan)
korean: From 앗 차가워 at chagaweo (Oh, it is cold!) and monkey
chineseMandarin: From 冷水 lěngshuǐ (cold water) and 猿 yuán (ape)
chineseCantonese: From 冷水 láahngséui (cold water) and 猿 yùhn (ape)

name: Munna
english: Munna may be a combination of 夢 mu (dream) and अन्न॑ ánna (Sanskrit for "food"). It may also involve luna (Latin for "moon"), manna (edible substance described in the Bible and the Quran), mana (spiritual force in Oceanic cultures), 花 hana (flower), and むにゃむにゃ munya munya (onomatopoeia for talking in one's sleep or talking with food in one's mouth).
japanese: From 夢 mu (dream), अन्न॑ ánna (Sanskrit for "food"), and possibly manna, mana, 花 hana (flower), and むにゃむにゃ munya munya (onomatopoeia for talking in one's sleep or talking with food in one's mouth)
german: From somnium (Latin for "dream") and mjam (yum) or njam (yum)
korean: From 몽 (夢) mong (dream) and अन्न॑ ánna (Sanskrit for "food")
chineseMandarin: From 食 shí (to eat) and 夢 / 梦 mèng (dream) reduplicated
chineseCantonese: From 食 sihk (to eat) and 夢 muhng (dream) reduplicated

name: Musharna
english: Musharna may be a combination of 夢 mu (dream), ムシャムシャ mushamusha (onomatopoeia for devouring), and प्रा॒ण prāṇá (Sanskrit for "breath" and "vitality") or अन्नपूर्णा Annapūrṇā (manifestation of Hindu goddess Parvati as the goddess of food and feeding). It may also involve luna (Latin for "moon"), manna (edible substance described in the Bible and the Quran), mana (spiritual force in Oceanic cultures), and 花 hana (flower)
japanese: From 夢 mu (dream), ムシャムシャ mushamusha (onomatopoeia for devouring), and प्रा॒ण prāṇá (Sanskrit for "breath" and "vitality") or अन्नपूर्णा Annapūrṇā
german: From somnium (Latin for "dream") and Latin suffix -vora (indicates an adjective that "feeds on something", analogous to English -vorous)
korean: From 몽 (夢) mong (dream), 얌얌 yam-yam (yum-yum), and प्रा॒ण prāṇá (Sanskrit for "breath" and "vitality") or अन्नपूर्णा Annapūrṇā
chineseMandarin: From 夢 / 梦 mèng (dream) and 蝕 / 蚀 shí (to nibble away at)
chineseCantonese: From 夢 muhng (dream) and 蝕 sihk (to nibble away at)

name: Pidove
english: Pidove may be a combination of pigeon and dove or love (referencing the heart motif).
japanese: From 忠実 mame (diligent) or 豆 mame (prefix meaning tiny; bean) and 鳩 hato (pigeon)
german: From dusselig (clumsy, lightheaded) and gurren (to coo)
korean: From 콩 kong (bean) and 비둘기 bidulgi (pigeon)
chineseMandarin: From 豆 dòu (bean) and 鴿 / 鸽 gē (pigeon, dove)
chineseCantonese: From 豆 dauh (bean) and 鴿 gap (pigeon, dove)

name: Tranquill
english: Tranquill may be a combination of tranquil (calm or unstressed) and quill (a feather from the tail of a bird).
japanese: From 鳩 hato (pigeon), 坊 bō (boy, monk), and possibly イーハトーヴォ Ihatovo (fictional ideal world in some works of Kenji Miyazawa)
korean: From U-turn, utopia and dove
chineseMandarin: From 咕咕 gūgū (onomatopoeia of a bird's coo) and 鴿 / 鸽 gē (pigeon, dove); Possibly from Japanese 波 ha, 波波 Bōbō (Pidgey), and 鴿 / 鸽 gē (pigeon, dove)
chineseCantonese: From 咕咕 gūgū (onomatopoeia of a bird's coo) and 鴿 gap (pigeon, dove); Possibly from Japanese 波 ha, 波波 Bōbō (Pidgey), and 鴿 gap (pigeon, dove)

name: Unfezant
english: Unfezant may be a combination of corruptions of unpleasant and pheasant. It may also involve unfazed.
japanese: From ケンホロロ kenhororo (onomatopoeia of pheasant cries) and けんもほろろ ken-mo-hororo (curt, brusque)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 高傲 gāo'ào (haughty) and 雉雞 / 雉鸡 zhìjī (pheasant); From 轟隆 / 轰隆 hōnglóng (sound of rumbling) and 雉雞 / 雉鸡 zhìjī (pheasant)
chineseCantonese: From 高傲 gōu'ngouh (haughty) and 雉雞 jihgāi (pheasant); From 轟隆 gwàhnglùhng (sound of rumbling) and 雉雞 jihgāi (pheasant)

name: Blitzle
english: Blitzle may be a combination of Blitz (German for "lightning") and little.
japanese: From 縞馬 shimauma (zebra)
french: From zébron (young zebra) and biberon (baby bottle)
korean: From 줄무늬 julmunui (stripe) and 마 (馬) ma (horse)
chineseMandarin: From 斑馬 / 斑马 bānmǎ (zebra)
chineseCantonese: From 斑馬 bāanmáh (zebra)

name: Zebstrika
english: Zebstrika may be a combination of zebra and lightning strike.
japanese: From zebra and 雷火 raika (flash of lightning)
german: From Zebra and Blitz (lightning) or britzel (onomatopoeia for crackling lightning)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 雷電 / 雷电 léidiàn (thunder and lightning) and 斑馬 / 斑马 bānmǎ (zebra)
chineseCantonese: From 雷電 lèuihdihn (thunder and lightning) and 斑馬 bāanmáh (zebra)

name: Roggenrola
english: Roggenrola may be derived from rock and rock and roll or rock-and-roller.
japanese: From 団子 dango and ゴロゴロ goro goro (onomatopoeia for the sound of a boulder rolling).
french: From nodule and -lithe (Greek suffix meaning stone)
korean: From 경단 gyeongdan, 데굴데굴 deguldegul (sound of rolling), and possibly 굴 (窟) gul (cave)
chineseMandarin: From 石 shí (stone) and 丸子 wánzi (ball)
chineseCantonese: From 石 sehk (stone) and 丸子 yúnjí (ball)

name: Boldore
english: Boldore may be combination of boulder, bold (outstanding or large), and ore.
japanese: From 岩 gan (rock) and mantle
french: From géode (geode) or géo- (geo- (prefix for Earth)) and -lithe (Greek suffix meaning stone)
german: From Sediment, Mantel (mantle), and Urgestein (bedrock, primitive rock)
korean: From 암 (岩) am (rock) and mantle
chineseMandarin: From 地幔 dìmàn (mantle) and 岩 yán (boulder)
chineseCantonese: From 地幔 deihmaahn (mantle) and 岩 ngàahm (boulder)

name: Gigalith
english: Gigalith may be a combination of γίγας gigas (Greek for "giant") and λίθος lithos (Greek for "stone"). It may also refer to megalith or monolith.
japanese: From γίγας gigas (Greek for "giant"), Gaia, Goliath, and earth
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 龐 / 庞 páng (enormous), 岩 yán (boulder), and 怪 guài (monster)
chineseCantonese: From 龐 pòhng (enormous), 岩 ngàahm (boulder), and 怪 gwaai (monster)

name: Woobat
english: Woobat may be a combination of woo and bat. It may also involve wool from its woolly appearance.
japanese: From 心 kokoro (heart) or コロコロ korokoro (onomatopoeia for lightly rolling) and 蝙蝠 kōmori (bat)
korean: From 또르르 ttoreureu (round and round) and 박쥐 bakjwi (bat)
chineseMandarin: From 滾滾 / 滚滚 gǔngǔn (to roll on) and 蝙蝠 biānfú (bat)
chineseCantonese: From 滾滾 gwángwán (to roll on) and 蝙蝠 pīnfūk (bat)

name: Swoobat
english: Swoobat may be a combination of swoon or swoop and bat. Its English name containing the English name of its pre-evolved form (Woobat) mirrors how its Japanese name (Kokoromori) contains the Japanese name of its pre-evolved form (Koromori).
japanese: From 心 kokoro (heart) and 蝙蝠 kōmori (bat)
german: From Fledermaus (bat) and ti amo (Italian for "I love you")
korean: From 마음 maeum (heart) and 박쥐 bakjwi (bat)
chineseMandarin: From 心 xīn (heart) and 蝙蝠 biānfú (bat)
chineseCantonese: From 心 sām (heart) and 蝙蝠 pīnfūk (bat)

name: Drilbur
english: Drilbur may be a combination of drill and burrow or burr.
japanese: From 土竜 mogura (mole) and screw
french: From rotation or rotor, taupe (mole), and possibly a pun on rototo (baby burp)
korean: From 두더지 dudeoji (mole) and screw
chineseMandarin: From 螺釘 / 螺钉 luódīng (screw), 地 dì (ground), and 地鼠 dìshǔ (mole)
chineseCantonese: From 螺釘 lòhdēng (screw), 地 deih (ground), and 地鼠 deihsyú (mole)

name: Excadrill
english: Excadrill may be a combination of excavate and drill.
japanese: From drill, 土竜 doryū (mole), 渦 uzu (spiral or swirl), and 竜頭 ryūzu (things in the shape of a dragon's head)
korean: From mole, drill, and screw
chineseMandarin: From 龍頭 / 龙头 lóngtóu (dragon head; leader), 地 dì (ground), and 地鼠 dìshǔ (mole)
chineseCantonese: From 龍頭 lùhngtàu (dragon head; leader), 地 deih (ground), and 地鼠 deihsyú (mole)

name: Audino
english: Audino may be derived from audio and a pun on the phrase "I dunno."
japanese: From a pun of 多分ね tabun ne (maybe) or 多聞 tabun (hearing many things) and possibly 耳朶 mimitabu (earlobe)
french: From ouïe (hearing) and a pun of non mais oui
german: From Ohr (ear), Doktor (doctor), and a pun of oh, doch
korean: From a pun of 다분히 dabunhi (quite)
chineseMandarin: From 差不多 chàbùduō (almost; more or less) and 娃娃 wáwa (doll)
chineseCantonese: From 差不多 chābātdō (almost; more or less) and 娃娃 wāwā (doll)

name: Timburr
english: Timburr is a corruption of timber and may also derive from burly.
japanese: From どっこらしょ dokkorasho (heave-ho) and possibly Δοκάρι dokári (Greek for "beam")
korean: From 으라차 euracha (heave-ho)
chineseMandarin: From 搬運 / 搬运 bānyùn (transport), 小 xiǎo (small), and 匠 jiàng (craftsman)
chineseCantonese: From 搬運 būnwahn (transport), 小 síu (small), and 匠 jeuhng (craftsman)

name: Gurdurr
english: Gurdurr may be derived from girder (support beam).
japanese: From 土木 doboku (engineering works) and 鉄骨 tekkotsu (steel frame)
korean: From 토목 (土木) tomok (engineering works), 쇠 soe (steel), and 골 (骨) gol (frame, bone)
chineseMandarin: From the Japanese 鉄骨 tekkotsu (steel frame), 土木 tǔmù (engineering works), and possibly 工人 gōngrén (worker)
chineseCantonese: From the Japanese 鉄骨 tekkotsu (steel frame), 土木 tóumuhk (engineering works), and possibly 工人 gūngyàhn (worker)

name: Conkeldurr
english: Conkeldurr may be a combination of concrete and elder. It may also involve conk, having meaning as both an especially large nose and to hit someone on the head.
japanese: From 老 rō (old) and 武神 bushin (warlord) or 普請 fushin (construction work)
korean: From 노 (老) no (old) and the hanja reading of the Japanese 普請 fushin (construction work)
chineseMandarin: From 修建 xiūjiàn (to construct), 老 lǎo (old), and 匠 jiàng (craftsman); From 修繕 / 修缮 xiūshàn (to repair or renovate) and 老頭 / 老头 lǎotóu (old man)
chineseCantonese: From 修建 sāugin (to construct), 老 lóuh (old), and 匠 jeuhng (craftsman); From 修繕 sāusihn (to repair or renovate) and 老頭 lóuhtàuh (old man)

name: Tympole
english: Tympole may be a combination of timpani or tympanum (both being types of drums), or tympanic membrane (eardrum; referring to the bumps on each side of its head), and tadpole.
japanese: From お玉杓子 otamajakushi (tadpole or musical notes) and 麿 maro (affectionate suffix for young men) or 麻呂眉 maro-mayu (shaved eyebrows)
korean: From 동글다 donggeulda (round) or 동 (童) dong (child) and 올챙이 olchaeng-i (tadpole)
chineseMandarin: From 圓 / 圆 yuán (round) and 蝌蚪 kēdǒu (tadpole)
chineseCantonese: From 圓 yùhn (round) and 蝌蚪 fōdáu (tadpole)

name: Palpitoad
english: Palpitoad may be a combination of palpitation (pulsation) and toad.
japanese: From 蝦蟇 gamagaeru (Japanese common toad)
korean: From 두꺼비 dukkeobi (toad)
chineseMandarin: From 藍 / 蓝 lán (blue) and 蟾蜍 chánchú (toad)
chineseCantonese: From 藍 làahm (blue) and 蟾蜍 sìhmsyùh (toad)

name: Seismitoad
english: Seismitoad may be a combination of seismic and toad.
japanese: From 蟇 gama (toad) and ゲロゲロ gerogero (onomatopoeia for croaking)
korean: From 두꺼비 dukkeobi (toad), big, and 개굴개굴 gaegul-gaegul (onomatopoeia for croaking)
chineseMandarin: From 蟾蜍 chánchú (toad) and 王 wáng (king)
chineseCantonese: From 蟾蜍 sìhmsyùh (toad) and 王 wòhng (king)

name: Throh
english: Throh may be derived from throw.
japanese: From 投げる nageru (to throw), 撃 geki (strike), and 鬼 ki (demon)
french: From judoka and crac (crack) or crack (slang term for a champion)
korean: From 던짐 deonjim (throwing) and suffix -이 i (-er)
chineseMandarin: From 投 tóu (to throw), 摔 shuāi (to throw down), and 鬼 guǐ (demon); From 投射 tóushè (to fling) and 鬼 guǐ (demon)
chineseCantonese: From 投 tàuh (to throw), 摔 sēut (to throw down), and 鬼 gwái (demon); From 投射 tàuhseh (to fling) and 鬼 gwái (demon)

name: Sawk
english: Sawk may be derived from sock (to punch).
japanese: From 打撃 dageki (blow, strike) and 鬼 ki (demon)
french: From karaté (karate) and raclée (slang term for a beating)
korean: From 타격 (打擊) tagyeok (blow, strike) and 귀 (鬼) gwi (demon)
chineseMandarin: From 打擊 / 打击 dǎjí / dǎjī (blow, strike), and 鬼 guǐ (demon)
chineseCantonese: From 打擊 dágīk (blow, strike) and 鬼 gwái (demon)

name: Sewaddle
english: Sewaddle may be a combination of sew and waddle (referring to how a baby walks) or swaddle (to wrap a baby in cloth).
japanese: From お包み okurumi (swaddle)
korean: From 두르다 dureuda (to wrap around, to wear) and 보 (褓) bo (swaddling cloth)
chineseMandarin: From 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug), 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby) and 包 bāo (to wrap)
chineseCantonese: From 蟲 chùhng (bug), 寶寶 bóubóu (baby) and 包 bāau (to wrap)

name: Swadloon
english: Swadloon may be a combination of swaddle (to wrap a baby in cloth) and cocoon.
japanese: From 包まる kurumaru (to be wrapped) or 繭 mayu (cocoon)
korean: From 두르다 dureuda (to wrap around, to wear) and cocoon
chineseMandarin: From 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby), 包 bāo (to wrap), and 繭 / 茧 jiǎn (cocoon)
chineseCantonese: From 寶寶 bóubóu (baby), 包 bāau (to wrap), and 繭 gáan (cocoon)

name: Leavanny
english: Leavanny is a combination of leaves and nanny. It may also derive from Levana, the ancient Roman goddess of newborn babies.
japanese: From 葉 ha (leaf), 母 haha (mother), and 子守 komori (babysitting)
korean: From 모 (母) mo (mother), 兒 a (child, children), 어머니 eomeoni (mother), and possibly armor
chineseMandarin: From 保母 / 保姆 bǎomǔ (nanny) and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug)
chineseCantonese: From 保母 bóumóuh (nanny) and 蟲 chùhng (bug)

name: Venipede
english: Venipede may be a combination of venom and centipede or millipede.
japanese: From 節 fushi (joint, segment) and 百足 mukade (centipede)
korean: From 마디 madi (joint) and 지네 jine (centipede)
chineseMandarin: From 百足 bǎizú (centipede; literally 'hundred foot') and 蜈蚣 wúgōng (centipede)
chineseCantonese: From 百足 baakjūk (centipede; literally 'hundred foot') and 蜈蚣 ngh-gūng (centipede)

name: Whirlipede
english: Whirlipede may be a combination of whirl and centipede or millipede.
japanese: From wheel and 毬 iga (sphere)
french: From scolopendre (centipede) and bolide (fast racing car)
korean: From wheel and 구 (毬) gu (sphere)
chineseMandarin: From 車輪 / 车轮 chēlún (car wheel) and 毬 / 球 qiú (ball, sphere)
chineseCantonese: From 車輪 chēlèuhn (car wheel) and 毬 kàuh (ball, sphere)

name: Scolipede
english: Scolipede may be a combination of Scolopendra (genus of centipedes) and centipede or millipede.
japanese: From Scolopendra
german: From κέρας kéras (Greek for "horn") and Scolopendra
korean: From Scolopendra
chineseMandarin: From 蜈蚣 wúgōng (centipede) and 王 wáng (king)
chineseCantonese: From 蜈蚣 nghgūng (centipede) and 王 wòhng (king)

name: Cottonee
english: Cottonee may be derived from cotton, cottony, cottonweed, and possibly wee (small).
japanese: From 木綿 momen (cotton)
french: From doudou (child talk for something soft and reassuring) and duvet (down feathers)
korean: From 소 (小) so (small) and 면 (綿) myeon (cotton)
chineseMandarin: From 木棉 mùmián (tree cotton) and 棉球 miánqiú (cotton ball)
chineseCantonese: From 木棉 muhkmìhn (tree cotton) and 棉球 mìhnkàuh (cotton ball)

name: Whimsicott
english: Whimsicott may be a combination of whimsical and cotton.
japanese: From elf and 風 fū (wind) or typhoon
german: From Elfe (elf) and Taifun (typhoon); also similar to the Japanese name
korean: From elf and 풍 (風) pung (wind)
chineseMandarin: From 風 / 风 fēng (wind) and 妖精 yāojing (elf, fairy, pixie)
chineseCantonese: From 風 fūng (wind) and 妖精 yíujīng (elf, fairy, pixie)

name: Petilil
english: Petilil may be a combination of petal, petite, petunia, or petiole, and lily or li'l (little).
japanese: From チューリップ chūrippu (tulip), 百合根 yurine (lily bulb), and 根 ne (root)
korean: From 치 (稚) chi (young) and lily
chineseMandarin: From 百合 bǎihé (lily), 根 gēn (root), and 娃娃 wáwá (doll, baby)
chineseCantonese: From 百合 baakhahp (lily), 根 gān (root), and 娃娃 wāwā (doll, baby)

name: Lilligant
english: Lilligant may be a combination of lily and elegant.
japanese: From dress, dear, lady, and Dianthus
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 裙 qún (skirt; dress), 兒 ér (child), and 小姐 xiǎojiě (young lady)
chineseCantonese: From 裙 kwàhn (skirt; dress), 兒 yìh (child), and 小姐 síujé (young lady)

name: Basculin
english: Basculin may be a combination of bass and masculine.
japanese: From bass and 丈夫 masurao (warrior, referring to its bold, violent nature) or bacalhau
french: From bar (bass) and Gargantua, a powerful giant in French literature
korean: From bass and 사나이 sana-i (man, hombre, bro (informal))
chineseMandarin: From 野蠻 yěmán (savage) and 鱸魚 lúyú (bass); From 勇士 yǒngshì (warrior) and 鱸魚 lúyú (bass)
chineseCantonese: From 野蠻 yéhmàahn (savage) and 鱸魚 lòuhyùh (bass); From 勇士 yúhngsih (warrior) and 鱸魚 lòuhyùh (bass)

name: Sandile
english: Sandile may be a combination of sand, crocodile, and possibly a play on sandal (footwear).
japanese: From 目黒 meguro (black-eyed) and crocodile
korean: From 깜깜 kkamkkam (pitch-black, very dark), 눈 nun (eye), and crocodile
chineseMandarin: From 黑眼 hēiyǎn (black-eyed) and 鱷魚 / 鳄魚 èyú (crocodile, alligator)
chineseCantonese: From 黑眼 hākngáahn (black-eyed) and 鱷魚 ngohkyùh (crocodile, alligator)

name: Krokorok
english: Krokorok may be a combination of crocodile, rock, and crook.
japanese: From 悪い warui (bad/evil/sinful), crocodile, and possibly びる biru (seems like...) and gavial
german: From Rocker or rock and Kaiman
korean: From 악어 (鰐魚) ageo (crocodile), 악 (惡) ak (evil), evil, and villain
chineseMandarin: From 混混 hùnhùn (slang term for rascal) and 鱷魚 / 鳄魚 èyú (crocodile, alligator)
chineseCantonese: From 混混 wahnwahn (slang term for rascal) and 鱷魚 ngohkyùh (crocodile, alligator)

name: Krookodile
english: Krookodile may be a combination of corruptions of crook and crocodile.
japanese: From 悪い warui (bad/evil/sinful), and gavial
korean: From 악어 (鰐魚) ageo (crocodile) or 악 (惡) ak (evil) and gavial
chineseMandarin: From 流氓 liúmáng (rogue) and 鱷魚 / 鳄魚 èyú (crocodile, alligator)
chineseCantonese: From 流氓 làuhmàhn (rogue) and 鱷魚 ngohkyùh (crocodile, alligator)

name: Darumaka
english: Darumaka and Darumakka seem to be a combination of Daruma and 真赤 makka (crimson) or a corruption of macaque.
japanese: From Daruma and 真赤 makka (crimson) or a corruption of macaque
french: From Daruma, rond (round) and possibly from marron
korean: From Daruma and 화 (火) hwa (fire)
chineseMandarin: From 火 huǒ (fire), 紅 / 红 hóng (red), 火紅 huǒhóng (blazing), and 不倒翁 bùdǎowēng (tumbler, roly-poly toy)
chineseCantonese: From 火 fó (fire), 紅 hùhng (red), 火紅 fóhùhng (blazing), and 不倒翁 bātdóuyūng (tumbler, roly-poly toy)

name: Darmanitan
english: Darmanitan may be a combination of Dharma (alternate spelling of daruma) and orangutan.
japanese: From 火 hi (fire), 緋 hi (scarlet), 狒々 hihi (baboon), Daruma, and 火達磨 hidaruma (the state of being on fire)
german: From Flamme (flame), Lampion (paper lantern), and Pavian (baboon)
korean: From 불 bul (fire), 비비 (狒狒) bibi (baboon), 비 (緋) bi (scarlet), and Daruma
chineseMandarin: From 達摩 / 达摩 Dámó (Daruma doll) and 狒狒 fèifèi (baboon)
chineseCantonese: From 達摩 Daahtmō (Daruma doll) and 狒狒 fātfāt (baboon)

name: Maractus
english: Maractus may be a combination of maraca and cactus.
japanese: From maraca, cactus and mariachi
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 沙鈴 / 沙铃 shālíng (maracas) and 仙人掌 xiānrénzhǎng (cactus); From 墨西哥街頭樂隊 / 墨西哥街头乐队 Mòxīgē-jiētóuyuèduì (mariachi) and 沙鈴 / 沙铃 shālíng (maracas)
chineseCantonese: From 沙鈴 sālìhng (maracas) and 仙人掌 sīnyàhnjéung (cactus); From 墨西哥街頭樂隊 Mahksāigō-gāaitàuhngohkdéui (mariachi) and 沙鈴 sālìhng (maracas)

name: Dwebble
english: Dwebble may be a combination of dwell or dwelling and pebble.
japanese: From 石 ishi (stone) and 住まい sumai (dwelling)
french: From crabe (crab), bicoque (slang term for a "small house" or "shack"), and coque (shell)
german: From the prefix litho- (relating to "stone") and Eremit (hermit)
korean: From 돌 dol (stone) and the suffix ～살이 -sari (equivalent to English "-living")
chineseMandarin: From 石 shí (stone) and 寄居蟹 jìjūxiè (hermit crab)
chineseCantonese: From 石 sehk (stone) and 寄居蟹 geigēuiháaih (hermit crab)

name: Crustle
english: Crustle may be a combination of crust, crustacean, crab, and castle.
japanese: From 岩 iwa (rock) and palace
german: From castellum (Latin for "castle") and suffix -lith (relating to "stone")
korean: From 암 (巖) am (boulder, rock) and palace
chineseMandarin: From 岩 yán (boulder, rock), 宮殿 / 宫殿 gōngdiàn (palace), and 寄居蟹 jìjūxiè (hermit crab)
chineseCantonese: From 岩 ngàahm (boulder, rock), 宮殿 gūngdihn (palace), and 寄居蟹 geigēuiháaih (hermit crab)

name: Scraggy
english: Scraggy may be derived from scraggy (scrawny) or scraggly. It may also involve scrappy (feisty), saggy, and baggy.
japanese: From 狡 zuru (sly fellow), 狡い zurui (crafty), ずるずる zuruzuru (onomatopoeia for dragging slowly), and sag
french: From baggy (baggy; loose-fitting trouser) and iguane (iguana)
german: From zurren (to drag), Rock (skirt), and Exuvie (molt) or Echse (lizard)
korean: From 곤죽 gonjuk (mess) and 헐렁이 바지 heolleong-i baji (loose pants)
chineseMandarin: From 滑 huá (cunning; to slide) and 小子 xiǎozi (boy, brat); From 滑頭 / 滑头 huátóu (crafty) and 小子 xiǎozi (boy, brat)
chineseCantonese: From 滑 waaht (cunning; to slide) and 小子 síují (boy, brat); From 滑頭 waahttáu (crafty ) and 小子 síují (boy, brat)

name: Scrafty
english: Scrafty may be a combination of scrappy (feisty), scruffy, or scraggy (scrawny), and crafty (being skilled at deceit to achieve one's goals).
japanese: From 狡 zuru (sly fellow), 狡い zurui (crafty), ずるずる zuruzuru (onomatopoeia for dragging slowly), 頭巾 zukin (hood), and possibly skin
french: From baggy and caïd (colloquial term for boss)
german: From Irokese (Mohawk) and Exuvie (molt) or Echse (lizard)
korean: From 두건 (頭巾) dugeon (hood), 건달 (乾達) geondal (hoodlum), and possibly dragon
chineseMandarin: From 頭巾 / 头巾 tóujīn (hood) and 混混 hùnhùn (rascal)
chineseCantonese: From 頭巾 tàuhgān (hood) and 混混 wahnwahn (rascal)

name: Sigilyph
english: Sigilyph may be a combination of sigil and glyph. It may also come from sylph, a mythological spirit of the air.
japanese: From symbol and bora or Ra
french: From cryptogramme (cryptogram) and πτερόν pterón (Greek for "wing")
german: From Symbol and volare (Latin for "to fly")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 象徵 / 象征 xiàngzhēng (symbol) and 鳥 / 鸟 niǎo (bird)
chineseCantonese: From 象徵 jeuhngjīng (symbol) and 鳥 níuh (bird)

name: Yamask
english: Yamask may be a combination of 闇 yami (darkness), や ya (bad), or Yama (lord of the dead in Hindu and Buddhist mythology), and mask.
japanese: From death mask
french: From Tutankhamun and fée (fairy), as well as pun of tout à fait
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 哭 kū (to cry) and 面具 miànjù (mask)
chineseCantonese: From 哭 hūk (to cry) and 面具 mihngeuih (mask)

name: Cofagrigus
english: Cofagrigus may be a combination of coffin and sarcophagus. It may also come from grim, grief, or egregious.
japanese: From death, 棺 kan (coffin) and a pun on です か desu ka ("Is it?")
french: From Tutankhamun and fer (iron). Also a pun on tant qu'à faire ("while we're at it")
german: From Echnaton (Akhenaten) and a pun with Echt? Na toll! ("Really? Great!" (ironic), "Shoot!")
korean: Corruption of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 死神 sǐshén (death god, Grim Reaper) and 棺 guān (coffin); From the transcription of Japanese name, 失 shī (lost) and 棺 guān (coffin)
chineseCantonese: From 死神 Séisàhn (death god, Grim Reaper) and 棺 gūn (coffin)

name: Tirtouga
english: Tirtouga may be a combination of turtle and a corruption of tortuga (Spanish for "turtle" or "tortoise").
japanese: From Protostega and tortuga (Spanish for "turtle")
french: From carapace and tortue des Galápagos (Galápagos tortoise)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 原蓋龜 / 原盖龟 Yuángàiguī (Protostega) and 海龜 / 海龟 hǎiguī (sea turtle)
chineseCantonese: From 原蓋龜 Yùhngoigwāi (Protostega) and 海龜 hóigwāi (sea turtle)

name: Carracosta
english: Carracosta may be a combination of carapace (exoskeleton or shell of certain animal groups, such as turtles) and costa (Latin for "rib"). It may also involve costa (Spanish and Portuguese for "coast") and accost (in the sense of assault), as well as allude to the Carrara fossil formation, which contains numerous trilobite fossils.
japanese: From 肋骨 abarabone (rib), 甲羅 kōra (shell), and possibly 暴れる abareru (to thrash or act violently)
french: From méga- (mega-) and tortue des Galápagos (Galápagos tortoise)
german: From Carapax (carapace), Rippe (rib), and possibly Karibik (Caribbean)
korean: From 늑골 (肋骨) neukgol (rib) and partial transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 肋骨 lèigǔ (ribs) and 海龜 / 海龟 hǎiguī (sea turtle)
chineseCantonese: From 肋骨 lahkgwāt (ribs) and 海龜 hóigwāi (sea turtle)

name: Archen
english: Archen may be derived from Archaeopteryx and/or the geological eon Archean.
japanese: From Archaeopteryx and Archean
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 始祖鳥 / 始祖鸟 Shǐzǔniǎo (Archaeopteryx) and 小 xiǎo (small, young)
chineseCantonese: From 始祖鳥 Chíjóuníuh (Archaeopteryx) and 小 síu (small, young)

name: Archeops
english: Archeops and Archeos may be derived from Archaeopteryx and -ops (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "face"). Archeops may also allude to Cheops, the Greek name for Egyptian pharaoh Khufu.
japanese: From Archaeopteryx
french: From aéro- (Greek-derived prefix for "air") and Archaeopteryx
german: From aero- (Greek-derived prefix for "air") and Archaeopteryx
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 始祖鳥 / 始祖鸟 Shǐzǔniǎo (Archaeopteryx) and 大 dà (big)
chineseCantonese: From 始祖鳥 Chíjóuníuh (Archaeopteryx) and 大 daaih (big)

name: Trubbish
english: Trubbish may be a combination of trash and rubbish.
japanese: From 破く yabuku (to tear) or 破ける yabukeru (to get torn), ぶくぶく bukubuku (loose-fitting), and 袋 fukuro (bag)
french: From miam miam (yummy yummy) and miasme (miasma)
korean: From 깨다 kkaeda (to break), 봉지 (封紙) bongji (bag), and the diminutive suffix -이 -i
chineseMandarin: From 破 pò (broken) and 袋 dài (bag)
chineseCantonese: From 破 po (broken) and 袋 doih (bag)

name: Garbodor
english: Garbodor may be a combination of garbage and odor. It could also be a reference to a garburator.
japanese: From dust, 出す dasu (to take out), and ゴミ出し gomidashi (taking out the trash).
german: From Deponie (landfill, dumping ground) and Toxin
korean: From dust and 나오다 naoda (to come out)
chineseMandarin: From 灰塵 / 灰尘 huīchén (dust) and 山 shān (mountain)
chineseCantonese: From 灰塵 fūichàhn (dust) and 山 sāan (mountain)

name: Zorua
english: Zorua may be a combination of zorro (Spanish for "fox") and rua (Irish for "red", possibly referring to its red fur; madra rua is Irish for "fox").
japanese: From zorro (Spanish for "fox") and rua (Irish for "red")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Zoroark
english: Zoroark may be a combination of zorro (Spanish for "fox"), roar, and dark, 悪 aku (evil), or arch- (prefix for "top" or "chief").
japanese: From zorro (fox in Spanish), roar, and dark, 悪 aku (evil), or arch-
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Minccino
english: Minccino may be a combination of mini (referring to its miniature size), mink (an animal known for its fur and its use in women's clothing), or mint (pristine condition), and chinchilla or chino cloth. The suffix -ino or -cino is also a diminutive to denote something small.
japanese: From chinchilla and charming
german: From piccolo (Italian for "small") or picobello (German colloquial for flawless) and Chinchilla
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 泡沫 pàomò (bubbles, foam) and 栗鼠 lìshǔ (chinchilla)
chineseCantonese: From 泡沫 póuhmut (bubbles, foam) and 栗鼠 leuhtsyú (chinchilla)

name: Cinccino
english: Cinccino and Chillaccino may be a combination of chinchilla and chino cloth. The suffix -ino or -cino is also a diminutive to denote something small.
japanese: From chinchilla and chino cloth
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From the partial transcription of the Japanese or possibly 卡布奇諾 / 卡布奇诺 Kǎbùqínuò (Cappuccino) and 栗鼠 lìshǔ (chinchilla)
chineseCantonese: From the partial transcription of the Japanese or possibly 卡布奇諾 Kāboukèihnohk (Cappuccino) and 栗鼠 leuhtsyú (chinchilla)

name: Gothita
english: Gothita may be derived from gothic and the Spanish feminine diminutive suffix -ita. It may also be a contraction of Gothic Lolita.
japanese: From Gothic and むちむち muchimuchi (chubby) or 予知夢 yochimu (precognitive dream)
french: From scruter (examine) and stella (Italian for "star") or -ella (Italian feminine diminutive suffix)
korean: From Gothic and 탱탱 taengtaeng (swollen)
chineseMandarin: From 哥德 Gēdé (Goth) and 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 哥德 Gōdāk (Goth) and 寶寶 bóubóu (baby)

name: Gothorita
english: Gothorita may be a combination of goth and señorita ("young woman" or the title "Miss" in Spanish), or a corruption of Gothic Lolita.
japanese: From gothic and 見る miru (to observe)
french: From mesmériser (mesmerize) and stella (Italian for "star") or -ella (Italian feminine diminutive suffix)
korean: From Gothic and 보다 boda (to see)
chineseMandarin: From 哥德 Gēdé (Goth) and 小童 xiǎotóng (child)
chineseCantonese: From 哥德 Gōdāk (Goth) and 小童 síutùhng (child)

name: Gothitelle
english: Gothitelle and Gothiruselle may be combinations of Gothic (referring to either Gothic art or the Goth subculture) and mademoiselle (Miss, French courtesy title for a young woman). Gothitelle may also involve stellar and foretell.
japanese: From Gothic and mademoiselle
french: From sidéral (sidereal, of the stars), sidérer (to dumbfound), and the Italian feminine diminutive suffix -ella
german: From morbid, Orbit, and Komtesse (countess) or the French feminine suffix -esse
korean: From Gothic and mademoiselle
chineseMandarin: From 哥德 Gēdé (Goth) and 小姐 xiǎojiě (miss)
chineseCantonese: From 哥德 Gōdāk (Goth) and 小姐 síujé (miss)

name: Solosis
english: Solosis may be a combination of solo (alone, single) and meiosis or mitosis (cell divisions).
japanese: From the numeral prefix uni- (one) and 卵 ran (egg cell)
german: From the numeral prefix mono- (one) and the suffix -zyt (used to form cell names, equivalent to English "-cyte"), as well as Monozyt (monocyte)
korean: From the prefix uni- (one) and 란 (卵) ran (egg cell)
chineseMandarin: From 單 / 单 dān (single), 卵細胞 / 卵细胞 luǎnxìbāo (egg cell), and 球 qiú (ball)
chineseCantonese: From 單 dāan (single), 卵細胞 léuhnsaibāau (egg cell), and 球 kàuh (ball)

name: Duosion
english: Duosion may be a combination of duo (two) and fission, division, or fusion.
japanese: From ダブル daburu (double) and 卵 ran (egg cell)
korean: From duo or 둘 dul (two) and 란 (卵) ran (egg cell)
chineseMandarin: From 雙 / 双 shuāng (double), 卵細胞 / 卵细胞 luǎnxìbāo (egg cell), and 球 qiú (ball)
chineseCantonese: From 雙 sēung (double), 卵細胞 léuhnsaibāau (egg cell), and 球 kàuh (ball)

name: Reuniclus
english: Reuniclus may be a combination of reunite and homunculus, nucleus, or cluster.
japanese: From 卵 ran (egg cell) and homunculus
german: From zyto- (cyto- (prefix for cell)) and mega-
korean: From 란 (卵) ran (egg cell) and homunculus
chineseMandarin: From 人造人 rénzàorén (homunculus) and 卵細胞 / 卵细胞 luǎnxìbāo (egg cell)
chineseCantonese: From 人造人 yàhnjouhyàhn (homunculus) and 卵細胞 léuhnsaibāau (egg cell)

name: Ducklett
english: Ducklett may be a corruption of ducklet, possibly combined with wet or -ette (suffix meaning small).
japanese: From 子 ko (child) or 小 ko (small) and 家鴨 ahiru (domestic duck)
korean: From 꼬마 kkoma (little kid) and 집오리 jib-ori (domestic duck)
chineseMandarin: From 鴨 / 鸭 yā (duck) and 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 鴨 aap (duck) and 寶寶 bóubóu (baby)

name: Swanna
english: Swanna is derived from swan and may be a combination of swan and ballerina.
japanese: From swan and ballerina
french: From Lakmé, cygne (swan), and Lac des Cygnes
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 舞 wǔ (dance) and 天鵝 / 天鹅 tiān'é (swan); From 首席 shǒuxí (chief, referring to the prima ballerina) and 天鵝 / 天鹅 tiān'é (swan)
chineseCantonese: From 舞 móuh (dance) and 天鵝 tīnngòh (swan); From 首席 sáujihk (chief, referring to the prima ballerina) and 天鵝 tīnngòh (swan)

name: Vanillite
english: Vanillite may be a combination of vanilla and lite (reduced) or possibly delight, as well as stalactite.
japanese: From vanilla and petit (French for "small")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 迷你 mínǐ (mini) and 冰 bīng (ice)
chineseCantonese: From 迷你 màihnéih (mini) and 冰 bīng (ice)

name: Vanillish
english: Vanillish may be a combination of vanilla and delish (slang term for delicious).
japanese: From vanilla and rich
french: From sorbet and boule (scoop of ice cream)
german: From gelato and troppo (Italian for "too much")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 多多 duōduō (much; yogurt drink) and 冰 bīng (ice)
chineseCantonese: From 多多 dōdō (much) and 冰 bīng (ice)

name: Vanilluxe
english: Vanilluxe may be a combination of vanilla and deluxe.
japanese: From 倍 bai (double), or bi (two), and vanilla
french: From sorbet, boule (scoop of ice cream) and bouboule (slang term for chubby)
korean: From 배 (倍) bae (double) and vanilla
chineseMandarin: From 雙倍 / 双倍 shuāngbèi (double), 多多 duōduō (much; yogurt drink), and 冰 bīng (ice)
chineseCantonese: From 雙倍 sēungpúih (double), 多多 dōdō (much), and 冰 bīng (ice)

name: Deerling
english: Deerling may be a combination of deer and darling or yearling (young animal between the age of one to two years old), with -ling being a common suffix to denote something that is small or immature; it may also reference the 1938 novel The Yearling, about a boy who adopts an orphaned fawn.
japanese: From 四季 shiki (four seasons) and 鹿 shika (deer)
french: From Vivaldi (composer of The Four Seasons) and daim (fallow deer)
korean: From 사철 sacheol (four seasons) and 록 (鹿) rok (deer)
chineseMandarin: From 四季 sìjì (four seasons) and 鹿 lù (deer)
chineseCantonese: From 四季 seigwai (four seasons) and 鹿 lúk (deer)

name: Sawsbuck
english: Sawsbuck may be a play on sawbuck (framework for holding wood to be sawn), which contains the word buck (male deer). SAWS may also be an acronym for the names of the seasons (summer, autumn, winter, and spring).
japanese: From 芽吹き mebuki (to bud) and 鹿 shika (deer)
french: From Haydn (composer of The Seasons) and daim (fallow deer)
german: From Krone (crown) and Kronjuwelen (crown jewels) and Wild (game animal)
korean: From 발아 (發芽) bar-a (germination; to sprout), 철 cheol (season), and 록 (鹿) rok (deer)
chineseMandarin: From 萌芽 méngyá (to sprout) and 鹿 lù (deer); From an orthographic borrowing of Japanese 芽吹き mebuki and 鹿 lù (deer)
chineseCantonese: From 萌芽 màhngngàh (to sprout) and 鹿 lúk (deer); From an orthographic borrowing of Japanese 芽吹き mebuki and 鹿 lúk (deer)

name: Emolga
english: Emolga may be a combination of 衣紋 emon (drapery) and モモンガ momonga (flying squirrel).
japanese: From 衣紋 emon (drapery) and モモンガ momonga (flying squirrel)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 電 / 电 diàn (electric) and 飛鼠 / 飞鼠 fēishǔ (flying squirrel); From 導電 / 导电 dǎodiàn (electrical conduction) and 飛鼠 / 飞鼠 fēishǔ (flying squirrel)
chineseCantonese: From 電 dihn (electric) and 飛鼠 fēisyú (flying squirrel); From 導電 douhdihn (electrical conduction) and 飛鼠 fēisyú (flying squirrel)

name: Karrablast
english: Karrablast may be a combination of Carabus blaptoides (snail-eating beetle, a species of ground beetles) and blast (referring to its defense mechanism). It may also involve carapace and plastron.
japanese: From 蝸牛被 maimaikaburi (snail-eating beetle) and possibly 甲虫 kabutomushi (beetle)
french: From carabe (ground beetle) and bing (onomatopeia indicating a sudden action or a collision)
german: From Laufkäfer (ground beetle) and Kappe (cap) or Kapsel (capsule)
korean: From 곤봉딱정벌레 gonbong-ttakjeongbeolle (snail-eating beetle)
chineseMandarin: From 蓋 / 盖 gài (covering) and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug, worm)
chineseCantonese: From 蓋 goi (covering) and 蟲 chùhng (bug, worm)

name: Escavalier
english: Escavalier may be a combination of escargot (French for "snail") and cavalier (French for "mounted soldier") or chevalier (French for "knight"), as well as pun of Excalibur.
japanese: From chevalier (French for "knight") and escargot (French for "snail")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 騎士 / 骑士 qíshì (knight) and 蝸牛 / 蜗牛 guāniú / wōniú (snail)
chineseCantonese: From 騎士 kèihsih (knight) and 蝸牛 wō'ngàuh (snail)

name: Foongus
english: Foongus may be a combination of fool (to deceive) and fungus. Together with its Evolution, their names are a corruption of the phrase, "Fungus among us." This is confirmed by Ali the Student in North Province (Area Two) in Pokémon Scarlet and Violet.
japanese: From 玉 tama (sphere), 魂消る tamageru (to be astonished), and 茸 take (mushroom)
korean: From 깜놀 kkamnol (contraction of the word surprised), 버섯 beoseot (mushroom), and 구슬 guseul (sphere)
chineseMandarin: From 哎呀 Āiyā! (interjection indicating surprise), 球 qiú (sphere, ball), and 菇 gū (mushroom); From 寶貝球 Bǎobèi-qiú (Poké Ball), 寶貝 bǎobèi (baby), 球 qiú (sphere, ball), and 菇 gū (mushroom)
chineseCantonese: From 哎呀 Āaiyā! (interjection indicating surprise), 球 kàu (sphere, ball), and 菇 gū (mushroom); From 精靈球 Jīnglìhng-kàuh (Poké Ball), 球 kàuh (sphere, ball), and 菇 gū (mushroom)

name: Amoonguss
english: Amoonguss may be a combination of amanita (a genus of mushroom) and fungus or humongous (huge). Together with its pre-Evolution, their names are a corruption of the phrase, "Fungus among us." This is confirmed by Ali the Student in North Province (Area Two) in Pokémon Scarlet and Violet.
japanese: From もろに moro ni (completely) and ばれる bareru (slang term meaning "to be exposed")
french: From gauler (to catch someone) and bolet
korean: From 뽀록나다 pporongnada (to be exposed)
chineseMandarin: From 敗露 / 败露 bàilù (to be exposed), 球 qiú (sphere, ball), and 菇 gū (mushroom); From 暴露 bàolù (to expose) and 菇 gū (mushroom)
chineseCantonese: From 敗露 baaihlouh (to be exposed), 球 kàu (sphere, ball), and 菇 gū (mushroom); From 暴露 bouhlouh (to expose) and 菇 gū (mushroom)

name: Frillish
english: Frillish may be a combination of frill and jellyfish.
japanese: From プルプル purupuru (onomatopoeia for jiggling) and frill
korean: From 탱글탱글 taengeultaengeul (mimetic word for round and taut) and frill
chineseMandarin: From 輕飄飄 / 轻飘飘 qīngpiāopiāo (lightly floating)
chineseCantonese: From 輕飄飄 hēngpīupīu (lightly floating)

name: Jellicent
english: Jellicent may be a combination of jellyfish and magnificent or translucent.
japanese: From ブルンブルン burunburun (onomatopoeia for shaking) and gel
korean: From 탱탱하다 taengtaenghada (to have a bouncy surface) and gel
chineseMandarin: From 胖嘟嘟 pàngdūdū (chubby)
chineseCantonese: From 胖嘟嘟 buhndyūtdyūt (chubby)

name: Alomomola
english: Alomomola may be a combination of aloha (Hawaiian for love), mom, and Mola mola (scientific name for the ocean sunfish).
japanese: From mama and 翻車魚 manbō (ocean sunfish)
german: From Mama and Molidae (ocean sunfish family)
korean: From mom or Japanese 翻車魚 manbō (ocean sunfish) and 개복치 gaebokchi (ocean sunfish)
chineseMandarin: From 保母 / 保姆 bǎomǔ (nanny) and 曼波魚 / 曼波鱼 mànbō-yú (ocean sunfish)
chineseCantonese: From 保母 bóumóuh (nanny) and 曼波魚 maahnbō-yùh (ocean sunfish)

name: Joltik
english: Joltik may be a combination of jolt and tick (a parasitic arachnid).
japanese: From バチバチ bachibachi (onomatopoeia for electric crackling) and tarantula
french: From électricité statique (static electricity) and tique (tick)
german: From Watt, zap, and anzapfen (to tap into)
korean: From 파직 pajik (onomatopoeia for electric crackling) and 쪼옥 jjo-ok (sound of sipping or sucking)
chineseMandarin: From 電 / 电 diàn (electricity) and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug)
chineseCantonese: From 電 dihn (electricity) and 蟲 chùhng (bug)

name: Galvantula
english: Galvantula may be a combination of galvanism and tarantula.
japanese: From 電池 denchi (battery), 電柱 denchū (utility pole), 虫 chū (bug), and tarantula
korean: From 전 (電) jeon (electricity) and tarantula
chineseMandarin: From 電 / 电 diàn (electricity) and 蜘蛛 zhīzhū (spider)
chineseCantonese: From 電 dihn (electricity) and 蜘蛛 jījyū (spider)

name: Ferroseed
english: Ferroseed may be a combination of ferrous (containing iron) and seed.
japanese: From 鉄 tetsu (iron) and seed
korean: From 철 (鐵) cheol (iron) and seed
chineseMandarin: From 種子 / 种子 zhǒngzǐ (seed) and 鐵球 / 铁球 tiěqiú (iron ball)
chineseCantonese: From 種子 júngjí (seed) and 鐵球 titkàuh (iron ball)

name: Ferrothorn
english: Ferrothorn may be a combination of ferrous (containing iron) and thorn.
japanese: From nut and 唖鈴 arei (dumbbell)
korean: From nut and 아령 (啞鈴) aryeong (dumbbell)
chineseMandarin: From 堅果 / 坚果 jiānguǒ (nut) and 啞鈴 / 哑铃 yǎlíng (dumbbell)
chineseCantonese: From 堅果 gīngwó (nut) and 啞鈴 álìhng (dumbbell)

name: Klink
english: Klink may be derived from clink (onomatopoeia for metal lightly striking a surface). It may also involve link or click.
japanese: From gear
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 齒輪 / 齿轮 chǐlún (gear) and 兒 / 儿 ér (child)
chineseCantonese: From 齒輪 chílèuhn (gear) and 兒 yìh (child)

name: Klang
english: Klang may be derived from clang (onomatopoeia for metal heavily striking a surface).
japanese: From gear
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 齒輪 / 齿轮 chǐlún (gear) and 組 / 组 zǔ (group)
chineseCantonese: From 齒輪 chílèuhn (gear) and 組 jóu (group)

name: Klinklang
english: Klinklang may be a combination of Klink and Klang, which in turn resemble clink and clang (onomatopoeias for metal striking a surface).
japanese: From gear
french: From cliquetis (clatter), as well as a combination of Tic (Klink) and Clic (Klang)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 齒輪 / 齿轮 chǐlún (gear) and 怪 guài (monster)
chineseCantonese: From 齒輪 chílèuhn (gear) and 怪 gwaai (monster)

name: Tynamo
english: Tynamo may be a combination of tiny or tyke and dynamo.
japanese: From 痺れ shibire (numbness) or 痺鰻 shibire-unagi (electric eel) and 白子 shirasu (whitebait)
german: From zappeln (to flounce), zap, Lamprete (lamprey), and Sardine
korean: From 저리다 jeorida (to be numb) and 어 (魚) eo (fish)
chineseMandarin: From 麻 má (numb), 小 xiǎo (small, young), and 魚 / 鱼 yú (fish)
chineseCantonese: From 麻 màh (numb), 小 síu (small, young), and 魚 yùh (fish)

name: Eelektrik
english: Eelektrik may be a combination of eel and electric.
japanese: From 痺れ shibire (numbness) or 痺鰻 shibire-unagi (electric eel), ビリビリ biribiri (onomatopoeic word for an electric shock sound), and イール īru (eel)
french: From lamproie (lamprey) and ampère (Ampere, unit of electric current)
german: From zappeln (to flounce), zap, Lamprete (lamprey), and Elektrizität (electricity)
korean: From 저리다 jeorida (to be numb) and eel
chineseMandarin: From 麻 má (numb) and 鰻魚 / 鳗鱼 mányú (eel)
chineseCantonese: From 麻 màh (numb) and 鰻魚 màahnyùh (eel)

name: Eelektross
english: Eelektross may be a combination of eel, electric, and boss or groß (German for "large").
japanese: From 痺れ shibire (numbness) or 痺鰻 shibire-unagi (electric eel) and don (Spanish for "lord; common suffix in extinct animal names derived from the Ancient Greek word for tooth")
german: From zappeln (to flounce), zap, Lamprete (lamprey), and Rang (rank)
korean: From 저리다 jeorida (to be numb) and possibly tough
chineseMandarin: From 麻 má (numb), 鰻魚 / 鳗鱼 mányú (eel), and 王 wáng (king)
chineseCantonese: From 麻 màh (numb), 鰻魚 màahnyùh (eel), and 王 wòhng (king)

name: Elgyem
english: Elgyem may be derived from the abbreviation LGM (little green men, a stereotypical depiction of extraterrestrials as diminutive green-skinned humanoids).
japanese: From little or little green men and greys
french: From Roswell partially spelled in reverse
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (small), 灰 huī (gray), 小灰人 xiǎohuīrén (greys), and 怪 guài (monster)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (small), 灰 fūi (gray), 小灰人 síufūiyàhn (greys), and 怪 gwaai (monster)

name: Beheeyem
english: Beheeyem may be a corruption of the abbreviation BEM (bug-eyed monster, a depiction of extraterrestrials as grotesque creatures with oversized eyes).
japanese: From 大 ō (large) and BEM
korean: From BEM and 크다 keuda (big, large)
chineseMandarin: From 大 dà (big), 宇宙 yǔzhòu (universe), and 怪 guài (monster)
chineseCantonese: From 大 daaih (big), 宇宙 yúhjauh (universe), and 怪 gwaai (monster)

name: Litwick
english: Litwick may be a combination of lit, little, wick, and possibly wicked.
japanese: From 火点し hitomoshi (lighting a lamp; person who leads a funeral procession with a torch)
korean: From 불 bul (fire, light), 켜다 kyeoda (to light a fire or lamp), and ～이 ~i (diminutive suffix )
chineseMandarin: From 燭光 / 烛光 zhúguāng (candle light) and 靈 / 灵 líng (spirit)
chineseCantonese: From 燭光 jūkgwōng (candle light) and 靈 lìhng (spirit)

name: Lampent
english: Lampent may be a combination of lamp, lambent (softly glowing), and possibly lament.
japanese: From lamp
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 燈火 / 灯火 dēnghuǒ (lights), 火 huǒ (fire), and 幽靈 / 幽灵 yōulíng (ghost, phantom)
chineseCantonese: From 燈火 dāngfó (lights), 火 fó (fire), and 幽靈 yāulìhng (ghost, phantom)

name: Chandelure
english: Chandelure may be a combination of chandelier and lure.
japanese: From chandelier and candela (Latin for "candle") or candelabra
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 水晶燈 / 水晶灯 shuǐjīngdēng (crystal chandelier), 燈火 / 灯火 dēnghuǒ (lights), 火 huǒ (fire), and 靈 / 灵 líng (spirit)
chineseCantonese: From 水晶燈 séuijīngdāng (crystal chandelier), 燈火 dāngfó (lights), 火 fó (fire), and 靈 lìhng (spirit)

name: Axew
english: Axew may be a combination of axe and chew or hew (to chop a material with a tool).
japanese: From 牙 kiba (tusk), 顎 ago (jaw), and dragon
french: From couper (to cut) and quenotte (child's tooth)
korean: From 턱 teok (jaw) and 엄니 eomni (tusk)
chineseMandarin: From 牙 yá (fang, tusk)
chineseCantonese: From 牙 ngàh (fang, tusk)

name: Fraxure
english: Fraxure may be a combination of fracture and axe.
japanese: From 斧 ono (axe), dragon, and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
korean: From axe and 도끼 dokki (axe)
chineseMandarin: From 斧 fǔ (axe), 牙 yá (fang, tusk), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 斧 fú (axe), 牙 ngàh (fang, tusk), and 龍 lùhng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)

name: Haxorus
english: Haxorus may be a combination of hack (to chop or cut down), axe, -saurus (common suffix in names of dinosaurs and extinct reptiles derived from the Ancient Greek word for lizard), and possibly hazardous.
japanese: From 斧 ono (axe), 戦く ononoku (to tremble), axe, and possibly -onychus (common suffix in dinosaur names derived from the Ancient Greek word for claw) and dragon
french: From trancher (to slice) and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
korean: From axe and surprise or rise
chineseMandarin: From 雙 / 双 shuāng (double), 斧 fǔ (axe), 戰 / 战 zhàn (battle), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 雙 sēung (double), 斧 fú (axe), 戰 jin (battle), and 龍 lùhng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)

name: Cubchoo
english: Cubchoo may be a combination of cub and ah-choo (sound of a sneeze).
japanese: From 熊 kuma (bear), くしゅん kushun (onomatopoeia of a sneeze), and possibly 熊 xióng (Chinese for bear)
german: From Meister Petz (Master Petz, common name for a bear in German fables) and schniefen (to sniff)
korean: From 코 ko (runny nose, nose), 꼬마 kkoma (little kid), 곰 gom (bear), ～이 -i (diminutive suffix), and possibly a pun of 코곪 kogom (snoring)
chineseMandarin: From 噴嚏 / 喷嚏 pēntì (sneeze) and 熊 xióng (bear)
chineseCantonese: From 噴嚏 pantai (sneeze) and 熊 hùhng (bear)

name: Beartic
english: Beartic may be a combination of bear and arctic. Notably, arctic itself derives from ἄρκτος arktos, Ancient Greek for bear. It may also incorporate the word beard, from the ice crystals around its snout giving the impression of a long beard.
japanese: From tundra, 氷柱 tsurara (icicle), and bear
german: From Sibirien (Siberia), Bär (bear), and ghiaccio (Italian for "ice")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 凍原 / 冻原 dòngyuán (tundra) and 熊 xióng (bear)
chineseCantonese: From 凍原 dungyúhn (tundra) and 熊 hùhng (bear)

name: Cryogonal
english: Cryogonal may be a combination of cry or cryo- (prefix for icy cold) and hexagonal.
japanese: From freeze or frigid and geometry
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 幾何 / 几何 jǐhé (geometry) and 雪花 xuěhuā (snowflake)
chineseCantonese: From 幾何 géihòh (geometry) and 雪花 syutfā (snowflake)

name: Shelmet
english: Shelmet may be a combination of shell and helmet.
japanese: From おちょぼ口 ochoboguchi (puckered-up mouth) and 巻貝 makigai (snail; conch)
korean: From 쪽 jjok (onomatopoeia for kissing), 조개 jogae (clam), and 말이 mari (roll)
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (small), 嘴 zuǐ (mouth), and 蝸 / 蜗 guā / wō (snail)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (small), 嘴 jéui (mouth), and 蝸 wō (snail)

name: Accelgor
english: Accelgor may be a combination of accelerate and escargot (French for "snail").
japanese: From アギル agiru (agile) and ライダー raidā (rider)
korean: From agility and rider
chineseMandarin: From 敏捷 mǐnjié (agile, nimble) and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug, worm)
chineseCantonese: From 敏捷 máhnjiht (agile, nimble) and 蟲 chùhng (bug, worm)

name: Stunfisk
english: Stunfisk may be a combination of stun and either fisk (fish in many Germanic languages), or fish and disk (in reference to its flat shape).
japanese: From mud and 魚 gyo (fish)
korean: From mud and 어 (魚) eo (fish)
chineseMandarin: From 泥巴 níbā (mud) and 魚 / 鱼 yú (fish)
chineseCantonese: From 泥巴 nàihbā (mud) and 魚 yùh (fish)

name: Mienfoo
english: Mienfoo may be a combination of ermine and kung fu.
japanese: From 白鼬 okojo (ermine) and kung fu
korean: From 족제비 jokjebi (Siberian weasel) and kung-fu
chineseMandarin: From 功夫 gōngfu (kung fu) and 鼬 yòu (weasel)
chineseCantonese: From 功夫 gūngfùh (kung fu) and 鼬 yauh (weasel)

name: Mienshao
english: Mienshao may be a combination of ermine and Shaolin.
japanese: From 白鼬 okojo (ermine) and 道 dō (teachings, path) or 道場 dōjō (dojo)
korean: From 족제비 jokjebi (Siberian weasel) and 도 (道) do (path, way) or 도장 (道場) dojang (dojo)
chineseMandarin: From 師父 / 师父 shīfù (master) and 鼬 yòu (weasel)
chineseCantonese: From 師父 sīfú (master) and 鼬 yauh (weasel)

name: Druddigon
english: Druddigon may be a combination of dragon and ruddy (reddish in color).
japanese: From crimson and 顔 gan (face) or 岩 gan (rock)
korean: From crimson and 안 (顔) an (face)
chineseMandarin: From 赤 chì (crimson), 面 miàn (face), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From 赤 chek (crimson), 面 mihn (face), and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Golett
english: Golett may be a combination of golem and the diminutive suffix -let.
japanese: From golem and bit or 小人 kobito (small person)

chineseMandarin: From 烈 liè (ardent; fierce), 箭 jiàn (arrow), and 鷹 / 鹰 yīng (hawk); From 烈 liè (ardent; fierce), 箭 jiàn (arrow), and 鶲 wēng (Old World flycatcher)
chineseCantonese: From 烈 liht (ardent; fierce), 箭 jin (arrow), and 鷹 yīng (hawk)

name: Scatterbug

name: Spewpa

chineseMandarin: From 鱗粉 / 鳞粉 línfěn (scale), 蝶 dié (butterfly), and 蛹 yǒng (chrysalis)
chineseCantonese: From 鱗粉 lèuhnfán (scale), 蝶 dihp (butterfly), and 蛹 yúng (chrysalis)

name: Vivillon

korean: Transcription of English/Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 彩 cǎi (variety of color), 鱗粉 línfěn (scale), and 蝶 dié (butterfly); From 碧 bì (jade), 鱗粉 línfěn (scale), and 蝶 dié (butterfly)

name: Litleo

name: Flabébé

chineseMandarin: From 花 huā (flower), 蓓 bèi (bud), and similar to the Japanese name

name: Gogoat

korean: Transcription of English/Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 坐騎 / 坐骑 zuòqí (mount) and 山羊 shānyáng (mountain goat)

chineseMandarin: From 妙 miào (mysterious) and 喵 miāo (meow)

english: Meowstic may be a combination of meow and mystic. It may also derive from stoic, referring to its generally emotionless facial expression.
japanese: From ニャー nyā (meow) and onyx or ὄνυξ ónyx (Greek for "claw"), and possibly psionics and Nyx
