name: Tyrantrum
english: Tyrantrum may be a combination of Tyrannosaurus, tyrant, and tantrum.
japanese: From ガチガチ gachigachi (teeth chattering), ガチ gachi (serious, for real), ガチン gachin (banging noise), がっちり gacchiri (stocky), チゴラス Chigoras (Tyrunt), and Tyrannosaurus
french: From Tyrannosaurus rex and maxillaire (maxilla (upper jaw))
korean: From 견고 (堅固) gyeongo (firm) and 티고라스 Tigoras (Tyrunt)
chineseMandarin: From 怪顎 / 怪颚 guài'è (strange jaw) and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon, a common suffix for dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 怪顎 gwaaingohk (strange jaw) and 龍 lùhng (dragon, a common suffix for dinosaur names)

name: Amaura
english: Amaura may be a combination of Amargasaurus and aurora.
japanese: From Amargasaurus
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 冰雪 bīngxuě (ice and snow) and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 冰雪 bīngsyut (ice and snow) and 龍 lùhng (dragon, a common suffix for dinosaur names)

name: Aurorus
english: Aurorus may be a combination of aurora and Amargasaurus.
japanese: From Amargasaurus
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 冰雪 bīngxuě (ice and snow), 巨 jù (giant), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 冰雪 bīngsyut (ice and snow), 巨 geuih (giant), and 恐龍 húnglùhng (dinosaur)

name: Sylveon
english: Sylveon may be a combination of sylph (elemental of air commonly identified with fairies), sylvan (an adjective used to describe wooded or rural areas), Silvanus (a Roman deity of the woods and uncultivated land), and eon (an immeasurably long period of time, possibly referring to how long evolution takes naturally). Eon is a suffix all Eeveelutions share and was Eevee's English prototype name.
japanese: From nymph
french: From nymph and -li (common suffix for all Eeveelutions in French)
german: From Fee (fairy), feeling, and -a (common suffix for all Eeveelutions in German)
korean: From 님프 nymph and the transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 仙子 xiānzǐ (fairy) and 伊布 Yībù (Eevee); From 仙子 xiānzǐ (fairy) and 精靈 / 精灵 jīnglíng (spirit, fairy, elf; former suffix for Eeveelutions in Mandarin)
chineseCantonese: From 仙子 sīnjí (fairy) and 伊布 Yībou (Eevee); From 仙子 sīnjí (fairy) and 伊貝 Yībui (former translation of Eevee)

name: Hawlucha
english: Hawlucha may be a combination of hawk and lucha libre, a form of Latin American professional wrestling.
japanese: From lucha libre and bull
german: From Wrestling, Adler (eagle), and -ero (Spanish agentive suffix)
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 摔角 shuāijiǎo (wrestling), 鷹 / 鹰 yīng (eagle), and 人 rén (person); From 戰鬥 zhàndòu (battle) and 飛鳥 fēiniǎo (bird)
chineseCantonese: From 摔角 sēutgok (wrestling), 鷹 yīng (eagle), and 人 yàhn (person); From 戰鬥 jindau (battle) and 飛鳥 fēiníuh (bird)

name: Dedenne
english: Dedenne may be a combination of 電気 denki (electricity), ヤマネ yamane (dormouse), and antenne (French for "antenna").
japanese: From 電気 denki (electricity), 山鼠 yamane (Japanese dormouse), and antenne (French for "antenna")
korean: Same as Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 咚咚 dōngdōng (onomatopoeia for pounding) and 鼠 shǔ (mouse)
chineseCantonese: From 咚咚 dūngdūng (onomatopoeia for pounding) and 鼠 syú (mouse)

name: Carbink
english: Carbink may be a combination of carbuncle (referring to the mythical creature and a type of gemstone), carbon (element diamonds are composed of), carat, and tink (to tinkle).
japanese: From melée (small cut diamonds), C (chemical symbol of carbon, the main constituent of diamonds), 珍しい mezurashii (rare, unusual), and 石 ishi (stone, rock)
french: From strass (rhinestone, a diamond simulant) and rhymes with Diancie
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (small) and 碎鑽 / 碎钻 suìzuàn (melée)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (small) and 碎鑽 seuijyūn (melée)

name: Goomy
english: Goomy may be a combination of goo and either gummy or slimy.
japanese: From 滑る numeru (to be slippery) and ぬらぬら nuranura (onomatopoetic word for slimy)
korean: From 미끄럽다 mikkeureopda (to be slippery)
chineseMandarin: From 黏 nián (sticky) and 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 黏 nìhm (sticky) and 寶寶 bóubóu (baby)

name: Sliggoo
english: Sliggoo may be a combination of slick, slither, slippery, slimy, or slug, and goo. The name may also be derived from the Irish word 'sliogán'—meaning shell—in reference to the shell on its back.
japanese: From 滑る numeru (to be slippery) and snail
korean: From 미끄럽다 mikkeureopda (to be slippery) and snail
chineseMandarin: From 黏 nián (sticky) and the transcription of the Japanese name with the incorporation of 美 měi (beautiful) and 兒 / 儿 er (child)
chineseCantonese: From 黏 nìhm (sticky), 美 méi (beautiful), and 兒 yìh (child)

name: Goodra
english: Goodra may be a combination of goo and dragon or Hydra. It may also be an inversion of Dragoon. It may also derive from good, referring to its kindly nature as opposed to the more violent dispositions of other Powerhouse Pokémon.
japanese: From 滑る numeru (to be slippery), gel, and dragon
korean: From 미끄럽다 mikkeureopda (to be slippery) and dragon
chineseMandarin: From 黏 nián (sticky), 美 měi (beautiful), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon); From 黏 nián (sticky), 美 měi (beautiful), 露 lù (dew), and 龍 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From 黏 nìhm (sticky), 美 méih (beautiful), and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Klefki
english: Klefki may be a combination of clef (French for "key"), key, and possibly kleftis (Κλέφτης, Greek for "thief").
japanese: From clef (French for "key")
french: From trousseau de clés (keychain) and gobelin (goblin)
german: From clāvis (Latin for "key") and possibly ion
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 鑰匙圈 / 钥匙圈 yàoshíquān (keyring) and 兒 / 儿 ér (diminutive suffix meaning child)
chineseCantonese: From 鑰匙圈 yeuhksìhhyūn (keyring) and 兒 yìh (diminutive suffix meaning child); From 鎖圈 sóhyūn (keyring) and 兒 yìh (diminutive suffix meaning child)

name: Phantump
english: Phantump may be a combination of phantom and stump.
japanese: From the alternative reading of 木霊 kodama
french: From Brocéliande, fantôme (ghost), and môme (kid, brat)
korean: From 나무 namu (tree), 나목 (裸木) namok (bare wood), and 령 (靈) ryeong (spirit, ghost)
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (small), 木 mù (wood), and 靈 / 灵 líng (spirit)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (small), 木 muhk (wood), and 靈 lìhng (spirit)

name: Trevenant
english: Trevenant may be a combination of tree, revenant, and possibly treant.
japanese: From 大 ō (big) and rot
french: From décès (death), dessécher (dry out), and Brocéliande
korean: From 대 (大) dae (big) and rot
chineseMandarin: From 朽木 xiǔmù (rotten wood) and 妖 yāo (goblin)
chineseCantonese: From 朽木 náumuhk (rotten wood) and 妖 yīu (goblin)

name: Pumpkaboo
english: Pumpkaboo may be a combination of pumpkin and boo (a common word used to startle people) or peek-a-boo.
japanese: From お化け obake (ghost) and 南瓜 kabocha (pumpkin)
french: From petit (small), pitre (jokester), citrouille (pumpkin), and trouille (fear)
korean: From 호박 (胡朴) hobak (pumpkin) and 귀 (鬼) gwi (ghost)
chineseMandarin: From 南瓜 nánguā (pumpkin) and 精 jīng (spirit)
chineseCantonese: From 南瓜 nàahmgwā (pumpkin) and 精 jīng (spirit)

name: Gourgeist
english: Gourgeist may be a combination of gourd and geist.
japanese: From pumpkin and 神 shin (deity, spirit), 人 jin (man), or jinn
korean: From pumpkin and 인 (人) in (man)
chineseMandarin: From 南瓜 nánguā (pumpkin) and 怪人 guàirén (strange being)
chineseCantonese: From 南瓜 nánguā (pumpkin) and 怪人 gwaaiyàhn (strange being)

name: Bergmite
english: Bergmite may be a combination of iceberg, mite, and possibly stalagmite.
japanese: From かちかち kachikachi (onomatopoeic word for frozen stiff), 凍る kōru (to freeze), and カチカチに凍る kachikachi ni kōru (to be frozen hard)
french: From grêlon (hailstone), grelotter (shivering), and glaçon (ice cube)
korean: From 꽁꽁 kkongkkong (frozen hard) and 얼음 eor-eum (ice)
chineseMandarin: From 冰 bīng (ice) and 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 冰 bīng (ice) and 寶寶 bóubóu (baby)

name: Avalugg
english: Avalugg may be a combination of avalanche and lug (to carry or drag heavy objects, or a big/clumsy person).
japanese: From クレバス crevasse and ベース base
german: From Arktis and Atlas or Atlas Mountains
korean: From 크레바스 crevasse and 베이스 base; same as Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 冰 bīng (ice), 岩 yán (boulder), and 怪 guài (monster)
chineseCantonese: From 冰 bīng (ice), 岩 ngàahm (boulder), and 怪 gwaai (monster)

name: Noibat
english: Noibat may be a combination of noise and bat.
japanese: From 音 on (sound), 音波 onpa (sound wave), and bat
korean: From 음 (音) eum (sound) and bat
chineseMandarin: From 嗡 wēng (onomatopoeia for buzzing or humming sound) and 蝠 fú (bat)
chineseCantonese: From 嗡 yūng (onomatopoeia for buzzing or humming sound) and 蝠 fūk (bat)

name: Noivern
english: Noivern may be a combination of noise and wyvern.
japanese: From 音 on (sound), 音波 onpa (sound wave), and wyvern
korean: From 음 (音) eum (sound) and wyvern
chineseMandarin: From 音波 yīnbō (sound wave) and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From 音波 yāmbō (sound wave) and 龍 lùhng (dragon); From 音波 yāmbō (sound wave) and 飛龍 fēilùhng (wyvern)

name: Xerneas
english: Xerneas begins with the letter X. It may be derived from cervus (Latin for "deer"), Cernunnos (a horned Celtic god), Ceryneian Hind, and アース āsu (earth).
japanese: From X, cervus (Latin for "deer"), Cernunnos, Ceryneian Hind, and earth
korean: Same as English name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Yveltal
english: Yveltal begins with the letter Y. It may be derived from yvel (a Middle English spelling of evil) and quetzal or talon.
japanese: From Y, yvel (archaic spelling of evil), and quetzal or talon
korean: Same as English name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name; Transcription of Japanese name

name: Zygarde
english: Zygarde begins with the letter Z, following the pattern established by Xerneas and Yveltal. It may also be derived from ζυγωτός zygōtos (Greek for "joined") or zygote, garde (French for "guard"), and garðr (Old Norse for enclosure; realm).
japanese: From Z, ζυγωτός zygōtos (Greek for "joined") or zygote, garde (French for "guard"), and garðr (Old Norse for 'enclosure, realm')
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Diancie
english: Diancie may be a combination of diamond, fancy, pixie, and 石 ishi (stone). The -cie could also come from メレシー Melecie (Carbink's Japanese name), reflecting Diancie’s status as a mutated Carbink.
japanese: From diamond, fancy, pixie, 石 ishi (stone, rock), and メレシー Melecie (Carbink)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Hoopa
english: Hoopa may be derived from hoop. It may also involve hoopla (something loud, attention-grabbing, and possibly misleading); or OOPArt (out-of-place artifact).
japanese: From hoop and possibly hoopla or OOPArt
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From the transcription of its Japanese name and possibly 胡 hú (recklessly)
chineseCantonese: From the Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name and possibly 胡 wùh (recklessly)

name: Volcanion
english: Volcanion may be a combination of volcano or volcanic and lion or union (given how it is both Water-type and Fire-type). It may also involve canyon or cañón (Spanish for "cannon").
japanese: From volcano, lion, and canyon or cañón (Spanish for "cannon and canyon")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Rowlet
english: Rowlet may be a combination of root, round, or arrow, and owlet (a young owl).
japanese: From 木 moku (wood) and 梟 fukurō (owl)
korean: From 나무 namu (tree) and 올빼미 olppaemi (owl)
chineseMandarin: From 木 mù (wood) and 梟 / 枭 xiāo (owl)
chineseCantonese: From 木 muhk (wood) and 梟 hīu (owl)

name: Dartrix
english: Dartrix may be a combination of dart and Strix (a genus of owls) or tricks.
japanese: From 梟 fukurō (owl) and throw
french: From chouette effraie (barn owl) and flèche (arrow)
german: From arbor (Latin for "tree"), Arboretum, and toss
korean: From 올빼미 olppaemi (owl) and throw
chineseMandarin: From 投 tóu (throw), 羽 yǔ (feather), and 梟 / 枭 xiāo (owl)
chineseCantonese: From 投 tàuh (throw), 羽 yúh (feather), and 梟 hīu (owl)

name: Decidueye
english: Decidueye may be a combination of deciduous, duel, and deadeye or bullseye.
japanese: From 樹 ju (tree), juniper, and sniper
french: From archer, duc (from certain owls such as Hibou moyen-duc (long-eared owl)), and archiduc (archduke)
korean: From 목 (木) mok (wood), juniper, and sniper
chineseMandarin: From 狙射 jūshè (snipe), 樹 / 树 shù (tree), 梟 / 枭 xiāo (owl)
chineseCantonese: From 狙射 jēuiyeh (snipe), 樹 syuh (tree), 梟 hīu (owl)

name: Litten
english: Litten may be a combination of lit, little, and kitten. It may also be a play on liten, Swedish for "small".
japanese: From ニャー nyā (meow), 火 hi (fire), and tabby
korean: From 야옹 yaong (meow) and 불 bul (fire)
chineseMandarin: From 火 huǒ (fire), 虎斑貓 / 虎斑猫 hǔbānmāo (tabby cat), and 喵 miāo (meow)
chineseCantonese: From 火 fó (fire), 虎斑貓 fúbāanmāau (tabby cat), and 喵 mīu (meow)

name: Torracat
english: Torracat may be a combination of torrid (very hot and dry), torrar (Portuguese and Spanish for "to roast" or "to toast"), or 虎 tora (Japanese for tiger), and cat.
japanese: From ニャー nyā (meow), 火 hi (fire), and heat
korean: From 야옹 yaong (meow) and heat
chineseMandarin: From 炎熱 / 炎热 yánrè (blazing hot) and 喵 miāo (meow)
chineseCantonese: From 炎熱 / 炎热 yìhmyiht (blazing hot) and 喵 mēu (meow)

name: Incineroar
english: Incineroar is a combination of incinerate and roar.
japanese: From ガオー gao (the sound of a roar) and 火炎 kaen (flame)
german: From fuego (fire in Spanish) and growl
korean: From 어흥 eoheung (growl) and 염 (炎) yeom (flame)
chineseMandarin: From 熾 chì (blazing, splendid), 焰 yàn (flame), 咆哮 páoxiāo (roar), and 虎 hǔ (tiger)
chineseCantonese: From 熾 chi (blazing, splendid), 焰 yìhm (flame), 咆哮 pàauhhāau (roar), and 虎 fú (tiger)

name: Popplio
english: Popplio may be a combination of sea lion pup, pop, pōpō (Hawaiian for ball), and ʻīlio-holo-i-ka-uaua (Hawaiian for the Hawaiian monk seal; meaning "dog that runs in rough water").
japanese: From 海驢 ashika (sea lion), 鞠 mari (ball), and marine
french: From otarie (sea lion), taquin (playful), and arlequin (harlequin)
korean: From 온눌 onnul (fur seal) and 공 gong (ball)
chineseMandarin: From 球 qiú (ball) and 海獅 / 海狮 hǎishī (sea lion)
chineseCantonese: From 球 kàuh (ball) and 海獅 hóisī (sea lion)

name: Brionne
english: Brionne may come from brio (vivacity of style or performance), sea lion, brine, sissonne (a ballet step), and ondine (a type of female water nymph or mermaid).
japanese: From オシャレ oshare (fashionable) or おしゃま oshama (precocious young girl), 鞠 mari (ball), and marine
korean: From 귀요미 gwiyomi (cutie) and 공 gong (ball)
chineseMandarin: From 花樣 / 花样 huāyàng (fancy), 漾 yàng (to ripple), and 海獅 / 海狮 hǎishī (sea lion)
chineseCantonese: From 花樣 fāyeuhng (fancy), 漾 yeuhng (to ripple), and 海獅 hóisī (sea lion)

name: Primarina
english: Primarina may be a combination of prima donna, marina, and ballerina.
japanese: From 海驢 ashika (sea lion) and sirène (French for "mermaid and Siren")
french: From oratorio, otarie (sea lion), and aria
german: From Primadonna (prima donna), marin (marine), and Sirene (Siren)
korean: From 온눌 onnul (fur seal) and sirène (French for "mermaid and Siren")
chineseMandarin: From 西施 Xī Shī, 海獅 / 海狮 hǎishī (sea lion), and 塞壬 Sāirén or 西壬 Xīrén (Siren)
chineseCantonese: From 西施 Sāi Sī, 海獅 hóisī (sea lion), and 塞壬 Choiyàhm or 西壬 Sāiyàhm (Siren)

name: Pikipek
english: Pikipek may be a combination of picus (Latin for "woodpecker"), pick, and peck.
japanese: From 突き tsutsuki (pecking) and 啄木鳥 keratsutsuki (woodpecker)
french: From pic (woodpecker), picasser (to make the sound of the woodpecker) and assaut (assault). Also a pun on the painter Pablo Picasso
korean: From 콕 kok (onomatopoeia for pecking sound), 꼬마 kkoma (little kid) and 딱따구리 ttakttaguri (woodpecker)
chineseMandarin: From 小兒 xiǎo'ér (child) and 篤篤 dǔdǔ (onomatopoeia for pecking sound)
chineseCantonese: From 小兒 síuyìh (child) and 篤篤 dūkdūk (onomatopoeia for pecking sound)

name: Trumbeak
english: Trumbeak may be a combination of trumpet and beak.
japanese: From 啄木鳥 keratsutsuki (woodpecker) and 喇叭 rappa (trumpet)
korean: From 큰 keun (big) and 나팔 napal (trumpet)
chineseMandarin: From 喇叭 lǎbā (trumpet) and 啄木鳥 / 啄木鸟 zhuómùniǎo (woodpecker)
chineseCantonese: From 喇叭 lābā (trumpet) and 啄木鳥 deukmuhkníuh (woodpecker)

name: Toucannon
english: Toucannon may be a combination of toucan and cannon.
japanese: From どでかい dodekai (huge) and 大嘴 ōhashi (toucan)
korean: From 왕 (王) wang (king) and 큰부리새 keunburisae (toucan)
chineseMandarin: From 銃 / 铳 chòng (firearm), 大 dà (big), and 巨嘴鳥 / 巨嘴鸟 jùzuǐniǎo (toucan)
chineseCantonese: From 銃 chung (firearm), 大 daai (big), and 巨嘴鳥 geuihjéuiníuh (toucan)

name: Yungoos
english: Yungoos and Youngoose may be a combination of young or ヤンキー yankī (a certain style of juvenile delinquent) and mongoose.
japanese: From young, ヤンキー yankī (juvenile delinquent), and mongoose
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 貓鼬 / 猫鼬 māoyòu (mongoose) and 少 shào (young; young master) or 惡少 / 恶少 èshào (ruffian)
chineseCantonese: From 貓鼬 māauyauh (mongoose) and 少 siu (young; young master) or 惡少 / 恶少 oksiu (ruffian)

name: Gumshoos
english: Gumshoos may be a combination of gumshoe (detective) and mongoose. It may also involve gumption.
japanese: From でか deka (slang term for detective) and mongoose
french: From argousin (slang term for police officer) and mangouste (mongoose)
korean: From 형사 (刑事) hyeongsa (detective) and mongoose
chineseMandarin: From 貓鼬 / 猫鼬 māoyòu (mongoose) and 探長 / 探长 tànzhǎng (chief inspector)
chineseCantonese: From 貓鼬 māauyauh (mongoose) and 探長 taamjéung (chief inspector)

name: Grubbin
english: Grubbin may be a combination of grub and grubbing (to scavenge or dig). Given its resemblance to an electrical plug, it may also be a play on the phrase "plug in".
japanese: From 顎 ago (jaw) and 地虫 jimushi (grub)
korean: From 턱 teok (jaw), 지충 (地蟲) jichung (grub), and ～이 -i (dimunitive suffix)
chineseMandarin: From 強顎 / 强颚 qiáng è (strong jaw) and 雞母蟲 / 鸡母虫 jīmǔchóng (grub)
chineseCantonese: From 強顎 kèuhng ngohk (strong jaw) and 雞母蟲 gāimóuhchùhng (grub)

name: Charjabug
english: Charjabug may be a combination of charge (as in to charge a battery) or charger and bug.
japanese: From 電池 denchi (battery) and 地虫 jimushi (grub)
korean: From 전지 (電池) jeonji (battery), 지충 (地蟲) jichung (grub), and 이 i (dimunitive suffix)
chineseMandarin: From 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug), 充電 / 充电 chōngdiàn (charge), 充電寶 / 充电宝 chōngdiànbǎo (powerbank), and 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 蟲 chùhng (bug), 充電 chūngdihn (charge), 充電寶 chūngdihnbóu (powerbank), and 寶寶 bóubóu (baby)

name: Vikavolt
english: Vikavolt may come from vise grip and volt.
japanese: From 鍬形虫 kuwagatamushi (stag beetle) and cannon
korean: From 투구풍뎅이 tugupungdeng-i (Japanese rhinoceros beetle) and cannon
chineseMandarin: From 鍬形蟲 / 锹形虫 qiāoxíngchóng (stag beetle) and 加農炮 / 加农炮 jiānóngpào (cannon)
chineseCantonese: From 鍬形蟲 chīuyìhngchùhng (stag beetle) and 加農炮 gānùhngpàauh (cannon)

name: Crabrawler
english: Crabrawler may be a combination of crab and brawler.
japanese: From 負けん気 makenki (hates to lose), 喧嘩 kenka (fight), and 蟹 kani (crab)
korean: From 오기 (傲氣) ogi (arrogance), 기지 (機智) giji (quick-witted), and 게 ge (crab)
chineseMandarin: From 好勝 / 好胜 hàoshèng (competitive; aggresive) and 蟹 xiè (crab)
chineseCantonese: From 好勝 housing (competitive; aggresive) and 蟹 háaih (crab)

name: Crabominable
english: Crabominable may be a combination of crab and abominable snowman (another name for the yeti).
japanese: From 毛蟹 kegani (horsehair crab) and 喧嘩 kenka (fight)
korean: From 모 (毛) mo (fur), 단단하다 dandanhada (tough), and 게 ge (crab)
chineseMandarin: From 好勝 / 好胜 hàoshèng (competitive; aggresive) and 毛蟹 máoxiè (horsehair crab)
chineseCantonese: From 好勝 housing (competitive; aggresive) and 毛蟹 mòuhháaih (horsehair crab)

name: Oricorio
english: Oricorio may be a combination of oriole and choreography. It may also incorporate oratorio. Its repetitive nature may reference Oricorio's ability Dancer's ability to copy moves.
japanese: From 踊り odori (dance), 鳥 tori (bird), and 色とりどり irotoridori (varicolored)
korean: From 춤추다 chumchuda (dance) and 새 sae (bird)
chineseMandarin: From 花舞 huāwǔ (fancy dance) and 鳥 / 鸟 niǎo (bird)
chineseCantonese: From 花舞 fāmóuh (fancy dance) and 鳥 níuh (bird)

name: Cutiefly
english: Cutiefly may be a combination of cutie and fly (including bee fly, fairyfly, butterfly, etc.), and a play on the phrase "cutie pie".
japanese: From 吊虻 tsuriabu (bee fly), lovely, and fairy
french: From bombyle (bee fly) and doux (sweet, soft, gentle)
german: From Wollschweber (bee fly), Wolle (wool), Hummel (bumblebee), and Bommel (bobble)
korean: From 재니등에 jaenideung-e (bee fly) and lovely
chineseMandarin: From 萌え moe (Japanese for cute) and 蜂虻 fēngméng (bee fly)
chineseCantonese: From 萌え moe (Japanese for cute) and 蜂虻 fūngmòhng (bee fly)

name: Ribombee
english: Ribombee may be a combination of ribbon, Bombyliidae (family of bee flies), and bee. It may also involve rimbombante (Spanish word for flamboyant) or bombinate (to buzz; hum).
japanese: From 吊虻 tsuriabu (bee fly) and ribbon
french: From ruban (ribbon), bombyle (bee fly) and belle (beautiful)
korean: From 재니등에 jaenideung-e (bee fly) and ribbon
chineseMandarin: From 蝴蝶結 / 蝴蝶结 húdiéjié (ribbon bow), 萌え moe (Japanese for cute), and 蜂虻 fēngméng (bee fly)
chineseCantonese: From 蝴蝶結 wùhdihpgit (ribbon bow), 萌え moe (Japanese for cute), and 蜂虻 fūngmòhng (bee fly)

name: Rockruff
english: Rockruff may be a combination of rock, ruff (onomatopoetic word for barking, or the fur around its neck), ruffle (referring to its collar's shape) and rough.
japanese: From 岩 iwa (rock), ワン wan (woof), わんこ wanko (doggy), and 子 ko (young animal)
korean: From 암 (岩) am (rock), 멍멍 meong-meong (onomatopoeia for the sound of a dog barking), and 이 i (diminutive marker)
chineseMandarin: From 岩 yán (rock) and 狗狗 gǒugǒu (doggy)
chineseCantonese: From 岩 ngàahm (rock) and 狗狗 gáugáu (doggy)

name: Lycanroc
english: Lycanroc may be a combination of lycanthrope and rock.
japanese: From loup-garou (French for "werewolf"), ガルル garuru (onomatopoeia for a dog's growling), and 岩 gan (rock)
korean: From loup-garou (French for "werewolf") and 암 (岩) am (rock)
chineseMandarin: From 鬃狼 zōngláng (maned wolf), 岩 yán (rock), 狼人 lángrén (werewolf)
chineseCantonese: From 鬃狼 jūnglòhng (maned wolf), 岩 ngàahm (rock), 狼人 lòhngyàhn (werewolf)

name: Wishiwashi
english: Wishiwashi may be a combination of wishy-washy, describing the weak state of its Solo Form; wash, in reference to its Water type; and 鰯 iwashi (Japanese for sardine).
japanese: From 弱い yowai (weak) or 弱々しい yowayowashii (frail) and 鰯 iwashi (sardine)
korean: From 약 (弱) yak (weakness) and 정어리 jeong-eori (sardine)
chineseMandarin: From 弱 ruò (weak) and 沙丁魚 / 沙丁鱼 shādīngyú (sardine)
chineseCantonese: From 弱 ruò (weak) and 沙甸魚 sādihnyùh (sardine)

name: Mareanie
english: Mareanie may be a combination of marine and meanie.
japanese: From 酷い hidoi (cruel) and 海星 hitode (sea star)
german: From garstig (nasty) and stella marina (Latin for "sea star")
korean: From 심하다 simhada (severe) and 불가사리 bulgasari (sea star)
chineseMandarin: From 好壞 / 好坏 hǎohuài (very bad) and 海星 hǎixīng (sea star)
chineseCantonese: From 好壞 hóuwaaih (very bad) and 海星 hóisīng (sea star)

name: Toxapex
english: Toxapex may be a combination of toxic and apex (as in "apex predator").
japanese: From ど酷い dohidoi (very cruel) and 海星 hitode (sea star)
german: From aggressiv (nasty), groß (big), and stella marina (Latin for "sea star")
korean: From 더 deo (more), 심하다 simhada (severe), and 불가사리 bulgasari (sea star)
chineseMandarin: From 超壞 / 超坏 chāohuài (super bad) and 海星 hǎixīng (sea star)
chineseCantonese: From 超壞 chīuwaaih (super bad) and 海星 hóisīng (sea star)

name: Mudbray
english: Mudbray may be a combination of mud and bray (cry of a donkey).
japanese: From 泥 doro (mud), 驢馬 roba (donkey), 輓馬 banba (draft horse), and 子 ko (young animal)
korean: From mud, 당나귀 dangnagwi (donkey), and 아기 agi (baby).
chineseMandarin: From 泥 ní (mud), 驢子 lǘzi (donkey), and 仔 zǎi (young animal)
chineseCantonese: From 泥 nàih (mud), 驢子 lèuihjí (donkey), and 仔 jái (young animal)

name: Mudsdale
english: Mudsdale may be a combination of mud and Clydesdale.
japanese: From 輓馬 banba (draft horse) and 泥 doro (mud)
french: From bourrique (donkey), bourrin (slang term for a donkey, a horse or someone brutal), and boue (mud)
korean: From 만마 (輓馬) manma (draft horse) and mud
chineseMandarin: From 重 zhòng (heavy), 泥 ní (mud), and 挽馬 / 挽马 wǎnmǎ (draft horse)
chineseCantonese: From 重 chúhng (heavy), 泥 nàih (mud), and 挽馬 wáahnmáh (draft horse)

name: Dewpider
english: Dewpider may be a combination of dew and spider, or refer to dewdrop spiders.
japanese: From 滴 shizuku (drop, of water or other liquids), 蜘蛛 kumo (spider), and 水蜘蛛 mizugumo (diving bell spider)
korean: From 물 mul (water) and 거미 geomi (spider) or 물거미 mulgeomi (diving bell spider)
chineseMandarin: From 滴 dī (drop) and 蜘蛛 zhīzhū (spider)
chineseCantonese: From 滴 dīk (drop) and 蜘蛛 jījyū (spider)

name: Araquanid
english: Araquanid may be a combination of arachnid and aqua.
japanese: From 鬼蜘蛛 onigumo (Araneus ventricosus), 鬼 oni (demon), 滴 shizuku (drop, of water or other liquids), 水蜘蛛 mizugumo (diving bell spider), 蜘蛛 kumo (spider), and Shizukumo (Dewpider)
korean: From 도깨비 dokkaebi, 물 mul (water), 거미 geomi (spider), and 물거미 mulgeomi (diving bell spider)
chineseMandarin: From 滴 dī (drop), 蜘蛛 zhīzhū (spider), and 霸 bà (tyrant)
chineseCantonese: From 滴 dīk (drop), 蜘蛛 jījyū (spider), and 霸 bà (tyrant)

name: Fomantis
english: Fomantis may be a combination of faux (French for both false and scythe) and mantis.
japanese: From 仮 kari (pseudo-), 刈 kari (prune), and 螳螂 kamakiri (praying mantis)
korean: From 가짜 gajja (fake) and 랑 (螂) rang (praying mantis)
chineseMandarin: From 偽 / 伪 wèi / wěi (fake), 螳螂 tángláng (praying mantis), and 草 cǎo (grass)
chineseCantonese: From 偽 ngaih (fake), 螳螂 tòhnglòhng (praying mantis), and 草 chóu (grass)

name: Lurantis
english: Lurantis may be a combination of lure, allure, fleur (French for "flower"), and mantis.
japanese: From 蘭 ran (orchid) and a corruption of mantis
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 蘭花 / 兰花 lánhuā (orchid) and 螳螂 tángláng (praying mantis) or 蘭花螳螂 / 兰花螳螂 lánhuā tángláng (orchid mantis)
chineseCantonese: From 蘭花 làahnfā (orchid) and 螳螂 tòhnglòhng (praying mantis) or 蘭花螳螂 làahnfā tòhnglòhng (orchid mantis)

name: Morelull
english: Morelull may be a combination of morel and lull.
japanese: From 寝 ne (sleep) and mushroom
french: From spore and dodo (childish way of saying sleep)
german: From Bubu (childish way of saying sleep) and fungus
korean: From 잠 jam (sleep) and mushroom
chineseMandarin: From 睡 shuì (to sleep) and 蘑菇 mógū (mushroom)
chineseCantonese: From 睡 seuih (to sleep) and 蘑菇 mòhgū (mushroom)

name: Shiinotic
english: Shiinotic may be a combination of shiitake, shine, and hypnotic.
japanese: From mushroom and lampshade
french: From lampe (lamp), champignon (mushroom), and lumignon (small light)
german: From Lampe (lamp), Lamelle (lamella, mushroom gill), and lux (Latin for "light")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 燈罩 / 灯罩 dēngzhào (lampshade), 夜 yè (night), and 蘑菇 mógū (mushroom)
chineseCantonese: From 燈罩 dāngjaau (lampshade), 夜 yeh (night), and 蘑菇 mòhgū (mushroom)

name: Salandit
english: Salandit may be a combination of salamander and bandit.
japanese: From 夜盗 yatō (burglar) and 井守 imori (newt)
korean: From 夜盜 (야도) yado (burglar) and 도롱뇽 dorongnyong (salamander)
chineseMandarin: From 夜盜 / 夜盗 yèdào (burglar), 火 huǒ (fire), and 火蜥蜴 huǒxīyì (salamander)
chineseCantonese: From 夜盜 yehdouh (burglar), 火 fó (fire), and 火蜥蜴 fósīkyihk (salamander)

name: Salazzle
english: Salazzle may be a combination of salamander and dazzle or sizzle.
japanese: From 炎 en (flame) or 艶 en (bewitching) and newt
korean: From 염 (炎) yeom (flame) or 염 (艷) yeom (bewitching) and newt
chineseMandarin: From 焰 yàn (flame), 艷后 yànhòu (bewitching queen), and 火蜥蜴 huǒxīyì (salamander)
chineseCantonese: From 焰 yihm (flame), 艷后 yihmhau (bewitching queen), and 火蜥蜴 fósīkyihk (salamander)

name: Stufful
english: Stufful may be derived from stuffed animal or a combination of stuff and full. It may also incorporate scuffle, for its aggressive nature and propensity to fight.
japanese: From ぬいぐるみ nuigurumi (stuffed animal) and 子熊 koguma (bear cub)
french: From nounours (teddy bear) and ourson (bear cub)
german: From Velours (velour), ursus (Latin for "bear"), and -i (diminutive suffix)
korean: From 포 (布) po (cloth), 포근 pogeun (snug), and 곰 gom (bear)
chineseMandarin: From 童 tóng (child), 玩偶 wán'ǒu (stuffed animal), and 熊 xióng (bear)
chineseCantonese: From 童 tùhng (child), 玩偶 wuhnngáu (stuffed animal), and 熊 hùhng (bear)

name: Bewear
english: Bewear may be a combination of beware, wear, and bear.
japanese: From 着てる kiteru (wearing), 着ぐるみ kigurumi (costume) and 熊 kuma (bear)
french: From chelou (verlan for shady) and ours (bear)
korean: From 입은 ibeun (wearing) and 곰 gom (bear)
chineseMandarin: From 穿着 / 穿着 chuānzhuó (wear) and 熊 xióng (bear)
chineseCantonese: From 穿着 chyūnjeuhk (wear) and 熊 hùhng (bear)

name: Bounsweet
english: Bounsweet may be a combination of bounce and sweet.
japanese: From 甘い amai (sweet) and 果実 kajitsu (fruit)
korean: From 달콤 dalkom (sweet) and 아기 agi (baby)
chineseMandarin: From 甜 tián (sweet) and 山竹 shānzhú (mangosteen)
chineseCantonese: From 甜 tìhm (sweet) and 山竹 sāanjūk (mangosteen)

name: Steenee
english: Steenee may be a combination of mangosteen and teeny or teenager. It may also incorporate the plant-based sweetener stevia.
japanese: From 甘い amai (sweet) and 舞子 maiko (dancing girl)
french: From sucre candi (candy sugar), coquine (naughty or flirty) and candide (innocent or naive)
korean: From 달콤 dalkom (sweet), 무녀 (舞女) munyeo (dancing girl), and ballerina
chineseMandarin: From 甜 tián (sweet), 舞女 wǔnǚ (dancing girl), and 妮 ní / nī (girl)
chineseCantonese: From 甜 tìhm (sweet), 舞女 móuhnéuih (dancing girl), and 妮 nèih (girl)

name: Tsareena
english: Tsareena may be a combination of tsarina (a Russian female monarch) and mangosteen. It may also incorporate queen.
japanese: From 甘い amai (sweet) and 女王 joō (queen)
korean: From 달콤 dalkom (sweet) and queen
chineseMandarin: From 甜 tián (sweet), 冷艷 / 冷艳 lěngyàn (cool and elegant), 美麗 / 美丽 měilì (beauty), and 后 hòu (queen)
chineseCantonese: From 甜 tìhm (sweet), 冷艷 láahngyihm (cool and elegant), 美麗 / 美丽 méihlaih (beauty), and 后 hauh (queen)

name: Comfey
english: Comfey may be a combination of comfy, comfort, comfrey, fey, and lei.
japanese: From cure, cute, 輪 wa (ring), and flower
korean: From cure and ring
chineseMandarin: From 花環 / 花环 huāhuán (garland) and 療法 liáofǎ (therapy)
chineseCantonese: From 花環 fāwàahn (garland) and 療法 lìuhfaat (therapy)

name: Oranguru
english: Oranguru may be a combination of orangutan and guru.
japanese: From やれ yare (do it) and オランウータン oran'ūtan (orangutan)
korean: From 하라 Hara (do it) and 오랑우탄 orang-utan (orangutan)
chineseMandarin: From 智慧 zhìhuì (wisdom), 指揮 / 指挥 zhǐhuī (to command), 智多星 zhìduōxīng (mastermind), and 猩猩 xīngxīng (orangutan)
chineseCantonese: From 智慧 jiwaih (wisdom), 指揮 jífāi (to command),, 智多星 jidōsīng (mastermind), and 猩猩 sīngsīng (orangutan)

name: Passimian
english: Passimian may be a combination of pass and simian. It may also be a play on prosimian.
japanese: From 投げつける nagetsukeru (to throw) and 猿 saru (monkey)
korean: From 내던지기 naedeonjigi (to throw) and 원숭이 wonsung-i (monkey)
chineseMandarin: From 投擲 / 投掷 tóuzhí / tóuzhì (to throw) and 猴 hóu (monkey)
chineseCantonese: From 投擲 tàuhjaahk (to throw) and 猴 hàuh (monkey)

name: Wimpod
english: Wimpod may be a combination of wimp and the taxonomic term pod (foot), such as in "isopod".
japanese: From 小 ko (small), 足 soku (feet) or 姑息 kosoku (cowardly; underhanded) and 虫 mushi (bug)
french: From Sauve qui peut ! (save yourself if you can) and pou (lice)
german: From Reißaus nehmen (run away) and Laus (louse)
korean: From 꼬마 kkoma (little kid), 꼬시다 kkosida (tempt, coax), and 벌레 beolle (bug)
chineseMandarin: From 膽小 / 胆小 dǎnxiǎo (cowardly) and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug)
chineseCantonese: From 膽小 dáamsíu (cowardly) and 蟲 chùhng (bug)

name: Golisopod
english: Golisopod may be a combination of Goliath and isopod.
japanese: From 大王具足虫 daiō-gusokumushi (giant isopod), 具足 gusoku (fully equipped), and 武者 musha (warrior)
german: From tectus (Latin for "protected" and "defended") and Assel (isopod)
korean: From 갑주 (甲冑) gapju (armor) and 무사 (武者) musa (warrior)
chineseMandarin: From 具甲 jùjiǎ (armor) and 武者 wǔzhě (warrior)
chineseCantonese: From 具甲 geuihgaap (armor) and 武者 móuhjé (warrior)

name: Sandygast
english: Sandygast may be a combination of sandy and ghast (evil spirit).
japanese: From 砂場 sunaba (sandbox) or 砂 suna (sand), bar, and いないいないばあ inai-inai-baa (peekaboo)
french: From bac à sable (sandbox) and bouh (boo)
korean: From 모래 morae (sand), 까꿍 kkakkung (peekaboo), and 궁 (宮) gung (palace)
chineseMandarin: From 沙丘 shāqiū (sand dune), 娃 wá (child), and 哇 wa (interjection indicating surprise or shock)
chineseCantonese: From 沙丘 sāyāu (sand dune), 娃 wā (child), and 哇 wā (interjection indicating surprise or shock)

name: Palossand
english: Palossand may be a combination of palace, loss, and sand, as well as a pun on pile of sand. It could also derive from pala (Spanish for "shovel") or involve colossal.
japanese: From 城ですな shiro desu na (that's a castle, huh), death, and 砂 suna (sand)
french: From trépas (death), sable (sand), and très passable (good enough)
german: From colosseum or colossal and Sand
korean: From 모래성이당 moraeseong-idang (that's a sand castle)
chineseMandarin: From 吞噬 tūnshì (to gobble), 沙堡 shābǎo (sand castle), 爺 / 爷 yé (elder man), and 是沙堡耶 Shì shābǎo yé (It's a sand castle!)
chineseCantonese: From 吞噬 tānsaih (to gobble), 沙堡 sābóu (sand castle), and 爺 yèh (elder man)

name: Pyukumuku
english: Pyukumuku may be a combination of puke, cucumber, and mucus. It may also involve the Hawaiian word pūʻukuʻuku (tiny, small).
japanese: From 海鼠 namako (sea cucumber) and 拳 kobushi (fist)
french: From concombre de mer (sea cucumber) and baffe (smack)
korean: From 해삼 (海蔘) haesam (sea cucumber) and 무기 (武器) mugi (weapon)
chineseMandarin: From 拳 quán (fist) and 海參 / 海参 hǎishēn (sea cucumber)
chineseCantonese: From 拳 kyùhn (fist) and 海參 hóisām (sea cucumber)

name: Type: Null
english: Type: Null is literally type and null (nothing).
japanese: From type and null
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 屬性 / 属性 shǔxìng (type) and 空 kōng (empty)
chineseCantonese: From 屬性 suhksing (type) and 空 hūng (empty)

name: Silvally
english: Silvally may be a combination of silver and ally.
japanese: From silver and buddy
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 銀 yín (silver), 伴 bàn (partner), 戰鬥 zhàndòu (fight), and 獸 shòu (beast)
chineseCantonese: From 銀 ngàhn (silver), 伴 buhn (partner), 戰鬥 jindau (fight), and 獸 sau (beast)

name: Minior
english: Minior may be derived from meteor. It may also involve any mixture of the words mini, minor, junior, armor, ore, and core.
japanese: From meteor and nano
french: Same as Japanese name; may also involve noyau
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (small) and 隕星 yǔnxīng (meteorite)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (small) and 隕星 wáhnsīng (meteorite)

name: Komala
english: Komala may be a combination of coma and koala.
japanese: From 根っ子 nekko (root; tree stump), 寝 ne (sleep), 子 ko (young animal), and koala
french: From dodo (childish way of saying sleep) and koala
german: From koala and La-Le-Lu (a German lullaby)
korean: From 잠 jam (sleep) and koala
chineseMandarin: From 樹 shù (tree), 無尾熊 wúwěixióng and 树袋熊 shùdàixióng (koala), and 枕頭 / 枕头 zhěntou (pillow)
chineseCantonese: From 樹 syuh (tree), 樹熊 syuhhùhng (koala), and 枕頭 jámtàuh (pillow)

name: Turtonator
english: Turtonator may be a combination of turtle and detonator.
japanese: From 爆発 bakuhatsu (explosion) and 亀 kame (turtle)
korean: From 폭 (爆) pok (explode) and 거북 geobuk (turtle)
chineseMandarin: From 爆炸 bàozhà (explosion), 火焰 huǒyàn (flame), 龜 / 龟 guī (turtle), and 獸 / 兽 shòu (beast)
chineseCantonese: From 爆炸 baauja (explosion), 火焰 fóyihm (flame), 龜 gwāi (turtle), and 獸 sau (beast)

name: Togedemaru
english: Togedemaru may be a combination of 棘 toge (thorn, spike) or 棘鼠 togenezumi (Ryūkyū spiny rats), 電気 denki (electricity), and 丸 maru (round), as well as a play on 棘で丸 toge de maru ("spiny and round").
japanese: From 棘 toge (thorn, spine) or 棘鼠 togenezumi (Ryūkyū spiny rats), 電気 denki (electricity), and 丸 maru (round), as well as a play on 棘で丸 toge de maru (spiny and round)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Mimikyu
english: Mimikyu and Mimikkyu may be derived from mimic and きゅうきゅう kyūkyū (onomatopoeia for squeaking, similar to Pikachu). It may also involve a corruption of 迷宮 meikyuu (mystery).
japanese: From 迷宮 meikyuu (mystery), mimic and きゅうきゅう kyūkyū (onomatopoeia for squeaking)
korean: From 따라하다 ttarahada (imitate; mimic) and 큐 kyu (adapted from the japanese kyūkyū or meikyuu)
chineseMandarin: From 謎 / 谜 mí (enigma), 模擬 / 模拟 mónǐ (imitate), and Q (adapted from the japanese kyūkyū or meikyuu)
chineseCantonese: From 謎 màih (enigma), 模擬 mòuhyíh (imitate), and Q (adapted from the japanese kyūkyū or meikyuu)

name: Bruxish
english: Bruxish may be a combination of bruxism and fish.
japanese: From 歯 ha (tooth), カワハギ kawahagi (filefish), ぎっしり gisshiri (densely packed), and 歯軋り hagishiri (bruxism)
french: From dent (tooth), crisse (gnash), or a pun on dentifrice (toothpaste)
korean: From 쥐치 jwichi (filefish), 치 (齒) chi (tooth) and 갈기 galgi (grind)
chineseMandarin: From 磨牙 móyá (bruxism), 彩 cǎi (streaks of color), 皮 pí (skin), and 魚 / 鱼 yú (fish)
chineseCantonese: From 磨牙 mòhngàh (bruxism), 彩 chói (streaks of color), 皮 pèi (skin), and 魚 yùh (fish)

name: Drampa
english: Drampa may be a combination of dragon and grampa (a variation on grandpa).
japanese: From 爺 jijī (informal term for old man) and 龍 / 龙 lóng (Chinese for "dragon")
french: From dragon and aïeul (grandfather; ancestor; old man)
german: From Senior and 神龍 / 神龙 shénlóng (Chinese for "divine dragon")
korean: From 할아버지 harabeoji (grandfather) and 龍 / 龙 lóng (Chinese for "dragon")
chineseMandarin: From 老翁 lǎowēng (old man) and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From 老翁 lóuhyūng (old man) and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Dhelmise
english: Dhelmise may be a combination of demise and helm (steering mechanism of a ship).
japanese: From 祟り tatari (cursed) and 舵輪 darin (rudder wheel)
german: From mors (Latin for "death"), modrig (moldy), and Ruder (rudder)
korean: From 타륜 (舵輪) taryun (rudder wheel)
chineseMandarin: From 破 pò (broken) and 舵輪 / 舵轮 duòlún (rudder wheel)
chineseCantonese: From 破 po (broken) and 舵輪 tòhlèuhn (rudder wheel)

name: Jangmo-o
english: Jangmo-o may derive from jangling and moʻo (Hawaiian for "lizard" or "dragon").
japanese: From ジャラジャラ jarajara (onomatopoetic sound for jingling), dracō (Latin for "dragon"), and 子 ko (young animal)
korean: From 짜랑 jjarang (onomatopoetic sound for jingling) and 꼬마 kkoma (little kid)
chineseMandarin: From 心 xīn (heart), 鱗 / 鳞 lín (scale), and 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 心 sām (heart), 鱗 lèuhn (scale), and 寶寶 bóubóu (baby)

name: Hakamo-o
english: Hakamo-o may be a combination of haka (a type of war dance present across various Polynesian cultures that involves vigorous movements and foot stamping) and moʻo (Hawaiian for "lizard" or "dragon").
japanese: From ジャラジャラ jarajara (onomatopoetic sound for jingling) and dragon
german: From medius (Latin for "middle"), Drache (dragon), and Rassel (rattle)

chineseCantonese: From 鱗甲 lèuhngaap (scale armor) and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Kommo-o
english: Kommo-o may be a combination of commotion (a period of noisy activity) and moʻo (Hawaiian for "lizard" or "dragon"). It may also incorporate combat, commander, and possibly Komodo dragon.

chineseCantonese: From 杖 jeuhng (staff), 尾 méih (tail), 鱗甲 lèuhngaap (scale armor), and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Tapu Koko
english: Tapu Koko may be a combination of the Polynesian word tapu (holy, sacred; forbidden; taboo) and kokō (Hawaiian onomatopoeia for a rooster's crowing), where the former is also the etymology of the word "taboo" in English.
japanese: From the Hawaiian word kapu and コケコッコー kokekokkō (cock-a-doodle-doo)
german: From the Hawaiian word kapu and kikeriki (cock-a-doodle-doo)
korean: From the Hawaiian word kapu and 꼬끼오 kkokki'o (cock-a-doodle-doo)

chineseCantonese: From the Mandarin-based transcription of its Japanese name and 鳴 mìhng (cry of an animal) with the latter character containing 鳥 níuh (bird)

name: Tapu Lele
english: Tapu Lele may be a combination of the Polynesian word tapu (holy, sacred; forbidden; taboo) and pulelehua (Hawaiian for "butterfly"), where the former is also the etymology of the word "taboo" in English.

french: From totem, tiki, and piscis (Latin for "fish")

name: Nihilego
english: Nihilego may be a combination of nihil (Latin for "indefinite nothing") and ego (Latin for "I"), which together roughly translates to "I am nothing" or "I have nothing". Ego may also refer to the part of the psychic apparatus that governs rational decision-making, and together with nihil reflects how the creature may have no ego, and only have an id (the survival and instinctual part of the psyche). The former may reflect its victims' lack of will outside their focus on Nihilego, while the latter may represent Nihilego's role in dominating the desires of its victims.
japanese: From 虚ろ utsuro (void), void, id, and possibly the suffix -oid (meaning "of similar form")
german: From ἀν- an- (ancient Greek prefix indicating "not" or "without") and ego
korean: From 텅빈 teongbin (hollow) and id
chineseMandarin: From 虛無 / 虚无 xūwú (void), 吾 wú (archaic form of "I"), and a partial transcription of its Japanese name or possibly 佛洛伊德 Fóluòyīdé / 弗洛伊德 Fúluòyīdé (Sigmund Freud, the founder of psychoanalysis who conceptualized the id, ego and superego)
chineseCantonese: From 虛無 hēuimòuh (void), 吾 ngh (archaic form of "I"), and possibly 佛洛伊德 Fahtlokyīdāk (Sigmund Freud)

name: Buzzwole

korean: From massive and 붕 boong (buzz)
chineseMandarin: From 爆 bào (explosive), 肌 jī (muscle), and 蚊 wén (mosquito)
chineseCantonese: From 爆 baau (explosive), 肌 gēi (muscle), and 蚊 mān (mosquito)

name: Pheromosa

korean: From pheromone and cockroach

name: Kartana

japanese: From 紙 kami (paper), 神 kami (deity), and 剣 tsurugi (sword)

The letter Z may symbolize an ending, as it is the final letter of the Latin alphabet, or may reference Z-Moves. It may also involve Project Ozma, an experiment conducted to search for extraterrestrial life.

korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 閃焰 / 闪焰 shǎnyàn (flare) and 王牌 wángpái (ace)
chineseCantonese: From 閃焰 símyihm (flare) and 王牌 wòhngpáai (ace)

name: Sobble
english: Sobble may be a combination of sob and bubble or dribble.
japanese: From メソメソ mesomeso (sobbing) and chameleon
korean: From 울먹이다 ulmeogida (close to tears)
chineseMandarin: From 淚眼 / 泪眼 lèiyǎn (tearful eyes) and 蜥蜴 xīyì (lizard)
chineseCantonese: From 淚眼 / 泪眼 leuih'ngáahn (tearful eyes) and 蜥蜴 sīkyihk (lizard)

name: Drizzile
english: Drizzile may be a combination of drizzle and reptile.
japanese: From じめじめ jimejime (damp, humid, clammy) and chameleon
french: From arroser (to water, sprinkle, spray) and lézard (lizard)
korean: From 눅눅하다 nungnukhada (damp, humid, soggy) and chameleon
chineseMandarin: From 變色龍 / 变色龙 biànsèlóng (chameleon), 澀 / 涩 sè (astringent), and 蜥蜴 xīyì (lizard)
chineseCantonese: From 變色龍 binsīklùhng (chameleon), 澀 saap (astringent), and 蜥蜴 sīkyihk (lizard)

name: Inteleon
english: Inteleon and Intereon may be a combination of intel (clipping of intelligence, as in secret information often obtained by spies) or intellect and chameleon.
japanese: From intelligence or intellect and chameleon
french: From lézard (lizard) and argus (archaic word for "watcher" and "spy" that is named after the mythological Argus)
german: From its Japanese and English name
korean: From intelligence and chameleon
chineseMandarin: From 千面 qiānmiàn (literally "thousand faces"; figurative chameleon) and 避役 bìyì (chameleon)
chineseCantonese: From 千面 chīnmihn (literally "thousand faces"; figurative chameleon) and 避役 beihyihk (chameleon)

name: Skwovet
english: Skwovet may be a combination of squirrel and covet.
japanese: From 欲しがる hoshigaru (to desire) and 栗鼠 risu (squirrel)
french: From ronger (to gnaw) or rongeur (rodent) and gourmand
german: From raffgierig (greedy) or raffen (to snatch) and squirrel
korean: From 탐 (貪) tam (greedy) and a partial transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 貪心 / 贪心 tānxīn (greedy) and 栗鼠 lìshǔ (chipmunk, squirrel)
chineseCantonese: From 貪心 tāamsām (greedy) and 栗鼠 leuhtsyú (chipmunk, squirrel)

name: Greedent
english: Greedent may be a combination of greed and rodent.
japanese: From 欲張り yokubari (greed), 栗鼠 risu (squirrel), and avarice
french: From ronger (to gnaw) or rongeur (rodent) and grigou (scrooge)
german: From Schlaraffenland (land of plenty in medieval folklore), raffen (to snatch), and squirrel
korean: From 욕심 (欲心) yoksim (greed) and a partial transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 藏 cáng (to store), 飽 / 饱 bǎo (to eat one's fill) and 栗鼠 lìshǔ (chipmunk, squirrel)
chineseCantonese: From 藏 chòhng (to store), 飽 báau (to eat one's fill) and 栗鼠 leuhtsyú (chipmunk, squirrel)

name: Rookidee
english: Rookidee may be a combination of rook, rookie, kid, and chickadee.
japanese: From 子 ko (child) and 小雀 kogara (willow tit) or 烏 karasu (crow)
german: From micro-, Meise (chickadee, tit), and crow
korean: From 파랑 parang (blue) and 꼬마 kkoma (little kid)
chineseMandarin: From 稚 zhì (young) and 山雀 shānquè (tit)
chineseCantonese: From 稚 jih (young) and 山雀 sāanjéuk (tit)

name: Corvisquire
english: Corvisquire may be a combination of corvid, squire and esquire.
japanese: From 青 ao (blue), 青雀 aogara (Eurasian blue tit), and 烏 karasu (crow, raven)
french: From bleu (blue), bleusaille (new recruit), and corneille (crow)
korean: From 파랑 parang (blue) and crow
chineseMandarin: From 藍 / 蓝 lán (blue) and 鴉 / 鸦 yā (crow)
chineseCantonese: From 藍 làahm (blue) and 鴉 ā (crow)

name: Corviknight
english: Corviknight may be a combination of corvid and knight.
japanese: From armor, ガアガア gāgā (sound of squawking), and 鴉 a (crow, raven)
korean: From armor, 까마귀 kkamagwi (crow, raven), 오 (烏) o (crow, raven), and 아 (鴉) a (crow, raven)
chineseMandarin: From 鋼 / 钢 gāng (steel), 鎧 / 铠 kǎi (armor), and 鴉 / 鸦 yā (crow, raven)
chineseCantonese: From 鋼 gōnghói (steel), 鎧 hói (armor) and 鴉 ā (crow, raven)

name: Blipbug
english: Blipbug may be a combination of blip (a small dot on a radar; the sound of a radar finding a target) and bug.
japanese: From 察知 satchi (sense), search, and 虫 mushi (bug)
korean: From 두루 duru (throughout), 찰지 (察知) chalji (sense), and 벌레 beollae (bug)
chineseMandarin: From 索 suǒ (search), 偵 / 侦 zhēn (detect), and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug)
chineseCantonese: From 索 sok (search), 偵 jīng (detect), and 蟲 chùhng (bug)

name: Dottler
english: Dottler may be a combination of dot and Doppler radar.
japanese: From radome and 天道虫 tentōmushi (ladybug)
korean: From 레이돔 radome and 벌레 beollae (bug)
chineseMandarin: From 天線罩 / 天线罩 tiānxiànzhào (radome) and 天道虫 tentōmushi (Japanese for ladybug)
chineseCantonese: From 天線罩 tīnsinjaau (radome) and 天道虫 tentōmushi (Japanese for ladybug)

name: Orbeetle
english: Orbeetle may be a combination of orb, orbit, orbital, and lady beetle.
japanese: From eol (Irish for knowledge), Io and orb
french: From ἄστρον ástron (Ancient Greek for "celestial body"), astronef (spacecraft) and coccinelle (lady beetle)
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Transcription of its Japanese name

name: Nickit
english: Nickit may be a combination of nick (slang for steal) and kit (young fox). It may also be a play on nick it.
japanese: From くすねる kusuneru (to pilfer) and 狐 kitsune (fox)
korean: From 훔치다 humchida (to steal) and 여우 yeou (fox)
chineseMandarin: From 偷 tōu (to steal), 兒 / 儿 ér (child), and 狐 hú (fox); From 狡猾 jiǎohuá (crafty), 小 xiǎo (little), and 狐 hú (fox)
chineseCantonese: From 偷 tāu (to steal), 兒 yìh (child), and 狐 wùh (fox)

name: Thievul
english: Thievul may be a combination of thieve/thief, evil, and vulpine (of or pertaining to foxes; foxlike).
japanese: From fox and sly
german: From Gauner (crook, sly person) and Fuchs (fox)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 狐 hú (fox), 大 dà (great), and 大盜 dàdào (thief); From 狡猾 jiǎohuá (crafty), 大 dà (great), and 狐 hú (fox)
chineseCantonese: From 狐 wùh (fox), 大 daaih (great), and 大盜 daaihdouh (thief)

name: Gossifleur
english: Gossifleur may be a combination of Gossypium (the cotton plant genus) and fleur (French for "flower"). It may also involve gossamer (light, delicate, silky).
japanese: From 姫 hime (princess; petite), 綿花 menka (raw cotton), and 花 ka (flower)
german: From cotton and tiny or mini
korean: From 꼬마 kkoma (little kid), 꽃 kkot (flower), and 목화 (木花) mokhwa (cotton)
chineseMandarin: From 幼 yòu (young), 棉 mián (cotton), and 幼麵麵 iùmīmī (Hokkien for delicate and tender)
chineseCantonese: From 幼 yau (young), 棉 mìhn (cotton), and 幼麵麵 iùmīmī (Hokkien for delicate and tender)

name: Eldegoss
english: Eldegoss may be a combination of elder and Gossypium (the cotton plant genus) or gossamer (something light or delicate). It could also originate from edelweiss, a flower with a furry coat.
japanese: From 綿 wata (cotton) and 白髪 shiraga (white hair)
korean: From 백 (白) baek (white), 솜 som (cotton), and 목화 (木花) mokhwa (cotton)
chineseMandarin: From 白蓬蓬 báipéngpéng (white and puffy)
chineseCantonese: From 白蓬蓬 baahkpùhngpùhng (white and puffy)

name: Wooloo
english: Wooloo may be a combination of wool and loom. It may also be derived from the Japanese name.
japanese: From wool
french: From moumoute (wig; sheepskin), mou (soft), and mouton (sheep)
german: From Wolle (wool) and possibly tiny or Dolly (female sheep that was the first mammal to be cloned)
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 羊毛 yángmáo (wool), 辮 / 辫 biàn (braid), and 羊 yáng (sheep)
chineseCantonese: From 羊毛 yèuhngmòuh (wool), 辮 bīn (braid), and 羊 yèuhng (sheep)

name: Dubwool
english: Dubwool may be a combination of double and wool.
japanese: From 倍 bai (twice), wool, and ウールー Wooluu (Wooloo)
french: From moumoute (sheepskin), mou (soft), and mouflon (a species of wild sheep)
german: From zweimal (twice), Wolle (wool), Locke (curl), and Bock (ram; buck (a male sheep, goat, deer, etc.))
korean: From 배 (倍) bae (double), wool, and 우르 Woolu (Wooloo)
chineseMandarin: From 羊毛 yángmáo (wool), 角 jiǎo (horn), and 羊 yáng (sheep, goat)
chineseCantonese: From 羊毛 yèuhngmòuh (wool), 角 gok (horn), and 羊 yèuhng (sheep, goat)

name: Chewtle
english: Chewtle may be a combination of chew and turtle.
japanese: From 噛む kamu (to bite) and 亀 kame (turtle)
french: From χελώνη khelṓnē (Ancient Greek for "tortoise") and croc (fang)
german: From 亀 kame (Japanese for turtle) and Happen (bite)
korean: From 깨물다 kkaemulda (to bite) and 거북이 geobugi (turtle)
chineseMandarin: From 咬 yǎo (to bite) and 龜 / 龟 guī (turtle)
chineseCantonese: From 咬 ngáauh (to bite) and 龜 gwāi (turtle)

name: Drednaw
english: Drednaw may be a combination of dread, gnaw, and dreadnought (a type of warship).
japanese: From 齧り付く kajiritsuku (to bite) and 亀 kame (turtle)
french: From tortue alligator (alligator snapping turtle) and mord (bites)
german: From Kamm (comb), 亀 kame (Japanese for turtle), and malmen (grind teeth loudly)
korean: From 갉아먹다 galgameokda (to gnaw) and 거북이 geobugi (turtle)
chineseMandarin: From 暴 bào (violent), 噬 shì (bite), and 龜 / 龟 guī (turtle)
chineseCantonese: From 暴 bouh (violent), 噬 saih (bite), and 龜 gwāi (turtle)

name: Yamper
english: Yamper may be a combination of yap, ampere, and scamper.
japanese: From ワンワン wanwan (onomatopoeia for barking) and パチパチ pachipachi (onomatopoeia for crackling)
german: From Volt, Hundi (dog; informal form of Hund), and possibly Waldi (a popular name for dogs in Germany)
korean: From 멍멍 meongmeong (onomatopoeia for barking) and partial transliteration of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 來 / 来 lái (come), 電 / 电 diàn (electricity), and 汪汪 wāngwāng (onomatopoeia for barking)
chineseCantonese: From 來 lòih (come), 電 dihn (electricity), and 汪汪 wōngwōng (onomatopoeia for barking)

name: Boltund
english: Boltund may be a combination of bolt and Hund (German and Swedish for dog) or hound.
japanese: From pulse and ワンワン wanwan (onomatopoeia for barking)
french: From fulgur (Latin for "lightning, thunderbolt") and dog
korean: From pulse and 멍멍 meongmeong (onomatopoeia for barking)
chineseMandarin: From 追風逐電 / 追风逐电 zhuīfēng-zhúdiàn ((lit. to chase wind and pursue lightning) proceeding at a tremendous pace) and 犬 quǎn (dog)
chineseCantonese: From 追風逐電 jēuifūng-juhkdihn ((lit. to chase wind and pursue lightning) proceeding at a tremendous pace) and 犬 hyún (dog)

name: Rolycoly
english: Rolycoly may be a combination of roly-poly and coal. It may also be a pun on rolling coal.
japanese: From 炭 tan (coal) and どん don (bang)
french: From charbon (coal) and petit (small) or ちび chibi (Japanese for runt, pipsqueak)
german: From klonk (onomatopoeia of something hard being hit), Kohle (coal), and Brikett (briquet)
korean: From 탄 (炭) tan (coal) and 동 (童) dong (child)
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (small), 炭 tàn (coal), and 仔 zǐ (young)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (small), 炭 taan (coal), and 仔 jí (young)

name: Carkol
english: Carkol may be a combination of car, cart, carbon, and coal or charcoal.
japanese: From トロッコ torokko (minecart) and wagon
korean: From 탄차 (炭車) tancha (minecart) and wagon
chineseMandarin: From 大 dà (big), 炭 tàn (coal), and 礦車 / 矿车 kuàngchē (minecart)
chineseCantonese: From 大 daaih (big), 炭 taan (coal), and 礦車 kwongchē (minecart)

name: Coalossal
english: Coalossal may be a combination of coal and colossal.
japanese: From 石炭 sekitan (coal) and 炭山 tanzan (mountain coal mine)
german: From monte (Italian for "mountain"), carbo (Latin for "carbon"), and a pun of Monte Carlo
korean: From 석탄 (石炭) seoktan (coal) and 탄산 (炭山) tansan (mountain coal mine)
chineseMandarin: From 巨 jù (giant), 炭 tàn (coal), and 山 shān (mountain)
chineseCantonese: From 巨 geuih (giant), 炭 taan (coal), and 山 sāan (mountain)

name: Applin
english: Applin may be a combination of apple and in.
japanese: From 齧る kajiru (to nibble), 果実 kajitsu (fruit), and 虫 chū (bug, worm)
french: From ver (worm), pomme (apple), and a play on vert pomme
korean: From 과 (果) gwa (fruit) or 사과 (沙果) sagwa (apple), 와사삭 wasasak (onomatopoeia for crunching), and 벌레 beollae (bug)
chineseMandarin: From 啃 kěn (to nibble), 果 guǒ (fruit), and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug)
chineseCantonese: From 啃 háng (to nibble), 果 gwó (fruit), and 蟲 chùhng (bug)

name: Flapple
english: Flapple may be a combination of flap and apple.
japanese: From apple and 竜 ryū (dragon)
french: From pomme d'Api (lady apple) and dragon
korean: From apple and 룡 (龍) ryong (dragon)
chineseMandarin: From 蘋果 / 苹果 píngguǒ (apple), 裹 guǒ (to wrap up; parcel), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From 蘋果 pìhnggwó (apple), 裹 gwó (to wrap up; parcel), and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Appletun
english: Appletun may be derived from apple, Appleton (a toponym denoting a place where apples grow), ton (unit of weight, referencing its bulk), apple turnover, and under.
japanese: From tart, 怠い tarui (sluggish), たっぷり tappuri (onomatopoetic word for plenty), and apple
german: From schlapp (weary), Schlupfkuchen (a German apple pie/cake) and Apfel (apple)
korean: From 단 dan (sweet), 지루하다 jiruhada (to be boring), and apple
chineseMandarin: From 豐 fēng (abundant), 蜜 mì (nectar, sweet), 蜂蜜 fēngmì (honey), and 龍 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From 豐 fūng (abundant), 蜜 maht (nectar, sweet), 蜂蜜 fūngmaht (honey), and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Silicobra
english: Silicobra may be a combination of silicon (basic constituent of sand) and cobra. It may also incorporate silt.
japanese: From 砂 suna (sand) and 蛇 hebi (snake)
french: From dune and the genus Naja (true cobras)
korean: From 모래 morae (sand) and 뱀 baem (snake)
chineseMandarin: From 沙 shā (sand), 包 bāo (to wrap; pouch) , 沙包 shābāo (sandbag, punching bag), and 蛇 shé (snake)
chineseCantonese: From 沙 sā (sand), 包 bāau (to wrap; pouch) , 沙包 sābāau (sandbag, punching bag), and 蛇 sèh (snake)

name: Sandaconda
english: Sandaconda may be a combination of sand and anaconda.
japanese: From 沙 sa (sand) and 大蛇 daija (serpent)
korean: From 사 (沙) sa (sand), 사 (蛇) sa (serpent), and a partial transliteration of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 沙 shā (sand), 螺 luó (conch; spiral), and 蟒 mǎng (python)
chineseCantonese: From 沙 sā (sand), 螺 lòh (conch; spiral), and 蟒 móhng (python)

name: Cramorant
english: Cramorant may be a combination of cram and cormorant.
japanese: From ウッ u~ (sound of choking or gasping) and 鵜 u (cormorant)
french: From nigaud (dimwitted or small cormorant) and gosier (gullet)
german: From Gurgel (gullet), urks (sound of choking), and Vogel (bird)
korean: From 가마우지 gamauji (cormorant) and 우걱우걱 ugeogugeok (sound of munching)
chineseMandarin: From 鶘 / 鹕 hú (pelican), may also incorporate 咕 gū (sound of gulping) and 噦 / 哕 yuě (sound of retching)
chineseCantonese: From 鶘 wùh (pelican)

name: Arrokuda
english: Arrokuda may be a combination of arrow and barracuda.
japanese: From 刺し sashi (pricking) and 梭子魚 kamasu (barracuda)
german: From Pike (a weapon), pike (a type of fish), and Barrakuda (barracuda)
korean: From 찌르다 jjireuda (to prick) and 꼬치고기 kkochigogi (barracuda)
chineseMandarin: From 刺 cì (to prick) and 梭魚 / 梭鱼 suōyú (barracuda)
chineseCantonese: From 刺 chi (to prick) and 梭魚 sōyùh (barracuda)

name: Barraskewda
english: Barraskewda may be a combination of barracuda and skewer.
japanese: From 梭子魚 kamasu (barracuda) and jaw
french: From hasta (Latin for "spear, pike") and barracuda
korean: From 꼬치고기 kkochigogi (barracuda) and jaw
chineseMandarin: From 戽斗 hùdǒu (protruding lower jaw; bailing bucket), 尖 jiān (sharp), and 梭魚 / 梭鱼 suōyú (barracuda)
chineseCantonese: From 戽斗 fudáu (protruding lower jaw; bailing bucket), 尖 jīm (sharp), and 梭魚 sōyú (barracuda)

name: Toxel
english: Toxel may be a combination of toxic, toddle, cell, electric, and little.
japanese: From electric and poison
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 毒 dú (poison), 電音 / 电音 diànyīn (electronic music), and 嬰 / 婴 yīng (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 毒 duhk (poison), 電 dihn (electric), and 嬰 yīng (baby)

name: Toxtricity
english: Toxtricity may be a combination of toxic or toxicity and electricity.
japanese: From string and salamander
french: From salamandre (salamander), larsen, arsenic and sale (dirty)
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 顫 / 颤 zhàn / chàn (tremble; vibrate), 弦 xián (string), and 蠑螈 / 蝾螈 róngyuán (salamander)
chineseCantonese: From 顫 jin (tremble; vibrate), 弦 yìhn (string), and 蠑螈 wìhngyùhn (salamander)

name: Sizzlipede
english: Sizzlipede may be a combination of sizzle and millipede or centipede.
japanese: From 焼く yaku (to burn) and 蚰蜒 yasude (millipede) or 百足 mukade (centipede)
german: From θερμός thermós (Ancient Greek for "hot") and Chilopoda
korean: From 태우다 taeuda (to burn) and 지네 jine (centipede)
chineseMandarin: From 燒火 / 烧火 shāohuǒ (to make fire) and 蜈蚣 wúgōng (centipede)
chineseCantonese: From 燒火 sīufó (to make fire) and 蜈蚣 ǹgh-gūng (centipede)

name: Centiskorch
english: Centiskorch may be a combination of centipede and scorch. It may also incorporate centigrade, an alternative name for the Celsius temperature scale.
japanese: From 丸焼け maruyake (completely burned), 馬陸 yasude (millipede) or 百足 mukade (centipede), and ヤクデ Yakude (Sizzlipede)
korean: From 다 da (all), 태우다 tae-uda (to burn), and 지네 jine (centipede)
chineseMandarin: From 焚 fén (to burn), 焰 yàn (flame), and 蜈蚣 wúgōng (centipede)
chineseCantonese: From 焚 fàhn (to burn), 焰 yihm (flame), and 蜈蚣 ǹgh-gūng (centipede)

name: Clobbopus
english: Clobbopus may be a combination of clobber and octopus.
japanese: From 叩く tataku (to strike), 戦い tatakai (fight, battle), attack, 蛸 tako (octopus), and 駄々っ子 dadakko (spoiled child)
french: From poulpe (octopus) and paf (onomatopoeia for a strike)
korean: From 때리다 ttaerida (to hit) and 문어 mun-eo (octopus)
chineseMandarin: From 拳 quán (fist) and 蛸 xiāo (octopus)
chineseCantonese: From 拳 kyùhn (fist) and 蛸 sīu (octopus)

name: Grapploct
english: Grapploct may be a combination of grapple, octopus, and locked.
japanese: From 落とす otosu (to take someone down) and octopus
french: From kraken and possibly Kratos (personification of strength in Greek mythology)
korean: From K.O. and octopus
chineseMandarin: From 八爪魚 / 八爪鱼 bāzhuǎyú (octopus) and 武師 / 武师 wǔshī (martial artist)
chineseCantonese: From 八爪魚 baatjáauyú (octopus) and 武師 móuhsī (martial artist)

name: Sinistea
english: Sinistea may be a combination of sinister and tea.
japanese: From やばい yabai (dangerous; terrible) and 茶 cha (tea)
german: From fatal or fatalité (French for "fatality") and Tee (tea)
korean: From danger and 차 (茶) cha (tea)
chineseMandarin: From 來 / 来 lái (come), 悲 bēi (sorrow), 茶 chá (tea), and a pun of 來杯茶 / 来杯茶 lái bēi chá (have some tea)
chineseCantonese: From 來 lòih (come), 悲 bēi (sorrow), and 茶 chàh (tea)

name: Polteageist
english: Polteageist may be a combination of poltergeist and tea.
japanese: From pot, death, and ポットです potto desu ("It's a teapot")
german: From mors (Latin for "death"), tea, and Pott (pot)
korean: From pot and death
chineseMandarin: From 怖 bù (terror), 思 sī (thought), 壺 hú (teapot), 不死 bùsǐ (undead), and 不是壺 bùshì hú ("Not a teapot")
chineseCantonese: From 怖 bou (terror), 思 sī (thought), and 壺 wùh (teapot)

name: Hatenna
english: Hatenna may be a combination of hat and antenna.
japanese: From 身振り miburi (gesture) and brim
french: From bibi (small lady's hat) and chut (shush)
korean: From 몸짓 momjit (gesture) and brim
chineseMandarin: Transcription of its Japanese name. Contains 迷 mí (bewitch, charm)
chineseCantonese: Transcription of its Japanese name. Contains 迷 màih (bewitch, charm)

name: Hattrem
english: Hattrem may be a combination of hat and tremble.
japanese: From 手振り teburi (hand gesture) and brim
korean: From 손짓 sonjit (hand gesture) and brim
chineseMandarin: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Transcription of its Japanese name

name: Hatterene
english: Hatterene may be a combination of hatter and serene.
japanese: From brim and 無音 muon (silence)
german: From silentium (Latin for "silence"), Salem, brim, and Simsalabim (magic incantation)
korean: From brim and 무음 (無音) mueum (silence)
chineseMandarin: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Transcription of its Japanese name

name: Impidimp
english: Impidimp may be a combination of imp, impede or impediment, and impudent (rude and disrespectful). It may also involve dimpsey, British dialect referring to the time around dusk, or dimple, alluding to its large smile.
japanese: From ベロ bero (tongue) and ベロベロバァ beroberobā (peekaboo)
german: From bäh (sound of sticking out one's tongue mockingly) and Dämon (demon) or Monster
korean: From 메롱 merong (onomatopoetic word for tongue sticking out) and 까꿍 kkakkung (peekaboo)
chineseMandarin: From 搗蛋 / 捣蛋 dǎodàn (to be mischievous), 小 xiǎo (small), and 妖 yāo (demon)
chineseCantonese: From 搗蛋 dóudáan (to be mischievous), 小 síu (small), and 妖 yīu (demon)

name: Morgrem
english: Morgrem may be a combination of morbid or morgue and gremlin. It may also come from grem, an old English and old German word for "to anger" or "to enrage". It may also reference Morgan le Fay, an enchantress, sometimes described as a fairy, from Arthurian legend.
japanese: From 欺罔 gimō (deception), 毛 mō (hair, fur), and demon
french: From fourbe (tricky fellow), malin (shrewd), and gobelin (goblin) or gremlin
korean: From 속여 sog-yeo (deceive) and 모 (毛) mo (hair, fur) or demon
chineseMandarin: From 詐唬 / 诈唬 zhàhǔ (to bluff) and 魔 mó (demon)
chineseCantonese: From 詐唬 jafú (to bluff) and 魔 mō (demon)

name: Grimmsnarl
english: Grimmsnarl may be a combination of grim, grimace, grimoire (a type of spellbook), or Grimm; and snarl. Its name could also incorporate the words gnarly.
japanese: From ogre and ロン毛 ronge (long hair)
korean: From ogre, long, and 털 teol (hair, fur)
chineseMandarin: From 長毛 / 长毛 chángmáo (long hair), 巨 jù (giant), and 魔 mó (demon)
chineseCantonese: From 長毛 chèuhngmòuh (long hair), 巨 geuih (giant), and 魔 mō (demon)

name: Obstagoon
english: Obstagoon may be a combination of obstacle or obstruct, raccoon, and goon.
japanese: From 立ち塞ぐ tachifusagu (to obstruct) and 洗熊 araiguma (raccoon) or 穴熊 anaguma (badger)
korean: From 가로막다 garomakda (to obstruct, to intercept) and 너구리 neoguri (raccoon)
chineseMandarin: From 堵 dǔ (block, stop), 攔 / 拦 lán (obstruct, impede), and 浣熊 wǎnxióng / huànxióng (raccoon)
chineseCantonese: From 堵 dóu (block, stop), 攔 làahn (obstruct, impede), and 浣熊 wúhnhùhng (raccoon)

name: Perrserker
english: Perrserker may be a combination of purr, Persian, and berserker.
japanese: From ニャー nyā (meow), Viking, and king
french: From berserker and katt (Norwegian and Swedish for cat)
german: From mauzen (a description of the sound a cat makes) and Wikinger (Viking)
korean: From 나옹 Naong (Meowth) and Viking
chineseMandarin: From 喵 miāo (meow) and 頭目 / 头目 tóumù (chieftain)
chineseCantonese: From 喵 mīu (meow) and 頭目 tàuhmuhk (chieftain)

name: Cursola
english: Cursola may be a combination of curse and Corsola. It may be derive from the female real-life name, Ursula.
japanese: From サニーゴ Sunnygo (Corsola), Gorgon, and gone
korean: From 산호 (珊瑚) sanho (coral) and Gorgon
chineseMandarin: From 魔 mó (demon), 靈 / 灵 líng (spirit), and 珊瑚 shānhú (coral)
chineseCantonese: From 魔 mō (demon), 靈 lìhng (spirit), and 珊瑚 sāanwùh (coral)

name: Sirfetch'd
english: Sirfetch'd may be a combination of Sir and Farfetch'd.
japanese: From 葱 negi (spring onion), giga-, knight, and possibly a pun on 葱がないと negi ga nai to ("must have a spring onion")
french: From paladin, artichaut (artichoke), and Pas l'artichaut ("Not the artichoke")
korean: From 창 (槍) chang (lance), 파 pa (spring onion), and knight
chineseMandarin: From 蔥 / 葱 cōng (spring onion), 遊 / 游 yóu (wander), 兵 bīng (soldier), and a pun on 蔥油餅 / 葱油饼 cōngyóubǐng (scallion pancake)
chineseCantonese: From 蔥 chūng (spring onion), 遊 yàuh (wander), 兵 bīng (soldier), and a pun on 蔥油餅 chūngyàuhbéng (scallion pancake)

name: Mr. Rime
english: Mr. Rime may be derived from the abbreviation of Mister and rime (a type of frost).
japanese: From barrier and 凍る kōru (to freeze)
french: From Monsieur (Mister), glaçon (icicle), and claquette (tap dancing)
korean: From mime and 꽁꽁 kkongkkong (frozen hard)
chineseMandarin: From 踢踏舞 tītàwǔ (tap dance), 冰 bīng (ice), and 人偶 rén'ǒu (puppet)
chineseCantonese: From 踢踏舞 tekdaahpmóuh (tap dance), 冰 bīng (ice), and 人偶 yàhnngáuh (puppet)

name: Runerigus
english: Runerigus may be a combination of rune and egregious or Cofagrigus.
japanese: From death and 板 ban (slab)
french: From Tutankhamun and a pun of tout est écrit ("everything is written")
german: From Ogham, Echnatoll (Cofagrigus), and a pun of Och, na toll! ("Oh, great!" (ironic))
korean: From death and 판 (板) pan (slab)
chineseMandarin: From 死神 sǐshén (death god, Grim Reaper) and 板 bǎn (slab); From the transcription of Japanese name, 失 shī (lost) and 板 bǎn (slab)
chineseCantonese: From 死神 séisàhn (death god, Grim Reaper) and 板 báan (slab)

name: Milcery
english: Milcery may be a combination of milk and sorcery.
japanese: From 魔法 mahō (magic) and milk
korean: From 마법 mabeop (magic) and milk
chineseMandarin: From 小仙子 xiǎoxiānzi (fairy) and 鮮奶 / 鲜奶 xiānnǎi (fresh milk)
chineseCantonese: From 小仙子 síusīnjí (fairy) and 鮮奶 sīnnáaih (fresh milk)

name: Alcremie
english: Alcremie may be a combination of alchemy and cream, crème, or creamy.
japanese: From 魔法 mahō (magic) and ホイップ hoippu (whipped cream)
korean: From 마법 mabeop (magic) and whipping cream
chineseMandarin: From 糖霜 tángshuāng (icing), 鮮奶油 xiānnǎiyóu (fresh cream), and 仙女 xiānnǚ (fairy)
chineseCantonese: From 糖霜 tòhngsēung (icing), 鮮奶油 sīnnáaihyàuh (fresh cream), and 仙女 sīnnéuih (fairy)

name: Falinks
english: Falinks may be a combination of phalanx and links.
japanese: From 隊列 tairetsu (a rank or formation of troops)
french: From hexa- (prefix for six) and escadron (squadron)
korean: From 대열 (隊列) daeyeol (troop formation)
chineseMandarin: From 列陣 / 列阵 lièzhèn (battle formation) and 兵 bīng (soldier)
chineseCantonese: From 列陣 lihtjahn (battle formation) and 兵 bīng (soldier)

name: Pincurchin
english: Pincurchin may be a combination of pincushion and sea urchin.
japanese: From バチン bachin (onomatopoeia for crackling electricity) and 海胆 uni (sea urchin)
german: From Blitz (lightning), britzeln (buzzing sound), and Seeigel (sea urchin)
korean: From 찌르다 jjireuda (to pierce) and 성게 seongge (sea urchin)
chineseMandarin: From 啪嚓啪嚓 pācāpācā (crackling sound) and 海膽 / 海胆 hǎidǎn (sea urchin)
chineseCantonese: From 啪嚓啪嚓 pāakchaatpāakchaat (crackling sound) and 海膽 hóidáam (sea urchin)

name: Snom
english: Snom may be a combination of snow, worm, and nom (slang for eating).
japanese: From 雪 yuki (snow) and 食み hami (eating)
korean: From 눈 nun (snow) and 먹이 meog-i (feed)
chineseMandarin: From 雪 xuě (snow), 吞 tūn (to swallow), and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug)
chineseCantonese: From 雪 syut (snow), 吞 tān (to swallow), and 蟲 chùhng (bug)

name: Frosmoth
english: Frosmoth may be a combination of frost and moth.
japanese: From moth and snow
french: From belle (beautiful) and boule de neige (snowball)
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 雪 xuě (snow), 絨 róng (velvet), 蛾 é (moth), and 絨蛾 róng'é (flannel moth)
chineseCantonese: From 雪 syut (snow), 絨 yùhng (velvet), 蛾 ngòh (moth), and 絨蛾 yùhngngòh (flannel moth)

name: Stonjourner
english: Stonjourner may be a combination of stone and sojourner (a person who resides temporarily in a place).
japanese: From 石 ishi (stone), Stonehenge, and 変人 henjin (weird or eccentric person)
german: From human or humanoid and megalith or monolith
korean: From 돌 dol (stone), Stonehenge, and 인 in (man)
chineseMandarin: From 巨石 jùshí (megalith) and 丁 dīng (man)
chineseCantonese: From 巨石 geuihsehk (megalith) and 丁 dīng (man)

name: Eiscue
english: Eiscue may be a combination of Eis (German for "ice") and ice cube.
japanese: From 氷 kōri (ice) and 立方 rippō (cube)
french: From bec (beak) and bac à glaçon (ice cube tray)
korean: From 빙 (冰) bing (ice) and cube
chineseMandarin: From 冰 bīng (ice), 砌 qì (to lay bricks), and 企鵝 / 企鹅 qì'é / qǐ'é (penguin)
chineseCantonese: From 冰 bīng (ice), 砌 chai (to lay bricks), and 企鵝 kéihngòh (penguin)

name: Indeedee
english: Indeedee may be derived from indeed and the phrase, "Yes indeedy."
japanese: From yessir and ～さん -san (honorific title)
german: From servant and sehr wohl (well, quite)
korean: From yes, sir
chineseMandarin: From 愛 ài (fond of, inclined in doing), 管 guǎn (to manage), 侍者 shìzhě (attendant, servant), and a pun of 愛管事 ài guǎn shì (hands-on, meddling)
chineseCantonese: From 愛 oi (fond of, inclined in doing), 管 gún (to manage), and 侍者 sihjé (attendant)

name: Morpeko
english: Morpeko may be a combination of モルモット morumotto (guinea pig) and 腹ペコ hara peko (hungry, starving). The "Hangry" in Morpeko's Hangry Mode may be a combination of hungry and angry.
japanese: From モルモット morumotto (guinea pig) and 腹ペコ hara peko (hungry, starving)
korean: Same as English/Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Cufant
english: Cufant may be a combination of Cu (element symbol for copper), cuprum (the Latin name for copper from which the symbol is derived), or cute, and elephant or infant.
japanese: From 象 zō (elephant) and 銅 dō (copper) or 童 dō (child), and 銅像 dōzō (bronze statue)
french: From charivari and barrir (to make the sound of an elephant's cry)
korean: From 코끼리 kokkiri (elephant), 동 (銅) dong (copper), and 동 (童) dong (child)
chineseMandarin: From 銅 / 铜 tóng (copper), 象 xiàng (elephant), and 銅像 / 铜像 tóngxiàng (bronze statue)
chineseCantonese: From 銅 tùhng (copper), 象 jeuhng (elephant), and 銅像 tùhngjeuhng (bronze statue)

name: Copperajah
english: Copperajah may be a combination of copper and Maharajah (Indian title of great king). It may also incorporate gajah (Indonesian and Malay for elephant), which in turn is derived from गज gaja (Sanskrit for elephant).
japanese: From 大王 daiō (great king) and 王道 ōdō (kingship), 黄銅 ōdō (brass), or 銅 dō (copper)
korean: From 대왕 (大王) daewang (great king), 코끼리 kokkiri (elephant), 동 (銅) dong (copper), and 동 (童) dong (child)
chineseMandarin: From 大王 dàwáng (great king), 銅 / 铜 tóng (copper), 象 xiàng (elephant), and 銅像 / 铜像 tóngxiàng (bronze statue)
chineseCantonese: From 大王 daaihwòhng (great king), 銅 tùhng (copper), 象 jeuhng (elephant), and 銅像 tùhngjeuhng (bronze statue)

name: Dracozolt
english: Dracozolt may be a combination of dracō (Latin for "dragon") and volt or jolt.
japanese: From パチパチ pachipachi (onomatopoeia for crackling) and dragon
korean: From the transcription of its Japanese name and dragon
chineseMandarin: From 雷 léi (thunder), 鳥 / 鸟 niǎo (bird), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 雷 lèuih (thunder), 鳥 níuh (bird), and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Arctozolt
english: Arctozolt may be a combination of arctic and volt or jolt.
japanese: From パチパチ pachipachi (onomatopoeia for crackling), chill, and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
french: From galvanique (galvanic) and glagla (onomatopeia suggesting coldness and shivering)
german: From elektrisch (electric), the prefix cryo- (relating to "cold" and "freezing"), and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 雷 léi (thunder), 鳥 / 鸟 niǎo (bird), and 海獸 / 海兽 hǎishòu (marine mammal)
chineseCantonese: From 雷 lèuih (thunder), 鳥 níuh (bird), and 海獸 hóisau (marine mammal)

name: Dracovish
english: Dracovish may be a combination of dracō (Latin for "dragon"), fish, and possibly vicious or Ordovician (geologic period in the Paleozoic era).
japanese: From 魚 uo (fish), the genitive particle の no, and dragon
french: From the prefix hydro- (relating to water) or Hydre (Hydra) and dragon
korean: From 어 (魚) eo (fish) and dragon
chineseMandarin: From 鰓 / 鳃 sāi (gills), 魚 / 鱼 yú (fish), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 鰓 sōi (gills), 魚 yùh (fish), and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Arctovish
english: Arctovish may be a combination of arctic, fish, and possibly vicious or Ordovician.
japanese: From 魚 uo (fish), chill, and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
french: From the prefix hydro- (relating to water) or Hydre (Hydra) and glagla (onomatopeia suggesting coldness and shivering)
german: From pesce (Italian for "fish"), the prefix cryo- (relating to "cold" and "freezing"), and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
korean: From 어 (魚) eo (fish), chill, and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
chineseMandarin: From 鰓 / 鳃 sāi (gills), 魚 / 鱼 yú (fish), and 海獸 / 海兽 hǎishòu (marine mammal)
chineseCantonese: From 鰓 sōi (gills), 魚 yùh (fish), and 海獸 hóisau (marine mammal)

name: Duraludon
english: Duraludon may be a combination of duralumin, durable, dragon, don (Spanish for "lord"), and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth").
japanese: From ジュラルミン duralumin, durable, dragon, don (Spanish for "lord"), and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 鋁 / 铝 lǚ (aluminum), 鋼 / 钢 gāng (steel), and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon; common suffix in dinosaur names)
chineseCantonese: From 鋁 léui (aluminum), 鋼 gong (steel), and 龍 lùhng (dragon, common suffix for dinosaur names)

name: Dreepy
english: Dreepy may be a combination of dragon or dreary and creepy.
japanese: From dragon and うらめしや urameshiya (Curse on you (phrase typically said by ghosts in popular culture))
korean: From dragon, 꼬마 kkoma (little kid), and 혼 (魂) hon (soul)
chineseMandarin: From the transcription of its Japanese name and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From the transcription of its Japanese name and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Drakloak
english: Drakloak may be a combination of dragon or drake and cloak.
japanese: From dragon and launch
korean: From dragon and launch
chineseMandarin: Transcription of its Japanese name. Contains 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon) and 奇 qí (strange)
chineseCantonese: Transcription of its Japanese name. Contains 龍 lùhng (dragon) and 奇 kèih (strange)

name: Dragapult
english: Dragapult and Dorapult may be combinations of dragon and catapult. It may also come from poltergeist or sepultura (Spanish and Portuguese for "grave").
japanese: From dragon and catapult
french: From lancer (to launch) or lance-missiles (missile launcher), and saurien (saurian)
korean: From dragon and catapult
chineseMandarin: From the transcription of its Japanese name and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From the transcription of its Japanese name and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Zacian
english: Zacian is derived from the cyan. The word the is conventionally transliterated into Japanese as ザ za, due to the lack of the /ð/ phoneme ("th") in Japanese. The Japanese word for cyan, シアン shian, is borrowed from Dutch rather than English, explaining the unusual pronunciation of the word.
japanese: From the cyan
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 蒼藍 / 苍蓝 cānglán (cyan) and the transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: From 蒼藍 chōnglàahm (cyan) and the Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Zamazenta
english: Zamazenta is derived from the magenta.
japanese: From the magenta
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 藏紅色 / 藏红色 zànghóngsè (a shade of dark red) and the transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: From 藏紅色 johnghùhngsīk (a shade of dark red) and the Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Eternatus
english: Eternatus may be derived from aether, eternal, eternity, aeternatus (Latin for "immortalized"), and Thanatus (Latin transliteration of Thanatos, the personification of death in Greek Mythology).
japanese: From 無限大な mugendai-na (infinite), ダイマックス Daimax (Dynamax), and possibly dynamic
