french: From éternel (eternal), éther (aether), and θάνατος thắnătos (Ancient Greek for "death")
german: From endlos (endless) or Ende (end) and Dynamax
korean: From 무한 (無限) muhan (infinity), 다이맥스 Daimax (Dynamax), and dino
chineseMandarin: From 無極 / 无极 wújí (limitless; wuji), 極巨化 / 极巨化 Jíjùhuà (Dynamax), and a partial transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: From 無極 mòuhgihk (limitless; wuji), 極巨化 Gihkgeuihfa (Dynamax), and a partial transcription of Japanese name

name: Kubfu
english: Kubfu may be a combination of cub and kung fu.
japanese: From 打 da (hit), 熊 kuma (bear), and 琢磨 takuma (cultivation of skill)
korean: From 치다 chida (hit), 곰 gom (bear), 꼬마 kkoma (little kid), and 탁마 (琢磨) takma (cultivation of skill)
chineseMandarin: From 熊 xióng (bear) and 徒弟 túdì (disciple)
chineseCantonese: From 熊 hùhng (bear) and 徒弟 tòuhdái (disciple)

name: Urshifu
english: Urshifu may be a combination of ursus (Latin for "bear") and shifu (Chinese for master). It may also involve kung fu.
japanese: From wushu, 老師 / 老师 lǎoshī (Chinese for teacher), and possibly ウラー urā (hurrah, battle cry) and 押忍 osu (interjection used in Japanese martial arts)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 武道 wǔdào (martial arts), 熊 xióng (bear), and 師 / 师 shī (master)
chineseCantonese: From 武道 móuhdouh (martial arts), 熊 hùhng (bear), and 師 sī (master)

name: Zarude
english: Zarude may be a combination of 猿 saru (monkey) and rude.
japanese: From 猿 saru (monkey) and rude
korean: Transcription of its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of its Japanese name and 殺戮 / 杀戮 shālù (to slaughter)
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of its Japanese name and 殺戮 saatluhk (to slaughter)

name: Regieleki
english: Regieleki may be a combination of regis (Latin for "royal") and エレキ ereki (Japanese for electric).
japanese: From regis (Latin for "royal") and エレキ ereki (electric)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Regidrago
english: Regidrago and Regidorago may be a combination of regis (Latin for "royal") and dragon.
japanese: From regis (Latin for "royal") and dragon
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Glastrier
english: Glastrier may be a combination of glacier and destrier, a type of medieval war horse.
japanese: From blizzard and ἵππος híppos (Greek for "horse") or horse
korean: Similar to Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 雪暴 xuěbào (snowstorm) and 馬 / 马 mǎ (horse)
chineseCantonese: From 雪暴 syutbouh (snowstorm) and 馬 máh (horse)

name: Spectrier
english: Spectrier may be a combination of spectre and destrier, a type of medieval war horse.
japanese: From wraith, 霊 rei (spirit) and ἵππος híppos (Greek for "horse") or horse
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 幽靈 / 幽灵 yōulíng (ghost, phantom) and 馬 / 马 mǎ (horse)
chineseCantonese: From 幽靈 yāulìhng (ghost, phantom) and 馬 máh (horse)

name: Calyrex
english: Calyrex may be a combination of calyx (Latin for "bud") and rex (Latin for "king") or carex. It may also incorporate cavalry, referring to its ability to mount Glastrier or Spectrier.
japanese: From bud and rex (Latin for "king")
french: From sylve (forest) and roy (archaic form of roi (French for "king"))
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 蕾 lěi (bud), 王冠 wángguàn (crown), and 王 wáng (king)
chineseCantonese: From 蕾 léuih (bud), 王冠 wòhnggun (crown), and 王 wòhng (king)

name: Wyrdeer
english: Wyrdeer may be a combination of wyrd (Anglo-Saxon concept roughly equivalent to fate or destiny), weird, and deer.
japanese: From 怪しい ayashii (strange), 鹿 shishi (archaism for deer), and 鹿威し shishi-odoshi
korean: From 신비 (神祕) sinbi (mystery) and 록 (鹿) rok (deer)
chineseMandarin: From 詭 / 诡 guǐ (weird), 角 jiǎo (antler), and 鹿 lù (deer)
chineseCantonese: From 詭 gwái (weird), 角 gok (antler), and 鹿 luhk (deer)

name: Kleavor
english: Kleavor seems to be a corruption of cleaver, or a combination of cleaver and razor. It may also involve ore (a natural and valuable rock) and cleavage (the tendency of crystals to split along defined structural planes).
japanese: From バッサリ bassari (with a single stroke), ばさら basara (acting without restraint), berserker, 鉞 masakari (broadaxe), and カマキリ kamakiri (mantis)
german: From Axt (axe) and possibly 螳螂 tōrō (Japanese for mantis)
korean: From 사마귀 samagwi (mantis) and 자르다 jareuda (to cut)
chineseMandarin: From 劈 pī (cleave), 斧 fŭ (axe), and 螳螂 tángláng (mantis)
chineseCantonese: From 劈 pek (cleave), 斧 fú (axe), and 螳螂 tòhnglòhng (mantis)

name: Ursaluna
english: Ursaluna may be a combination of ursa (Latin for "bear") and luna (Latin for "moon").
japanese: From 月輪 gachirin (round moon) and 熊 kuma (bear)
french: From ursa (Latin for "bear"), king, and similar to Ursaring
korean: From 달 dal (moon), 다툼 datum (quarrel), and 곰 gom (bear)
chineseMandarin: From 月 yuè (moon) and 熊 xióng (bear)
chineseCantonese: From 月 yuht (moon) and 熊 hùhng (bear)

name: Basculegion
english: Basculegion may be a combination of Basculin and legion (an army or a vast amount of people) or Legion (a Biblical demon or group of demons).
japanese: From 偉大 idai (great), 哀悼 aitou (mourning), and イトウ itou (Sakhalin taimen)
french: From Parahucho (genus of the Sakhalin taimen), paranormal, cruel, and Pantagruel, a powerful giant in French literature
german: From salmo (Latin for "salmon") and magnis (Latin for "grand")
korean: From 대 (大) dae (great), bass, and 연어 yeoneo (salmon)
chineseMandarin: From 幽玄 yōuxuán (mysterious), 幽靈 / 幽灵 yōulíng (ghost), 尾 wěi (tail), and 魚 / 鱼 yú (fish)
chineseCantonese: From 幽玄 yāuyùhn (mysterious), 幽靈 yāulìhng (ghost), 尾 méih (tail), and 魚 yùh (fish)

name: Sneasler
english: Sneasler may be a combination of Sneasel and ruler. It could also be a combination of Sneasel and the comparative suffix -er, meaning more (thus "more Sneasel", alluding to it being physically similar to Hisuian Sneasel apart from its larger size).
japanese: From 大 ō (big), 大入道 ōnyūdō, and ニューラ Nyula (Sneasel)
french: From Farfuret (Sneasel), rex (Latin for "king"), and possibly furax (slang for furious)
korean: From 포푸니 Popuni (Sneasel) and 큰 keun (big)
chineseMandarin: From 大 dà (big) and 狃拉 Niǔlā (Sneasel)
chineseCantonese: From 大 daaih (big) and 狃拉 Náulāai (Sneasel)

name: Overqwil
english: Overqwil may be a combination of overkill and Qwilfish.
japanese: From ハリーセン Harysen (Qwilfish) and 針千本 harisenbon (porcupinefish) with 千 sen (thousand) replaced with 万 man (ten thousand, myriad)
korean: From 장 (長) jang (long; chief), 침 (針) chim (needle), 바늘 baneul (needle), balloon, and 침바루 Chimbaru (Qwilfish)
chineseMandarin: From 千針魚 / 千针鱼 Qiānzhēnyú (Qwilfish) with the 千 qiān (thousand) replaced with 萬 / 万 wàn (ten thousand)
chineseCantonese: From 千針魚 Chīnjāmyùh (Qwilfish) with the 千 chīn (thousand) replaced with 萬 maahn (ten thousand)

name: Enamorus
english: Enamorus may be a combination of enamor, amorous, and Aeolus (ruler of the winds in Greek mythology).
japanese: From love and Αἴολος Aiolos, also possibly ラブとロス rabu to rosu (love and loss)
french: From amour (love) and Vénus (Venus, the Roman goddess of love, beauty and fertility)
german: From Cupido (Cupid, the Roman god of love) and Aiolos
korean: Partial transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 眷戀 / 眷恋 juànliàn (yearning), 戀 / 恋 liàn (love), and 雲 / 云 yún (cloud)
chineseCantonese: From 眷戀 gyunlyún (yearning), 戀 lyún (love), and 雲 wàhn (cloud)

name: Sprigatito
english: Sprigatito may be a combination of sprig and gatito (Spanish for "kitten").
japanese: From ニャー nyā (meow), hoja (Spanish for "leaf"), and 葉 ha (leaf)
french: From pousse (sprout), chat (cat), and possibly herbe à chat (catnip)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name and 냐오 nyao (meow)
chineseMandarin: From 新 xīn (new, fresh), 新芽 xīnyá (sprout, bud), 葉 / 叶 yè (leaf), and 喵 miāo (meow)
chineseCantonese: From 新 sān (new, fresh), 新芽 sānngaa (sprout, bud), 葉 yihp (leaf), and 喵 mīu (meow)

name: Floragato
english: Floragato may be a combination of flora or flor (Spanish and Portuguese for "flower") and gato (Spanish and Portuguese for "cat").
japanese: From ニャー nyā (meow) and brote (Spanish for "sprout" or "plant bud")
german: From felis (Latin for "cat"), Knospe (plant bud), and Flora
korean: From 냐오 nyao (meow) and transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 蒂 dì (stem), 蕾 lěi (bud), and 喵 miāo (meow)
chineseCantonese: From 蒂 dai (stem), 蕾 léuih (bud), and 喵 mīu (meow)

name: Meowscarada
english: Meowscarada may be a combination of meow and mascarada (Spanish and Portuguese for "masquerade").
japanese: From masquerade and ニャー nyā (meow)
german: From Maske (mask) and gato (Spanish and Portuguese for "cat")
korean: From the transcription of Japanese name and 냐오 nyao (meow)
chineseMandarin: From 魔幻 móhuàn (magical), 假面 jiǎmiàn (mask), and 喵 miāo (meow)
chineseCantonese: From 魔幻 mōwaahn (magical), 假面 gámihn (mask), and 喵 mīu (meow)

name: Fuecoco
english: Fuecoco may be a combination of fuego (Spanish for "fire") and cocodrilo (Spanish for "crocodile"). It may also come from fuocoso (Italian for "fiery, especially relating to music").
japanese: From 火 ho (fire), ほげー hogē (onomatopoeia for being dumbfounded), fogata (Spanish for "campfire"), hoguera (Spanish for "bonfire"), gator, malagueta, and melegueta
german: From Krokodil (crocodile) and Fackel (torch) or kokeln (to play with fire)
korean: From 뜨겁다 tteugeopda (hot) and 악어 (鰐魚) ageo (crocodile)
chineseMandarin: From 呆 dāi (simple-minded), 火 huǒ (fire), and 鱷魚 / 鳄鱼 èyú (crocodile)
chineseCantonese: From 呆 ngòih (simple-minded), 火 fó (fire), and 鱷魚 ngohkyùh (crocodile)

name: Crocalor
english: Crocalor may be a combination of crocodile and calor (Spanish and Portuguese for "heat"). It may also involve vocal or coloratura (an ornamentation of vocal melody).
japanese: From あちち achichi ("Hot!"), mariachi, and alligator
german: From Lohe (archaic word for flame) and Krokodil (crocodile)
korean: From 악어 (鰐魚) ageo (crocodile; alligator) and 뜨겁다 tteugeopda (hot)
chineseMandarin: From 炙 zhì (to broil; to cauterize), 燙 / 烫 tàng (boiling hot), and 鱷魚 / 鳄鱼 èyú (crocodile; alligator)
chineseCantonese: From 炙 jek (to broil; to cauterize), 燙 tong (boiling hot), and 鱷魚 ngohkyùh (crocodile; alligator)

name: Skeledirge
english: Skeledirge may be a combination of skeleton and dirge (a song or hymn performed in mourning, such as during funerals).
japanese: From laúd (Spanish lute), loud, and bone
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 骨紋 / 骨纹 gǔwén (bone-patterned), 巨聲 / 巨声 jùshēng (loud sound), and 鱷魚 / 鳄魚 èyú (crocodile; alligator)
chineseCantonese: From 骨紋 gwāt (bone-patterned), 巨聲 geuihsēng (loud sound), and 鱷魚 ngohkyùh (crocodile; alligator)

name: Quaxly
english: Quaxly may be a combination of quack, wax (referring to hair wax), and duckling.
japanese: From クワック kuwakku (quack) and an anagram of ワックス wakkusu (wax)
french: From coiffe or coiffure (headwear or hairstyle) and caneton (duckling)
korean: From 꽥꽥 kkwaek-kkwaek (quack) and 왁스 wakseu (wax)
chineseMandarin: From 潤 / 润 rùn (wet), 水 shuǐ (water), 鴨 / 鸭 yā (duck), and 水鴨 shuǐyā (teal)
chineseCantonese: From 潤 yeuhn (wet), 水 séui (water), 鴨 aap (duck), and 水鴨 séuiaap (teal)

name: Quaxwell
english: Quaxwell may be a combination of quack, aqua, wax (referring to hair wax), well, swell (series of ocean waves) and the name Maxwell.
japanese: From well or swell and 鴨 kamo (duck), as well as well combed
french: From canard (duck), cabello (Spanish for "hair"), and bello (Spanish for "beautiful")
korean: From aqua, 꽥꽥 kkwaek-kkwaek (quack), and 왁스 wakseu (wax)
chineseMandarin: From 湧 / 涌 yǒng (to gush), 踴躍 / 踊跃 yǒngyuè (enthusiastic), and 鴨 / 鸭 yā (duck)
chineseCantonese: From 湧 yúng (to gush), 踴躍 yúngyeuhk (enthusiastic), and 鴨 aap (duck)

name: Quaquaval
english: Quaquaval may be a combination of quá-quá (Spanish and Portuguese onomatopoeia for duck sounds), aqua, and carnaval (Spanish and Portuguese for "carnival"). The name also appears to draw from the adjective quaquaversal, referring to a pattern that radiates in all directions from a common center; such is the case for the water feathers that fan out from Quaquaval's tail during battle.
japanese: From wave and carnival
german: From baile (Spanish and Portuguese for "dance") and onda (Spanish and Portuguese for "wave")
korean: From wave and carnival
chineseMandarin: From 狂歡 / 狂欢 kuánghuān (merriment), 浪 làng (wave), 舞 wǔ (dance), and 鴨 / 鸭 yā (duck)
chineseCantonese: From 狂歡 kòhngfūn (merriment), 浪 lohng (wave), 舞 móuh (dance), and 鴨 aap (duck)

name: Lechonk
english: Lechonk may be a combination of lechón (Spanish for "suckling piglet") and chonk (slang term for a fat or large animal).
japanese: From gourmet, glutton, and 豚 ton (pig)
korean: From 맛보다 matboda (to taste) and 돈 (豚) don (pig)
chineseMandarin: From 愛吃 / 爱吃 àichī (to love to eat) and 豚 tún (pig)
chineseCantonese: From 愛吃 oihek (to love to eat) and 豚 tyùhn (pig)

name: Oinkologne
english: Oinkologne may be a combination of oink (the sound a pig makes) and cologne. It may also involve bologna, a type of pork meat.
japanese: From perfume and 豚 ton (pig)
korean: From 퍼퓸 peopyum (perfume) and 돈 (豚) ton (pig)
chineseMandarin: From 飄香 / 飘香 piāoxiāng (wafting fragrance) and 豚 tún (pig)
chineseCantonese: From 飄香 pīuhēung (wafting fragrance) and 豚 tyùhn (pig)

name: Tarountula
english: Tarountula may be a combination of tarantula and round.
japanese: From 球 tama (sphere) and tarantula
korean: From 타래 tarae (skein) and 타란툴라 tarantulla (tarantula)
chineseMandarin: From 團 / 团 tuán (sphere), 珠 zhū (bead), and 蜘蛛 zhīzhū (spider)
chineseCantonese: From 團 tyùhn (sphere), 珠 jyū (bead), and 蜘蛛 jījyū (spider)

name: Spidops
english: Spidops may be a combination of spider, spy, ops (abbreviation of "operations"), and possibly Deinopis (genus of the ogre-faced spider).
japanese: From 罠 wana (trap), spider, and Schneider (German for "tailor" and "long-legged arachnid")
french: From fil (string), trappe (trap), and possibly a pun on philanthrope (philanthropist)
korean: From trap and spider
chineseMandarin: From 操 cāo (to control), 陷阱 xiànjǐng (trap), and 蜘蛛 zhīzhū (spider)
chineseCantonese: From 操 chōu (to control), 陷阱 haahmjihng (trap), and 蜘蛛 jījyū (spider)

name: Nymble
english: Nymble may be a combination of nymph (immature form of an insect) and nimble.
japanese: From 豆 mame (prefix for small) and 飛蝗 batta (locust; grasshopper)
korean: From 콩알 kong-al (bean; figurative term for small) and 메뚜기 mettugi (short-horned grasshopper; locust)
chineseMandarin: From 豆 dòu (bean) and 蟋蟀 xīshuài (cricket)
chineseCantonese: From 豆 dauh (bean) and 蟋蟀 sīksēut (cricket)

name: Lokix
english: Lokix may be a combination of locust and kicks or crickets, or a pun on low kicks.
japanese: From extreme and leg
french: From gambette (slang for leg) and extreme
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 烈 liè (fierce), 腿 tuǐ (leg; kick), and 蝗 huáng (locust)
chineseCantonese: From 烈 liht (fierce), 腿 téui (leg; kick), and 蝗 wòhng (locust)

name: Pawmi
english: Pawmi may be a combination of paw, palm, and mini or 鼠 nezumi (Japanese for mouse).
japanese: From パチパチ pachipachi (onomatopoeia for crackling), palm, marmot, dynamo, and mho (unit of electric conductance)
french: From paume (palm) and ohm (unit of electrical resistance)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 布 bù (cloth) and 土撥鼠 / 土拨鼠 tǔbōshǔ (marmot)
chineseCantonese: From 布 bou (cloth) and 土撥鼠 tóubuhtsyú (marmot)

name: Pawmo
english: Pawmo may be a combination of Pawmi, marmot, and dynamo.
japanese: From パモ Pamo (Pawmi) and marmot
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 布 bù (cloth) and 土撥鼠 / 土拨鼠 tǔbōshǔ (marmot)
chineseCantonese: From 布 bou (cloth) and 土撥鼠 tóubuhtsyú (marmot)

name: Pawmot
english: Pawmot may be a combination of Pawmi or Pawmo and marmot.
japanese: From パモ Pamo (Pawmi), パモット Pamot (Pawmo), and marmot
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 巴掌 bāzhang (palm), 布 bù (cloth) and 土撥鼠 / 土拨鼠 tǔbōshǔ (marmot)
chineseCantonese: From 巴掌 bājéung (palm), 布 bou (cloth) and 土撥鼠 tóubuhtsyú (marmot)

name: Tandemaus
english: Tandemaus may be a combination of tandem and Maus (German for "mouse").
japanese: From 輪っか wakka (loop) and 鼠 nezumi (mouse)
korean: From 둘 dul (two) and 쥐 jwi (mouse)
chineseMandarin: From 一對 / 一对 yīduì (pair) and 鼠 shǔ (mouse)
chineseCantonese: From 一對 yātdeui (pair) and 鼠 syú (mouse)

name: Maushold
english: Maushold may be a combination of Maus (German for "mouse") and household. It may also be a pun on mouse hole.
japanese: From 一家 ikka (a family) and 鼠 nezumi (mouse)
french: From famille (family), mignon (cute), and campagnol (vole, field mouse)
korean: From family and 쥐 jwi (mouse)
chineseMandarin: From 一家 yījiā (a family) and 鼠 shǔ (mouse)
chineseCantonese: From 一家 yātgā (a family) and 鼠 syú (mouse)

name: Fidough
english: Fidough may be a combination of Fido (Spanish/Italian for "loyal", also a stereotypical name for a pet dog), filo, and dough.
japanese: From puppy and もっちり mocchiri (doughy, springy) or 餅 mochi
french: From pâte à choux (choux pastry; a type of pastry dough) and chiot (puppy)
german: From Hefe (yeast) and Dackel (dachshund; a dog breed)
korean: From 쫀득쫀득 jjondeuk-jjondeuk (glutinous), 쫀드기 jjondeugi, and doggy
chineseMandarin: From 狗仔 gǒuzǎi (puppy) and 包 bāo (bun)
chineseCantonese: From 狗仔 gáujái (puppy) and 包 bāau (bun)

name: Dachsbun
english: Dachsbun may be a combination of dachshund and bun.
japanese: From bow wow (onomatopoeia for a dog's bark) and pretzel
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 麻花 máhuā and 犬 quǎn (dog)
chineseCantonese: From 麻花 màhfā and 犬 hyún (dog)

name: Smoliv
english: Smoliv may be a combination of small or smol (diminutive spelling of small) and olive.
japanese: From mini and olive
korean: From mini and 올리브 ollibeu (olive)
chineseMandarin: From 迷你 mínǐ (mini) and the transcription of the Japanese name
chineseCantonese: From 迷你 màihnéih (mini) and the transcription of the Japanese name

name: Dolliv
english: Dolliv may be a combination of doll and olive.
japanese: From olive and aliño (Spanish for "condiment") or -inho (Portuguese diminutive suffix)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Transcription of Japanese name

name: Arboliva
english: Arboliva may be a combination of arbor (shelter formed from trees and vines; tree) or árbol (Spanish for "tree"), olive or oliva ("olive" in various Romance languages), and dīva (Latin for "goddess") or diva (female celebrity).
japanese: From oliva ("olive" in various Romance languages) and dīva (Latin for "goddess") or diva
german: From Olive and Athena (Greek goddess of wisdom, whose symbol was the olive tree)
korean: From olive, diva, and possibly hierba (Spanish for "herb")
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Squawkabilly
english: Squawkabilly may be a combination of squawk, bill (beak), and rockabilly.
japanese: From イキり ikiri (slang for a cocky person) and 鸚哥 inko (parrot)
korean: From 시비 (是非) sibi (dispute) and 잉꼬 ingkko (parrot)
chineseMandarin: From 怒 nù (rage) and 鸚哥 / 鹦哥 yīnggē (parrot)
chineseCantonese: From 怒 nouh (rage) and 鸚哥 yīnggō (parrot)

name: Nacli
english: Nacli may be a combination of NaCl (chemical formula for sodium chloride; table salt) and little or salty. The -i at the end of its name may also refer to iodine, a common element added to salt to prevent iodine deficiency.
japanese: From 小 ko (small), 子 ko (child), 塩 shio (salt), and geo- (prefix for earth)
german: From geo- (prefix for earth) and salis (Latin for "salt")
korean: From bébé (French for "baby") and salt
chineseMandarin: From 石鹽 / 石盐 shíyán (rock salt), 寶石 / 宝石 bǎoshí (jewel), and 寶寶 / 宝宝 bǎobao (baby)
chineseCantonese: From 石鹽 sehkyìhm (rock salt), 寶石 bóusehk (jewel), and 寶寶 bóubóu (baby)

name: Naclstack
english: Naclstack may be a combination of NaCl (chemical formula for sodium chloride; table salt) and stack, possibly in reference to dry stack (method of stone structure building that doesn't use mortar).
japanese: From 塩 shio (salt), the prefix geo- (relating to "earth") or geode, and 積む tsumu (to stack)
korean: From stack and salt
chineseMandarin: From 石鹽 / 石盐 shíyán (rock salt) and 壘 / 垒 lěi (to pile)
chineseCantonese: From 石鹽 sehkyìhm (rock salt) and 壘 léuih (to pile)

name: Garganacl
english: Garganacl may be a combination of gargantuan and NaCl (chemical formula for sodium chloride; table salt). It may also borrow from tabernacle.
japanese: From 巨人 kyojin (giant), 塩 shio (salt), and geo- (prefix for earth)
korean: From colossal and salt
chineseMandarin: From 石鹽 / 石盐 shíyán (rock salt), 巨 jù (giant), and 靈 / 灵 líng (spirit)
chineseCantonese: From 石鹽 sehkyìhm (rock salt), 巨 geuih (giant), and 靈 lìhng (spirit)

name: Charcadet
english: Charcadet may be a combination of char (to burn), charcoal, and cadet.
japanese: From carbón (Spanish for "charcoal"), carbon, and 坊 bō (boy)
korean: From carbón (Spanish for "charcoal")
chineseMandarin: From 炭 tàn (coal), 小 xiǎo (small; young), and 侍 shì (attendant)
chineseCantonese: From 炭 taan (coal), 小 síu (small; young), and 侍 sih (attendant)

name: Armarouge
english: Armarouge may be a combination of arma (Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian for "weapon"), armadura (Spanish and Portuguese for "armor") or armatura (Italian for "armor"), and rouge (French for "red").
japanese: From 紅蓮 guren (crimson), arma (Italian, Spanish and Portuguese for "weapon"), and armadura (Spanish and Portuguese for "armor") or armatura (Italian for "armor")
french: From carmin (carmine; a deep red color) and armadura (Spanish and Portuguese for "armor")
korean: From cardinal, arma (Italian, Spanish and Portuguese for "weapon"), and armadura (Spanish and Portuguese for "armor") or armatura (Italian for "armor")
chineseMandarin: From 紅蓮 / 红莲 hónglián (crimson lotus), 鎧 / 铠 kǎi (armor), and 騎士 / 骑士 qíshì (knight)
chineseCantonese: From 紅蓮 hùhnglìhn (crimson lotus), 鎧 hói (armor), and 騎士 kèihsih (knight)

name: Ceruledge
english: Ceruledge may be a combination of cerulean (a shade of dark blue), cruel, and edge.
japanese: From 蒼 sō (azure), soul, and blades, also possibly blaze or wraith
french: From mal (evil), malva (Spanish for "mauve") and lame (blade)
german: From azur (Spanish and Portuguese for "azure") and gladius (Latin for "sword")
korean: From 파랑 parang (blue) and blaze or blades
chineseMandarin: From 蒼 / 苍 cāng (azure), 炎 yán (flame), 刃 rèn (blade), and 鬼 guǐ (ghost)
chineseCantonese: From 蒼 chōng (azure), 炎 yìh (flame), 刃 myah (blade), and 鬼 ngwái (ghost)

name: Tadbulb
english: Tadbulb may be a combination of tadpole and light bulb.
japanese: From 頭 zu (head) and ピカピカ pikapika (onomatopoeia for sparkling)
french: From têtard (tadpole) and ampoule (light bulb), also a pun on tête d'ampoule (egghead)
korean: From 빛나다 binnada (to shine) and 두 (頭) du (head)
chineseMandarin: From 光 guāng (light), 蝌蚪 kēdǒu (tadpole), and 仔 zǎi (young animal)
chineseCantonese: From 光 gwōng (light), 蝌蚪 fōdáu (tadpole), and 仔 jái (young animal)

name: Bellibolt
english: Bellibolt may be a combination of belly and bolt.
japanese: From 腹 hara (belly) and バリバリ baribari (onomatopoeia for crackling)
french: From amphibien (amphibian), ampère (ampere) or ampoule (light bulb), and bidou (childish way of saying 'bidon' (tummy))
german: From Wampe (colloquial term for potbelly) and Blitz (lightning)
korean: From 찌릿 jjirit (onomatopoeia for crackling), 배 bae (belly), and 개구리 gaeguri (frog)
chineseMandarin: From 電 / 电 diàn (electric), 肚 dù (belly), and 蛙 wā (frog)
chineseCantonese: From 電 dihn (electric), 肚 tóuh (belly), and 蛙 wā (frog)

name: Wattrel
english: Wattrel may be a combination of watt and petrel.
japanese: From 海 kai (sea), 海燕 kaien (northern storm petrel), and 雷電 raiden (thunder and lightning)
korean: From 찌릿찌릿 jjirit-jjirit (onomatopoeia for crackling) and 바다제비 badajaebi (northern storm petrel)
chineseMandarin: From 電 / 电 diàn (electric), 海 hǎi (sea), and 海燕 hǎiyàn (northern storm petrel)
chineseCantonese: From 電 dihn (electric), 海 hói (sea), and 海燕 hóiyin (northern storm petrel)

name: Kilowattrel
english: Kilowattrel may be a combination of kilowatt and petrel; it can also be deconstructed as "kilo-" + Wattrel.
japanese: From 大 tai (big; great), 大海 taikai (ocean), 海燕 kaien (northern storm petrel), and 雷電 raiden (thunder and lightning)
french: From fulmar, fulgur (Latin for "lightning, thunderbolt"), sac gulaire (gular sac), and possibly aero- (Latin prefix for air) or airo (Portuguese for "common murre")
korean: From 찌릿찌릿 jjirit-jjirit (onomatopoeia for crackling), 바다제비 badajaebi (northern storm petrel), and beak
chineseMandarin: From 大 dà (big; great), 電 / 电 diàn (electric), 海 hǎi (sea), and 海燕 hǎiyàn (northern storm petrel)
chineseCantonese: From 大 daaih (big; great), 電 dihn (electric), 海 hói (sea), and 海燕 hóiyin (northern storm petrel)

name: Maschiff
english: Maschiff may be a combination of mastiff and mischief.
japanese: From オラつく oratsuku (slang word to describe a rude or irreverent person) and マスチフ masuchifu (mastiff)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From the phrase 我驕傲 / 我骄傲 Wǒ jiāo'ào (I'm proud), 叫 jiào (to bark), and 獒犬 áoquǎn (mastiff)
chineseCantonese: From the phrase 我驕傲 Ngóh gīu'ngouh (I'm proud), 叫 giu (to bark), and 獒犬 ngòuhhyún (mastiff)

name: Mabosstiff
english: Mabosstiff may be a combination of mafia, mob, boss, and mastiff.
japanese: From mafia and mastiff
german: From Mastiff and mafioso (mobster in various Romance languages)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 獒犬 áoquǎn (mastiff) and 教父 jiàofù (godfather)
chineseCantonese: From 獒犬 ngòuhhyún (mastiff) and 教父 gaaufuh (godfather)

name: Shroodle
english: Shroodle may be a combination of shrew (insectivore mammal), shrewd, and doodle.
japanese: From 汁 shiru (juice), しるし shirushi (mark, sign), shrew, and シュルシュル shurushuru (onomatopoeia for rustling)
korean: From 땃쥐 ttatjwi (musk shrew) and shrew
chineseMandarin: From 滋 zī (to squirt), 汁 zhī (juice), and 鼴鼠 / 鼹鼠 yǎnshǔ (talpid)
chineseCantonese: From 滋 jī (to squirt), 汁 jāp (juice), and 鼴鼠 yínsyú (talpid)

name: Grafaiai
english: Grafaiai may be a combination of graffiti and aye-aye. It may also be derived from Urdaibai (natural reserve home to the painted Oma forest).
japanese: From tagging, 猿 saru (monkey), and possibly jungle
french: From tag with the name formatted similarly to aye-aye
korean: From tagging and the transcription of the Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 塗鴉 / 涂鸦 túyā (graffiti), 標籤 / 标签 biāoqiān (tag), and 客 kè (agentive suffix for one who engages in a certain activity)
chineseCantonese: From 塗鴉 tòuh'ā (graffiti), 標籤 bīuchīm (tag), and 客 haak (agentive suffix for one who engages in a certain activity)

name: Bramblin
english: Bramblin may be a combination of bramble and rambling, goblin, or gremlin.
japanese: From あの草 ano kusa (that grass)
french: From virevoltant (tumbleweed) and virer au vent (to drift with the wind)
german: From Wehe (drift), woher (where from), and Latin herba
korean: From 그 풀 geu pul (that grass)
chineseMandarin: From 納 / 纳 nà (to receive), 噬 shì (to bite), 草 cǎo (grass), and a pun of 那是草 Nà shì cǎo (That is grass)
chineseCantonese: From 納 naahp (to receive), 噬 saih (to bite), and 草 chóu (grass)

name: Brambleghast
english: Brambleghast may be a combination of bramble and ghastly, ghast (a name used for various types of undead in fantasy fiction), or aghast.
japanese: From the phrase あのほら草 ano hora kusa (Um... Look! Grass) and horror
korean: From 공포 (恐怖) gongpo (horror) and 풀 pul (grass)
chineseMandarin: From 怖 bù (terror), 納 / 纳 nà (to receive), 噬 shì (to bite), 草 cǎo (grass), and 不，那是草 Bù, nà shì cǎo (No, that is grass)
chineseCantonese: From 怖 bou (terror), 納 naahp (to receive), 噬 saih (to bite), and 草 chóu (grass)

name: Toedscool
english: Toedscool may be a combination of toadstool (another name for mushroom), toed (having toes), and Tentacool.
japanese: From 野 no (field), 木耳 kikurage (jelly ear), and メノクラゲ Menokurage (Tentacool)
korean: From 들 deul (field) and 왕눈해 Wangnunhe (Tentacool)
chineseMandarin: From 原野 yuányě (field) and 瑪瑙水母 / 玛瑙水母 Mǎnǎoshuǐmǔ (Tentacool)
chineseCantonese: From 原野 yùhnyéh (field) and 瑪瑙水母 Máhnóuhséuimóuh (Tentacool)

name: Toedscruel
english: Toedscruel may be a combination of toadstool (another name for mushroom), toed (having toes), and Tentacruel.
japanese: From 陸 riku (land), 木耳 kikurage (jelly ear), and ドククラゲ Dokukurage (Tentacruel)
korean: From 육 (陸) yuk (land) and 독파리 Tokpari (Tentacruel)
chineseMandarin: From 陸地 / 陆地 lùdì (land) and 毒刺水母 Dúcìshuǐmǔ (Tentacruel)
chineseCantonese: From 陸地 luhkdeih (land) and 毒刺水母 Duhkchiséuimóuh (Tentacruel)

name: Klawf
english: Klawf may be a combination of claw and cliff.
japanese: From 崖 gake (cliff) and 蟹 kani (crab) or 毛蟹 kegani (horsehair crab)
korean: From 절벽 jeolbyeok (cliff) and 게 ge (crab)
chineseMandarin: From 毛蟹 máoxiè (Chinese mitten crab) and 崖 yái / yá (cliff)
chineseCantonese: From 毛蟹 mòuhháaih (Chinese mitten crab) and 崖 ngàaih (cliff)

name: Capsakid
english: Capsakid may be a combination of capsaicin (active component of chili peppers) or Capsicum (the genus of chili peppers), kappa, and kid.
japanese: From capsaicin and 児 ji (child)
french: From piment (chili pepper) and chiquito (Spanish for "little boy")
korean: From capsaicin and 아이 ai (child)
chineseMandarin: From 熱 / 热 rè (hot), 辣 là (spicy), and 娃 wá (child)
chineseCantonese: From 熱 yiht (hot), 辣 laaht (spicy), and 娃 wā (child)

name: Scovillain
english: Scovillain may be a combination of Scoville (as in the Scoville scale, the measurement scale for chili pepper pungency) and villain.
japanese: From Scoville scale and villain
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 狠 hěn (vicious) and 辣椒 làjiāo (chili pepper)
chineseCantonese: From 狠 hán (vicious) and 辣椒 laahtjīu (chili pepper)

name: Rellor
english: Rellor may be derived from roller spelled backwards.
japanese: From a backward spelling of 糞転がし funkorogashi (colloquial term for dung beetle)
french: From Verlan for roulé-boulé (roll) and possibly boue (mud)
korean: From 쇠똥구리 soettungguri (dung beetle) and a corruption of 굴리다 gullida (to tumble)
chineseMandarin: From 滾屎蟲 / 滚屎虫 gǔnshǐchóng (dialectal name for dung beetle) and 泥 ní (mud)
chineseCantonese: From 滾屎蟲 gwánsíchùhng (dialectal name for dung beetle) and 泥 nàih (mud)

name: Rabsca
english: Rabsca may be derived from scarab with the syllables transposed. It may also pull from Ra, the Egyptian sun god sometimes associated with scarabs. The name is also an anagram of "scarab."
japanese: From スカラベ sukarabe (scarab) spelled in reverse
korean: From 스카라베 seukarabe (scarab) spelled in reverse
chineseMandarin: From 聖甲蟲 / 圣甲虫 shèngjiǎchóng (scarab) spelled in reverse
chineseCantonese: From 聖甲蟲 singgaapchùhng (scarab) spelled in reverse

name: Flittle
english: Flittle may be a combination of flitter (a fluttering movement) and little.
japanese: From ひらひら hirahira (onomatopoetic word for fluttering) and 雛 hina (chick)
korean: From 하늘하늘 haneul-haneul (buoyantly) and 아기 agi (baby)
chineseMandarin: From 飄飄 / 飘飘 piāopiāo (fluttering in the wind) and 雛 chú (chick)
chineseCantonese: From 飄飄 pīupīu (fluttering in the wind) and 雛 chòh (chick)

name: Espathra
english: Espathra may be a combination of ESP, telepath, and Cleopatra.
japanese: From cuello (Spanish for "neck"), ESP, and Cleopatra
german: From the prefix Psi- and Kleopatra (Cleopatra)
korean: From Cleopatra and esper
chineseMandarin: From 超能力 chāonénglì (extrasensory perception), 豔后 / 艳后 yànhòu (bewitching queen; alias for Cleopatra), and 鴕鳥 / 鸵鸟 tuóniǎo (ostrich)
chineseCantonese: From 超能力 chīunàhnglihk (extrasensory perception), 豔后 yihmhau (bewitching queen; alias for Cleopatra), and 鴕鳥 tòhníuh (chick)

name: Tinkatink
english: Tinkatink may be a combination of tinker (itinerant tinsmith) and pink or tink (sharp metallic sound).
japanese: From 鍛冶 kanuchi (blacksmith) and ～ちゃん -chan (Japanese diminutive suffix)
french: From forgeron (blacksmith) and -ette (French feminine diminutive suffix)
german: From forge and -ita (Spanish feminine diminutive suffix)
korean: From 어리다 eorida (young) and 대장장이 daejangjang-i (blacksmith)
chineseMandarin: From 小 xiǎo (small), 鍛 / 锻 duàn (to forge) and 鐵匠 / 铁匠 tiějiàng (blacksmith)
chineseCantonese: From 小 síu (small), 鍛 dyun (to forge) and 鐵匠 titjeuhng (blacksmith)

name: Tinkatuff
english: Tinkatuff may be a combination of tinker (itinerant tinsmith) and tough.
japanese: From 中 naka (middle), 鍛冶 kanuchi (blacksmith), and ～ちゃん -chan (Japanese diminutive suffix)
french: From forger (to forge) and -ella (Italian feminine diminutive suffix)
german: From taff (tough), forge and -ita (Spanish feminine diminutive suffix)
korean: From 벼리다 byeorida (to forge) and 대장장이 daejangjang-i (blacksmith)
chineseMandarin: From 巧 qiǎo (skillful), 鍛 / 锻 duàn (to forge) and 鐵匠 / 铁匠 tiějiàng (blacksmith)
chineseCantonese: From 巧 háau (skillful), 鍛 dyun (to forge) and 鐵匠 titjeuhng (blacksmith)

name: Tinkaton
english: Tinkaton may be a combination of tinker (itinerant tinsmith) and ton or gigaton.
japanese: From でかい dekai (huge), 鍛冶 kanuchi (blacksmith), and ～ちゃん -chan (Japanese diminutive suffix)
french: From forger (to forge) and -elina (Italian feminine diminutive suffix)
german: From gran (Italian and Spanish for "great"), forge and -ita (Spanish feminine diminutive suffix)
korean: From 두드리다 dudeurida (to knock) and 대장장이 daejangjang-i (blacksmith)
chineseMandarin: From 巨 jù (giant), 鍛 / 锻 duàn (to forge) and 鐵匠 / 铁匠 tiějiàng (blacksmith)
chineseCantonese: From 巨 geuih (giant), 鍛 dyun (to forge) and 鐵匠 titjeuhng (blacksmith)

name: Wiglett
english: Wiglett may be a combination of wiggle, water or white, and Diglett.
japanese: From 海 umi (sea) and ディグダ Digda (Diglett)
korean: From 바다 bada (sea) and 디그다 Digda (Diglett)
chineseMandarin: From 海 hǎi (sea) and 地鼠 Dìshǔ (Diglett)
chineseCantonese: From 海 hói (sea) and 地鼠 Deihsyú (Diglett)

name: Wugtrio
english: Wugtrio may be a combination of Wiglett, water, or wug (a word used to describe any creature with worm-like features) and Dugtrio.
japanese: From 海 umi (sea) and Dugtrio
korean: From 바다 bada (sea) and 닥트리오 Daktrio (Dugtrio)
chineseMandarin: From 海 hǎi (sea) and 三地鼠 Sāndìshǔ (Dugtrio)
chineseCantonese: From 海 hói (sea) and 三地鼠 Sāamdeihsyú (Dugtrio)

name: Bombirdier
english: Bombirdier may be a combination of bombardier and bird.
japanese: From 落とし otoshi (dropping of object) and 鳥 tori (bird)
french: From lest (ballast, dead weight), laisse tomber (drop it), and aile (wing)
german: From Meister Adebar (name of the stork said to deliver babies in German fairy tales) and Bombe (bomb)
korean: From 떨구다 tteolguda (to drop) and 새 sae (bird)
chineseMandarin: From the idiom 落井下石 lùojǐng-xiàshí (to kick someone when they are down; literally "to throw stones at someone who fell down a well") and 鳥 / 鸟 niǎo (bird)
chineseCantonese: From the idiom 落井下石 lohkjéng-hahsehk (to kick someone when they are down; literally "to throw stones at someone who fell down a well") and 鳥 níuh (bird)

name: Finizen
english: Finizen may be a combination of fin, delfín (Spanish for "dolphin"), and citizen or denizen.
japanese: From 波 nami (wave), 並み nami (ordinary), and 海豚 iruka (dolphin)
french: From dauphin (dolphin); is also identical to the Picard language word for dolphin
korean: From man and dolphin
chineseMandarin: From 波 bō (wave), 普通 pǔtōng (ordinary), and 海豚 hǎitún (dolphin)
chineseCantonese: From 波 bō (wave), 普通 póutūng (ordinary), and 海豚 hóityùhn (dolphin)

name: Palafin
english: Palafin may be a combination of paladin or pal (since another player is needed to evolve it) and fin or delfín (Spanish for "dolphin").
japanese: From 海豚 iruka (dolphin) and man
french: From super and dauphin (dolphin) or Dofin (Finizen)
korean: From dolphin and man
chineseMandarin: From 海豚 hǎitún (dolphin) and 俠 / 侠 xiá (common suffix used in translations of superhero names)
chineseCantonese: From 海豚 hóityùhn (dolphin) and 俠 hahp (common suffix used in translations of superhero names)

name: Varoom
english: Varoom may be derived from vroom (onomatopoetic sound of engine revving up).
japanese: From ぶろろろ burororo (onomatopoeia for engine sounds) and ぶるん burun (vroom)
french: From vroum (vroom) and vrombir (to emit a buzzing or roaring sound)
korean: From 부르릉 bureureung (vroom) and the transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 噗 pū (onomatopoetic sound for release of gas) and 隆隆 lónglóng (onomatopoetic sound for rumbling)
chineseCantonese: From 噗 pok (onomatopoetic sound for release of gas) and 隆隆 lùhnglùhng (onomatopoetic sound for rumbling)

name: Revavroom
english: Revavroom may be a combination of rev (to increase the running speed of an engine by pressing on the accelerator) and vroom (onomatopoetic sound of engine revving up).
japanese: From ぶろろろ burororo (onomatopoeia for engine sounds), vroom, and possibly roam
french: From vroum (vroom), vrombir (to emit a buzzing or roaring sound) and motor or rotor
korean: From 부르릉 bureureung (vroom) and the transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 隆隆 lónglóng (onomatopoetic sound for rumbling) and the transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: From 隆隆 lùhnglùhng (onomatopoetic sound for rumbling) and the transcription of Japanese name

name: Cyclizar
english: Cyclizar may be a combination of cycle and lizard.
japanese: From moto (Spanish and Portuguese for "motorcycle") and 蜥蜴 tokage (lizard)
korean: From motorcycle and 도마뱀 domabaem (lizard)
chineseMandarin: From 摩托車 / 摩托车 mótuō-chē (motorcycle) and 蜥蜴 xīyì (lizard)
chineseCantonese: From 摩托車 mōtok-chē (motorcycle) and 蜥蜴 sīkyihk (lizard)

name: Orthworm
english: Orthworm may be a combination of ore, ortho- (prefix meaning "straight" or "upright"), orthoclase (a mineral), and earthworm.
japanese: From 蚯蚓 mimizu (earthworm) and ズズズ zuzuzu (onomatopoeia for burrowing through the ground)
french: From fer (iron) and ver de terre (earthworm)
german: From schleppen (to tow or haul) and Wurm (worm)
korean: From 꿈틀꿈틀 kkumteul-kkumteul (wriggling) and 지렁이 jireong-i
chineseMandarin: From 拖 tuō (to drag) and 蚯蚓 qiūyǐn (earthworm)
chineseCantonese: From 拖 tō (to drag) and 蚯蚓 yāuyáhn (earthworm)

name: Glimmet
english: Glimmet may be a combination of glimmer and the suffix -et (indicating something is small or lesser) or emit.
japanese: From キラキラ kirakira (onomatopoeia for glittering) or 煌めく kirameku (to glitter), killer and 芽 me (bud)
french: From germe (sprout) and éclat (radiance or shard)
german: From luminare (Latin for "to shine") and Spross (sprout)
korean: From 초롱초롱 chorong-chorong (onomatopoeia for glittering) and 순 (筍) sun (sprout)
chineseMandarin: From 晶 jīng (crystal), 光 guāng (light), and 芽 yá (bud)
chineseCantonese: From 晶 jīng (crystal), 光 gwōng (light), and 芽 ngàh (bud)

name: Glimmora
english: Glimmora may be a combination of glimmer and flora. It may also include ore.
japanese: From キラキラ kirakira (onomatopoeia for glittering), 煌めく kirameku (to glitter), killer, and flor (Spanish and Portuguese for "flower")
french: From flora (Latin for "flower") and éclat (radiance or shard)
german: From luminare (Latin for "to shine") and flora (Latin for "flower")
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 晶 jīng (crystal), 光 guāng (light), and 花 huā (flower)
chineseCantonese: From 晶 jīng (crystal), 光 gwōng (light), and 花 fā (flower)

name: Greavard
english: Greavard may be a combination of graveyard, grieve, greaves (a byproduct of a historical method of candlemaking; typically used as dog food), and Briard (a long-haired dog breed).
japanese: From 墓地 bochi (graveyard), ポチ Pochi (a common name for a pet dog), and ひとりぼっち hitoribocchi (loneliness)
korean: From 망 (亡) mang (death) and 멍멍이 meongmeong-i (childish term for dog)
chineseMandarin: From 墓仔埔 bōng-á-poo (Hokkien for graveyard) and 狗仔 gǒuzǎi (puppy)
chineseCantonese: From 墓仔埔 bōng-á-poo (Hokkien for graveyard) and 狗仔 gáujái (puppy)

name: Houndstone
english: Houndstone may be a combination of hound and headstone.
japanese: From 墓 haka (tomb) and dog
korean: From 묘 (墓) myo (tomb) and 바둑이 badugi (spotted dog)
chineseMandarin: From 墓 mù (tomb), 揚 / 扬 yáng (to raise), and 牧羊犬 mùyángquǎn (sheepdog)
chineseCantonese: From 墓 mouh (tomb), 揚 yèuhng (to raise), and 牧羊犬 muhkyèuhnghyún (sheepdog)

name: Flamigo
english: Flamigo may be a combination of flamingo and amigo (Spanish and Portuguese for "friend").
japanese: From 絡む karamu (to entangle; to intertwine) and flamingo
french: From flamant rose (flamingo) and enrouler (to coil)
korean: From 꼬다 kkoda (twist; writhe) and flamingo
chineseMandarin: From 纏繞 / 缠绕 chánrào (to entwine) and 紅鸛 / 红鹳 hónghè (flamingo)
chineseCantonese: From 纏繞 chìhnyíu (to entwine) and 紅鸛 hùhnghohk (flamingo)

name: Cetoddle
english: Cetoddle may be a combination of cetacean or Cetus (a sea monster in Greek mythology whose name became the etymology for the word cetacean) and toddle (to walk unsteadily) or toddler.
japanese: From 歩く aruku (to walk) and 鯨 kujira (whale)
korean: From 터벅거리다 teobeokgeorida (to totter) and 고래 gorae (whale)
chineseMandarin: From 走 zǒu (to walk) and 鯨 / 鲸 jīng (whale)
chineseCantonese: From 走 jáu (to run) and 鯨 kìhng (whale)

name: Cetitan
english: Cetitan may be a combination of cetacean or Cetus (a sea monster in Greek mythology whose name became the etymology for the word cetacean) and titan.
japanese: From hulk, 歩く aruku (to walk), 鯨 kujira (whale), and 歯鯨 hakujira (toothed whale)
korean: From 우락부락하다 urakburakhada (to look threatening) and 고래 gorae (whale)
chineseMandarin: From 浩大 hàodà (vast) and 鯨 / 鲸 jīng (whale)
chineseCantonese: From 浩大 houhdaaih (vast) and 鯨 kìhng (whale)

name: Veluza
english: Veluza may be a combination of veloz (Spanish and Portuguese for "fast") and merluza (Spanish and Portuguese for "hake").
japanese: From 身軽 migaru (nimble) and merluza (Spanish for "hake")
french: From délester (to unburden) and possibly colin (generic term for various species of fish that includes the hake fish) or festin (feast)
german: From agil (agile) and merluza (Spanish and Portuguese for "hake")
korean: From 가볍다 gabyeopda (to be light) and merluza (Spanish for "hake")
chineseMandarin: From 輕身 / 轻身 qīngshēn (lightweight) and 無鬚鱈 / 无须鳕 wúxūxuě (hake)
chineseCantonese: From 輕身 hēngsān (lightweight) and 無鬚鱈 mòuhsōusyut (hake)

name: Dondozo
english: Dondozo may be a combination of don (Spanish for "lord") and どうぞ dōzo (Japanese for "please (help yourself)"; typically said when offering something). Don also refers to a crime boss, which may allude to Dondozo's relationship with Tatsugiri, who acts as its consigliere. It may also derive from bozo, in reference to Dondozo's dimwitted nature.
japanese: From へいらっしゃい heirasshai ("Hey, come on in"), the agentive suffix ～者 -sha or -er, and possibly Rusher Itamae
french: From 親方 oyakata (Japanese for "master") and poisson-chat (catfish)
german: From Herr (Sir) or Heer (army) and へいらっしゃい heirasshai (Japanese for "Hey, come on in")
korean: From 어서 오세요 eoseo oseyo ("Come on in") and a transcription of rusher from its Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 吃 chī (to eat), 吼 hǒu (to roar), 霸 bà (overlord), and possibly a pun of 食予飽 tsia̍h-hōo-pá (Hokkien for "eat one's fill")
chineseCantonese: From 吃 hek (to eat), 吼 háu (to roar), 霸 ba (overlord), and possibly a pun of 食予飽 tsia̍h-hōo-pá (Hokkien for "eat one's fill")

name: Tatsugiri
english: Tatsugiri may be a combination of 竜 tatsu (Japanese for dragon) and 握り寿司 nigirizushi.
japanese: From シャリ shari (sushi rice) and 竜 tatsu (dragon)
french: From 握り寿司 nigirizushi and dragon
german: From 握り寿司 nigirizushi and dragon
korean: From the transcription of Japanese name and 용 (龍) yong (dragon)
chineseMandarin: From 米粒 mǐlì (rice grain) and 龍 / 龙 lóng (dragon)
chineseCantonese: From 米粒 máihlāp (rice grain) and 龍 lùhng (dragon)

name: Annihilape
english: Annihilape may be a combination of annihilate and ape.
japanese: From この世を去る kono yo o saru (to leave this world; to die) and 猿 saru (monkey)
korean: From 저승 갔음 jeongseung gasseum (passed on to the other world) and 원숭이 wonsung-i (monkey)
chineseMandarin: From 棄世 / 弃世 qìshì (to pass away) and 猴 hóu (monkey)
chineseCantonese: From 棄世 heisai (to pass away) and 猴 hàuh (monkey)

name: Clodsire
english: Clodsire may be a combination of clod (lump of earth), sire or Siren (a genus of salamander), and Quagsire.
japanese: From 土 do (earth, ground), 毒 doku (poison), 王 ō (king), 大山椒魚 ōsanshōuo (Japanese giant salamander), and ヌオー Nuoh (Quagsire)
german: From suelo (Spanish for "ground, soil"), Lord, and Morlord (Quagsire)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 土 tǔ (earth), 王 wáng (king), and 沼王 Zhǎowáng (Quagsire)
chineseCantonese: From 土 tóu (earth), 王 wòhng (king), and 沼王 Jíuwòhng (Quagsire)

name: Farigiraf
english: Farigiraf is an inversion of Girafarig. This may reflect Farigiraf's physical inversion, with its tail moving to its head.
japanese: From 力 riki (power), 麒麟 kirin (giraffe), and an anagram of キリンリキ Kirinriki (Girafarig)
korean: From an anagram of 키링키 Kilingki (Girafarig)
chineseMandarin: From an anagram of 麒麟奇 Qílínqí (Girafarig)
chineseCantonese: From an anagram of 麒麟奇 Kèihlèuhnkèih (Girafarig)

name: Dudunsparce
english: Dudunsparce may be derived from a partial repetition of Dunsparce and redundant, in reference to the former's multi-segmented appearance as well as having an appearance nearly identical to its pre-Evolution. It may also be a combination of double or dud (possibly referencing its pre-Evolution's almost-useless wings and tendency to remain motionless and inactive, or Dudunsparce's aforementioned relative lack of visual changes from its pre-Evolution) and Dunsparce.
japanese: From a partial repetition of ノコッチ Nokocchi (Dunsparce)
german: From a partial repetition of Dummisel (Dunsparce)
korean: From a partial repetition of 노고치 Nogochi (Dunsparce)
chineseMandarin: From 土龍 / 土龙 tǔlóng (tsuchinoko), 土龍弟弟 / 土龙弟弟 Tǔlóngdìdì (Dunsparce), 節 / 节 jiē (segment), and possibly a pun of 姐姐 jiějie (older sister)
chineseCantonese: From 土龍 tóulùhng (tsuchinoko), 土龍弟弟 Tóulùhngdàihdái (Dunsparce), and 節 jit (segment)

name: Kingambit
english: Kingambit may be a combination of king and gambit; both words are applicable terms used in chess, including in the opening known as the King's Gambit. It may also be derived from karambit.
japanese: From ど do (very much), 土下座 dogeza (kneeling down on the ground), and 斬 zan (to slash)
french: From scalper (to scalp) or scalpel and empereur (emperor)
korean: From 대 (太) dae (great), 대도 (太刀) daedo (long sword), 각 (刻) gak (carve), and 참 (斬) cham (behead)
chineseMandarin: From 仆 pū (to lie prostrate), 斬 zhǎn (to slash), and 將軍 jiāngjūn (general; shogun); From 仆 pū (to lie prostrate), 刀 dāo (blade, sword), and 将军 jiāngjūn (general; shogun)
chineseCantonese: From 仆 pūk (to lie prostrate), 斬 jáam (to slash), and 將軍 jēunggwān (general; shogun)

name: Great Tusk
english: Great Tusk is literally great tusk.
japanese: From 偉大な牙 idai-na kiba (great tusk)
german: From the prefix riesen- (gigantic) and Stoßzahn (tusk)
korean: From 위대한엄니 widae-han eomni (great tusk)
chineseMandarin: From 雄偉 / 雄伟 xióngwěi (majestic) and 牙 yá (tusk)
chineseCantonese: From 雄偉 hùhngwáih (majestic) and 牙 ngàh (tusk)

name: Scream Tail
english: Scream Tail is literally scream tail.
japanese: From 叫ぶ尻尾 sakebu shippo (screaming tail)
korean: From 우렁찬꼬리 ureongchan kkori (roaring tail)
chineseMandarin: From 吼叫 hǒujiào (to roar) and 尾 wěi (tail)
chineseCantonese: From 吼叫 haugiu (to roar) and 尾 méih (tail)

name: Brute Bonnet
english: Brute Bonnet is literally brute bonnet. The word bonnet may refer to both a type of hat and the common bonnet, a species of mushroom.
japanese: From 荒ぶる茸 araburu take (savage mushroom)
korean: From 사나운버섯 sanaun beoseot (savage mushroom)
chineseMandarin: From 猛惡 / 猛恶 měng'è (savage) and 菇 gū (mushroom)
chineseCantonese: From 猛惡 máahng'ok (savage) and 菇 gū (mushroom)

name: Flutter Mane
english: Flutter Mane is literally flutter mane.
japanese: From 羽ばたく髪 habataku kami (fluttering hair)
french: From flotter (to flutter) and mèche (strand of hair)
korean: From 날개치는머리 nalgaechineun meori (fluttering hair)
chineseMandarin: From 振 zhèn (to flap), 翼 yì (wings), and 髮 / 发 fǎ / fà (hair)
chineseCantonese: From 振 jan (to flap), 翼 yihk (wings), and 髮 faat (hair)

name: Slither Wing
english: Slither Wing is literally slither wing.
japanese: From 地を這う羽 chi o hau hane (wings slithering on the ground)
korean: From 땅을기는날개 ttang-eulgineun nalgae (crawling wings)
chineseMandarin: From 爬 pá (to crawl), 地 dì (ground), and 翅 chì (wings)
chineseCantonese: From 爬 pàh (to crawl), 地 deih (ground), and 翅 chi (wings)

name: Sandy Shocks
english: Sandy Shocks is literally sandy shocks. The word shock may refer to both a burst of electrical energy and a tuft of hair or fur.
japanese: From 砂の毛皮 suna no kegawa (sandy fur)
korean: From 모래털가죽 morae teolgajuk (sandy fur)
chineseMandarin: From 沙 shā (sand), 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron), and 皮 pí (skin)
chineseCantonese: From 沙 sā (sand), 鐵 tit (iron), and 皮 pèih (skin)

name: Iron Treads
english: Iron Treads is literally iron treads.
japanese: From 鉄の轍 tetsu no wadachi (iron treads)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 바퀴 bakwi (wheel)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 轍跡 / 辙迹 chèjī / zhéjì (tread marks)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 轍跡 chitjīk (tread marks)

name: Iron Bundle
english: Iron Bundle is literally iron bundle.
japanese: From 鉄の包み tetsu no tsutsumi (iron bundle)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 보따리 bottari (bundle)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 包袱 bāofu (bundle wrapped in cloth)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 包袱 bāaufuhk (bundle wrapped in cloth)

name: Iron Hands
english: Iron Hands is literally iron hands.
japanese: From 鉄の腕 tetsu no kaina (iron arms)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 손 son (hand)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 臂膀 bìbǎng (arm)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 臂膀 beibóng (arm)

name: Iron Jugulis
english: Iron Jugulis is literally iron jugulis (with jugulis being derived from the Latin word jugulum, meaning throat or neck).
japanese: From 鉄の首 tetsu no kōbe (iron head)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 머리 meori (head)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 脖頸 / 脖颈 bógěng (nape)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 脖頸 buhtgéng (nape)

name: Iron Moth
english: Iron Moth is literally iron moth.
japanese: From 鉄の毒蛾 tetsu no dokuga (iron venomous moth)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 독나방 dongnabang (venomous moth)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 毒蛾 dú'é (venomous moth)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 毒蛾 duhkngòh (venomous moth)

name: Iron Thorns
english: Iron Thorns is literally iron thorns.
japanese: From 鉄の棘 tetsu no ibara (iron thorns)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 가시 gasi (thorn)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 荊棘 / 荆棘 jīngjí (brambles)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 荊棘 gīnggīk (brambles)

name: Frigibax
english: Frigibax may be a combination of frigid, back, and axe.
japanese: From 背びれ sebire (dorsal fin) and 冷え hie (coldness)
french: From frigorifique (frigorific), dos (back), and dragon de Komodo (Komodo dragon)
korean: From 등 deung (back) and 차다 chada (cold)
chineseMandarin: From 涼 / 凉 liáng (cool), 脊 jǐ (spine), and 棘龍 / 棘龙 jílóng (Spinosaurus)
chineseCantonese: From 涼 lèuhng (cool), 脊 jek (spine), and 棘龍 gīklùhng (Spinosaurus)

name: Arctibax
english: Arctibax may be a combination of arctic, back, and axe.
japanese: From 背 se (back) and 凍る kōru (freeze)
french: From cryo- (Greek prefix for cold), dos (back), and dragon de Komodo (Komodo dragon)
korean: From 등 deung (back) and 꽁꽁 얼다 kkong-kkong eolda (freeze solid)
chineseMandarin: From 凍 / 冻 dòng (to freeze; frozen), 脊 jǐ (spine), and 棘龍 / 棘龙 jílóng (Spinosaurus)
chineseCantonese: From 凍 dung (to freeze; frozen), 脊 jek (spine), and 棘龍 gīklùhng (Spinosaurus)

name: Baxcalibur
english: Baxcalibur may be a combination of back and Excalibur (mythical sword belonging to King Arthur).
japanese: From 背 se (back) and glaive
french: From glaive, dos (back), dragon de Komodo (Komodo dragon), and Quasimodo
german: From espina (Spanish for "spine"), Spinosaurus, and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for "tooth")
korean: From 등 deung (back) and glaive
chineseMandarin: From 戟 jǐ (halberd), 脊 jǐ (spine), and 棘龍 / 棘龙 jílóng (Spinosaurus)
chineseCantonese: From 戟 gīk (halberd), 脊 jek (spine), and 棘龍 gīklùhng (Spinosaurus)

name: Gimmighoul
english: Gimmighoul may be a combination of gimme (informal pronunciation of "give me"), gimmick, mimic, and ghoul. Altogether, it sounds like the phrase "Give me gold."
japanese: From collect, 霊 rei (spirit), and これくれ kore kure (Give me this)
korean: From 모으다 moeuda (to collect) and 령 (靈) ryeong (spirit)
chineseMandarin: From 索 suǒ (to search), 財 / 财 cái (wealth), and 靈 / 灵 líng (spirit)
chineseCantonese: From 索 sok (to search), 財 chòih (wealth), and 靈 lìhng (spirit)

name: Gholdengo
english: Gholdengo may be a combination of ghoul or ghost, golden, and possibly go (as in GO, the game its pre-Evolution Gimmighoul first debuted in; Gholdengo's model itself was in the game's files before it was officially revealed). It may also come from tengo (Spanish for "I have") or деньги den'gi (Russian for money, itself from denga, a historical unit worth 1/200th of a Russian ruble).
japanese: From surf, 富豪 fugō (wealthy person), gold, and GO
french: From gros (big), magot (loot), and Pokémon GO
german: From Moneten (slang for "money"), amigo (Spanish and Portuguese for "friend"), and Pokémon GO
korean: From 타보자고 Tabojago (Let's ride; Let's surf), 부자 (富者) buja (wealthy person), and Pokémon GO
chineseMandarin: From 賽 / 赛 sài (to compete), 曬富 / 晒富 shàifù (to show off wealth), and 富豪 fùháo (wealthy person)
chineseCantonese: From 賽 choi (to compete) and 富豪 fuhòuh (wealthy person)

name: Wo-Chien
english: Wo-Chien may be a combination of 蝸 / 蜗 wō (Chinese for snail) and 簡 / 简 jiǎn (Chinese for bamboo slips). The name is formatted in Wade–Giles, a romanization system used in the Anglosphere for most of the 20th century.
japanese: From 蟲 / 虫 chóng (Chinese for bug) and 簡 / 简 jiǎn (Chinese for bamboo slips)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 古 gǔ (ancient), 簡 / 简 jiǎn (bamboo slips), and 蝸牛 / 蜗牛 guāniú / wōniú (snail)
chineseCantonese: From 古 gú (ancient), 簡 gáan (bamboo slips), and 蝸牛 wō'ngàuh (snail)

name: Chien-Pao
english: Chien-Pao and Paojian may be a combination of 劍 / 剑 jiàn (Chinese for sword) or 寶劍 / 宝剑 bǎojiàn (Chinese for treasure sword) and 豹 bào (Chinese for leopard). The English name is formatted in Wade–Giles, a romanization system used in the Anglosphere for most of the 20th century.
japanese: From 豹 bào (Chinese for leopard) and 劍 / 剑 jiàn (Chinese for sword)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 古 gǔ (ancient), 劍 / 剑 jiàn (sword), and 豹 bào (leopard, panther)
chineseCantonese: From 古 gú (ancient), 劍 gim (sword), and 豹 paau (leopard, panther)

name: Ting-Lu
english: Ting-Lu and Dinlu may be a combination of 鼎 dǐng (ancient Chinese cauldron) and 鹿 lù (Chinese for deer). The English name is formatted in Wade–Giles, a romanization system used in the Anglosphere for most of the 20th century.
japanese: From 鼎 dǐng and 鹿 lù (Chinese for deer)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 古 gǔ (ancient), 鼎 dǐng, and 鹿 lù (deer)
chineseCantonese: From 古 gú (ancient), 鼎 díng, and 鹿 lúk (deer)

name: Chi-Yu
english: Chi-Yu may be a combination of 鯽魚 / 鲫鱼 jìyú (Chinese for crucian carp, from which goldfish are domesticated) and 玉 yù (Chinese for jade). The name is formatted in Wade–Giles, a romanization system used in the Anglosphere for most of the 20th century.
japanese: From 玉 yù (Chinese for jade) and 魚 yú (Chinese for fish)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 古 gǔ (ancient), 玉 yù (jade), and 魚 / 鱼 yú (fish)
chineseCantonese: From 古 gú (ancient), 玉 yuhk (jade), and 魚 yùh (fish)

name: Roaring Moon
english: Roaring Moon is literally roaring moon.
japanese: From 轟く月 todoroku tsuki (roaring moon)
korean: From 고동치는달 godongchineun dal (pulsating moon)
chineseMandarin: From 轟鳴 / 轰鸣 hōngmíng (to roar) and 月 yuè (moon)
chineseCantonese: From 轟鳴 gwāngmìhng (to roar) and 月 yuht (moon)

name: Iron Valiant
english: Iron Valiant is literally iron valiant.
japanese: From 鉄の武人 tetsu no bujin (iron warrior)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 무인 (武人) muin (warrior)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 武者 wǔzhě (warrior)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 武者 móuhjé (warrior)

name: Koraidon
english: Koraidon may be a combination of 古来 korai (from time immemorial) or 古代 kodai (ancient times), ライド raido (ride), and dragon, don (Spanish for "lord"), or -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for tooth).
japanese: From 古来 korai (from time immemorial) or 古代 kodai (ancient times), ride, dragon, don (Spanish for "lord"), and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 故 gù (old) and the transcription of the Japanese name
chineseCantonese: From 故 gu (old) and the transcription of the Japanese name

name: Miraidon
english: Miraidon may be a combination of 未来 mirai (future), ライド raido (ride), and dragon, don (Spanish for "lord"), or -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals derived from the Ancient Greek word for tooth).
japanese: From 未来 mirai (future), ride, dragon, don (Spanish for "lord"), and -don (common suffix in taxonomic names of prehistoric animals)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseCantonese: Mandarin-based transcription of Japanese name

name: Walking Wake
english: Walking Wake is literally walking wake. A wake is a movement of water created by a moving object.
japanese: From うねる水面 uneru minamo (undulating water's surface)
french: From serpenter (to snake, to wind) and eau (water)
italian: From acqua (water) and crespo (curly, creased) or increspato (rippled)
korean: From 굽이치는 물결 gubichineun mulgyeol (undulating wave)
chineseMandarin: From 波 bō (wave), 盪 / 荡 dàng (to undulate), and 水 shuǐ (water)
chineseCantonese: From 波 bō (wave), 盪 dohng (to undulate), and 水 séui (water)

name: Iron Leaves
english: Iron Leaves is literally iron leaves.
japanese: From 鉄の斑葉 tetsu no isaha (iron mottled leaves)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 잎새 ipsae (leaf)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 斑葉 / 斑叶 bānyè (mottled leaf)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 斑葉 bāanyihp (mottled leaf)

name: Dipplin
english: Dipplin may be a combination of di- (prefix meaning double), dip, and Applin.
japanese: From 果 ka (fruit), 花蜜 kamitsu (nectar), 虫 chū (bug; worm), and カジッチュ Kajicchu (Applin)
french: From pomme d'amour (candy apple) and dragon
korean: From 과 (果) gwa (fruit) or 사과 (沙果) sagwa (apple), 화밀 (花蜜) hwamil (nectar), and 미르 mireu (dragon)
chineseMandarin: From 蘋裹龍 / 苹裹龙 Píngguǒlóng (Flapple), 果蜜 guǒmì (fruit nectar), and 蟲 / 虫 chóng (bug)
chineseCantonese: From 蘋裹龍 Pìhnggwólùhng (Flapple), 果蜜 gwómaht (fruit nectar), and 蟲 chùhng (bug)

name: Poltchageist
english: Poltchageist may be a combination of poltergeist and 抹茶 matcha, following the same naming pattern as Polteageist.
japanese: From 抹茶 matcha, death, and a pun of 茶です cha desu ("It's tea")
german: From mors (Latin for "death") or mort (French for "death") and Matcha
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 斯 sī (this), 魔 mó (demon), 茶 chá (tea), and a pun of 是抹茶 shì mǒchá ("It's matcha")
chineseCantonese: From 斯 sī (this), 魔 mō (demon), 茶 chàh (tea), and a pun of 是抹茶 sih mutchàh ("It's matcha")

name: Sinistcha
english: Sinistcha may be a combination of sinister and 抹茶 matcha, following the same naming pattern as Sinistea.
japanese: From やばい yabai (dangerous; terrible), ヤバチャ Yabacha (Sinistea), and 粗茶 socha (low grade tea, coarse tea)
french: From thé (tea), froid (cold), Théffroi (Sinistea), and effroyable (terrifying)
german: From fatal or fatalité (French for "fatality"), Fatalitee (Sinistea), and 抹茶 matcha
korean: From green, 우린 urin (brewed) and 차 (茶) cha (tea)
chineseMandarin: From 來悲茶 / 来悲茶 Láibēichá (Sinistea) and 粗茶 cūchá (low grade tea)
chineseCantonese: From 來悲茶 Lòihbēichàh (Sinistea) and 粗茶 chōuchàh (low grade tea)

name: Okidogi
english: Okidogi may be a combination of okie-dokie (variant of "okay") and dog. "Dogi" may also be a reference to training uniforms used for martial arts, hence the Fighting typing.
japanese: From いいね ii ne (interjection to express approval) and 犬 inu (dog)
french: From félicité (felicity, happiness) and canis (Latin for "dog")
german: From bon (French for "good") and 犬 inu (Japanese for dog)
korean: From 좋다고 jotago (interjection to express approval) and 구 (狗) gu (dog)
chineseMandarin: From 夠 / 够 gòu (good enough), 讚 / 赞 zàn (to like) and 狗 gǒu (dog)
chineseCantonese: From 夠 gau (good enough), 讚 jaan (to like) and 狗 gáu (dog)

name: Munkidori
english: Munkidori may be a combination of monkey and hunky dory (slang meaning that things are good).
japanese: From 増し mashi (better, improving) and 猿 mashira (archaic word for monkey or ape)
french: From fortune and simia (Latin for "monkey or ape")
german: From bene (Italian for "good") and 猿 saru (Japanese for monkey or ape)
korean: From 이야호 iyaho (Hooray) and 후 (猴) hu (monkey)
chineseMandarin: From 願 / 愿 yuàn (to desire), 增 zēng (to increase), and 猿 yuán (ape)
chineseCantonese: From 願 yuhn (to desire), 增 jāng (to increase), and 猿 yùhn (ape)

name: Fezandipiti
english: Fezandipiti may be a combination of pheasant and serendipity (an unexpected but auspicious happening).
japanese: From 吉 kichi (fortune) and 雉子 kigisu (pheasant)
french: From faveur (favor), avian, and φασιανός fasianós (Greek for "pheasant")
german: From beatus (Latin for "prosperous") and 鳥 tori (Japanese for bird)
korean: From 길하다 gilhada (auspicious), 그렇지 geureohji (interjection to express approval), and 치 (雉) chi (pheasant)
chineseMandarin: From 吉 jí (fortune) and 雉雞 / 雉鸡 zhìjī (pheasant)
chineseCantonese: From 吉 gāt (fortune) and 雉雞 jihgāi (pheasant)

name: Ogerpon
english: Ogerpon may be derived from ogre and ponkan or dekopon (varieties of orange), as well as ～ぽん -pon, a cutesy suffix applied to names as a form of endearment.
japanese: From ogre and ponkan or ～ぽん -pon (cutesy suffix for names)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From the transcription of the Japanese name, 鬼 guǐ (demon; oni), and 椪柑 pènggān (ponkan)
chineseCantonese: From the transcription of the Japanese name, 鬼 gwái (demon; oni), and 椪柑 punggām (ponkan)

name: Archaludon
english: Archaludon may be a combination of arch (meaning principal or superlative, as well as referring to a type of bridge), Duraludon, and possibly Archosaur.
japanese: From bridge, ジュラルドン Duraludon, and ソーラス -saurus (Greek-derived suffix for dinosaur names)
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: From 鋁鋼龍 / 铝钢龙 Lǚgānglóng (Duraludon) and 橋 / 桥 qiáo (bridge)
chineseCantonese: From 鋁鋼龍 Léuihgonglùhng (Duraludon) and 橋 kìuh (bridge)

name: Hydrapple
english: Hydrapple may be a combination of Hydra, dragon, and apple. The term "syrpent" may be a combination of syrup or wyrm and serpent.
japanese: From 果 ka (fruit), 花蜜 kamitsu (nectar), and 大蛇 orochi (large snake)
french: From Pomdramour (Dipplin), pomme d'or (golden apple), and 大蛇 orochi (large snake)
korean: From 과 (果) gwa (fruit) or 사과 (沙果) sagwa (apple), 화밀 (花蜜) hwamil (nectar), and Hydra
chineseMandarin: From 蜜 mì (honey; sweet), 密集 mìjí (concentrated; crowded together), and 大蛇 dàshé (large snake)
chineseCantonese: From 蜜 maht (honey; sweet), 密集 mahtjaahp (concentrated; crowded together), and 大蛇 daaihsèh (large snake)

name: Gouging Fire
english: Gouging Fire is literally gouging fire.
japanese: From 穿つ炎 ugatsu homura (piercing flame)
korean: From 꿰뚫는 화염 kkwettulleun hwayeom (piercing flame)
chineseMandarin: From 破空 pòkōng (to break through the sky) and 焰 yàn (flame)
chineseCantonese: From 破空 pohūng (to break through the sky) and 焰 yihm (flame)

name: Raging Bolt
english: Raging Bolt is literally raging bolt.
japanese: From 猛る雷鼓 takeru raiko (furious thunderclap) and ライコウ Raikou
korean: From 날뛰는 우레 nalttwineun ure (rampaging thunder)
chineseMandarin: From 猛 měng (fierce) and 雷鼓 léigǔ (thunderclap; thunder drum)
chineseCantonese: From 猛 máahng (fierce) and 雷鼓 lèuihgú (thunderclap; thunder drum)

name: Iron Boulder
english: Iron Boulder is literally iron boulder.
japanese: From 鉄の巌 tetsu no iwao (iron boulder)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 암석 (岩石) amseok (rock)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron), 磐 pán (boulder), and 岩石 yánshí (boulder)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron), 磐 pùhn (boulder), and 岩石 ngàahmsehk (boulder)

name: Iron Crown
english: Iron Crown is literally iron crown. Crown may refer to the head adornment, the top of a person's head, or a reigning monarch or leader.
japanese: From 鉄の頭 tetsu no kashira (iron head; iron leader)
german: From Eisen (iron) and Haupt (poetic word for head; leader)
korean: From 무쇠 musoe (cast iron) and 감투 gamtu (horsehair cap worn by officials)
chineseMandarin: From 鐵 / 铁 tiě (iron) and 頭殼 / 头壳 tóuké (dialectal word for head)
chineseCantonese: From 鐵 tit (iron) and 頭殼 tàuhhok (dialectal word for head)

name: Terapagos
english: Terapagos may be a combination of stal, terrapin, and galápagos (a Spanish word for turtles, most recognizable because of the Galápagos Islands).
japanese: From stal, terrapin, and galápagos (old Spanish word for turtles) or Galápagos Islands
korean: Transcription of Japanese name
chineseMandarin: Transcription of the Japanese name and 太晶化 Tàijīnghuà (Terastal phenomenon)
chineseCantonese: Transcription of the Japanese name and 太晶化 Taaijīngfa (Terastal phenomenon)

name: Pecharunt
english: Pecharunt may be a combination of peach or Pecha Berry and runt or petulant.
japanese: From 桃太郎 Momotarō, 桃 momo (peach), 悪し waroshi ("bad" or "inferior" in classical Japanese), and 和郎 warō (boy)
french: From pêche (peach) or Baie Pêcha (Pecha Berry) and minus (shortie, runt)
german: From infam (malicious; infamous), īnfāns (Latin for "infant") and 桃 momo (Japanese for "peach")
korean: From 복숭아 boksung-a (peach) and 악동 (惡童) akdong (brat)
chineseMandarin: From 桃太郎 Táotàiláng (Momotarō), 桃 táo (peach), and 歹 dǎi (wicked)
chineseCantonese: From 桃太郎 Tòuhtaailòhng (Momotarō), 桃 tòuh (peach), and 歹 dáai (wicked)
